Watch your thermometer — when water temps push above 70 degrees, fish stress quickly, and moving to shaded reaches or calling it early protects these wild fish for the next angler.

Casco Bay runs a reliable seasonal parade of species. Striped bass show first in spring as water temperatures climb through the mid-50s, moving into the harbor flats and creek mouths on the hunt for baitfish and worms. Mackerel pour in by early summer, drawing bluefish close behind — both species push schools of sand eels and herring against the islands and ledges scattered across the bay. By fall, stripers stack up heavy and aggressive before migrating south, and cod can be found holding in deeper rocky structure throughout the colder months when surface action slows.

Work the tide transitions hard — the two hours before and after a moving tide push baitfish through channel edges and around the bay's many rocky points, which is exactly where stripers and blues ambush. On the drop, look for rips forming off island points. Soft plastic paddle tails and epoxy jigs in white or chartreuse cover water efficiently, while fresh mackerel chunks or live eels will always out-fish hardware when blues are finicky. When wind chop puts a little texture on the water, fish tighter to structure. Clear, slack-water days call for finesse — lighter leaders and smaller profiles make a real difference.

Boothbay Harbor sits at the mouth of the Sheepscot River, and that estuary system drives everything. Striped bass arrive first in spring, following baitfish into the river channels and cove edges. By early summer, bluefish push in behind them and the action turns aggressive around the outer ledges. Fluke settle into sandy bottom areas off the islands once water temperatures climb into the low 60s, while black sea bass stack on the rockpiles deeper offshore. Tautog are here year-round on structure, best in shoulder seasons. Weakfish and kingfish show up opportunistically in warmer months, typically in calmer back-bay shallows.

Work the tide transitions hard — Boothbay's tidal range is significant, and stripers and blues ambush bait where current pinches around points and island corners. On the ebb, fish the mouths of the coves where smaller fish get pushed out. Soft plastic eels and paddle tails on jigheads produce well for stripers along rocky structure. Fluke want a bucktail with a Gulp trailer dragged slowly over sandy patches. For tog, use green crab tight to submerged rockpiles with minimal drift. Northwest wind after a blow generally clears the water fastest here, and once surface temps drop back into the 50s in fall, the striper bite often peaks before the fish push south.

The Piscataqua River mouth and surrounding coast offer a varied season that keeps serious anglers busy from ice-out through late fall. Striped bass arrive first in spring, staging along current seams as water temperatures climb through the mid-40s, with fish lingering well into fall. Bluefish push in during summer and can be aggressive through the river mouth on strong outgoing tides. Fluke settle onto sandy bottom patches in warmer months, while black sea bass hold around rockier structure. Tautog favor the same hard bottom and peak in shoulder seasons. Weakfish and kingfish show up as bonus catches during warmer summer periods, often near softer bottom in calmer reaches.

The Piscataqua runs fast, so tide timing is everything here — the two hours before and after peak outgoing tide concentrate baitfish and predators at the river mouth, channel edges, and rip lines where current breaks. Stripers respond well to large soft plastics, bucktails, and live mackerel worked through current seams. For fluke, drift sandy edges with bucktail-and-trailer combos or live-lined small baitfish. Tautog and black sea bass want green crabs or fiddlers worked tight to structure with minimal lead. When water temperatures exceed 68 degrees, bluefish activity surges and metal lures or chunked bunker draw strikes fast. Watch northwest wind — it clears water and sharpens fishing noticeably.

Frenchman Bay runs cold and deep, and that shapes everything. Striped bass move in as water temperatures climb into the low 50s, often the first serious action of the season, and they stick around well into fall. Bluefish show up mid-summer in blitzing schools, especially near the surface when bait is pushed up. Fluke and black sea bass work the rockier bottom structure, though both are near the northern edge of their comfortable range here, so numbers can be inconsistent. Tautog hold tight to ledges and mussel beds. Weakfish and kingfish are opportunistic visitors rather than reliable targets in these waters.

Work the rocky points, kelp edges, and drop-offs on the moving tide rather than slack water — stripers and blues feed aggressively on the flood and ebb when bait gets flushed through. For stripers, swimming plugs, soft plastics on jig heads, and live mackerel or herring are hard to beat. Fluke and black sea bass respond well to squid strips and gulp-style baits bounced along the bottom. Northwest winds tend to push bait toward the bay's protected western shore. Once surface temps drop below 55 degrees, fish push deeper or begin migrating out — that's your signal to follow them down or call the season.

The Piscataqua River corridor and the Isles of Shoals offer remarkably varied fishing through the seasons. Striped bass arrive first in spring, moving up with baitfish into the river current and along the rocky island edges. By midsummer, bluefish show in force around the Shoals alongside keeper-sized fluke burying into sandy bottom structure off the river mouth. Black sea bass and tautog work the rockpile and ledge habitat around the islands all summer, with tautog holding well into fall. Weakfish and kingfish are less consistent but appear during warmer-water years, typically mid to late summer in calmer inshore areas.

On the Piscataqua, fish the rip edges and eddies formed by bridge structure and channel bends, especially during moving tides when baitfish concentrate. Stripers and blues respond well to swim shads, bucktails, and live mackerel drifted through current seams. At the Shoals, anchor or drift the rocky ledges for tautog using green crab or Asian crab tight to structure, and drop diamond jigs or squid strips for black sea bass. Fluke want a slow drift with bucktail tipped with squid and a strip bait over sandy transition zones. Water temperature above 55 degrees generally signals consistent striper action, and southwest winds tend to push bait onto the productive western faces of the islands.

The Merrimack River mouth and Plum Island Sound offer some of New England's most varied inshore fishing. Striped bass are the anchor species, moving through from spring into fall with the largest fish often appearing during the late-spring herring runs that flood the river. Bluefish arrive in summer and can turn the mouth into a frenzy. Fluke settle onto the sandy flats off Plum Island through the warmer months, while black sea bass hold on nearshore rocky structure. Tautog favor the jetties and rip-rap early and late in the season when water cools. Weakfish appear occasionally during warm-water years, and kingfish show up in the surf and shallow sandy edges mid-summer.

Tides do most of the work here. Fish the outgoing tide hard at the river mouth, where baitfish funnel through the channel edges and stripers and blues stack up to ambush them. Soft plastics on jig heads, bucktails, and live eels work well for bass in the current seams. For fluke, drift the sandy shallows parallel to the island with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp strip. Tautog respond to green crab on the jetty rocks on a slow retrieve. Water temperature is the key trigger — once surface temps push into the mid-50s, fish start showing, and the bite intensifies as it climbs toward the low 60s.

Cape Cod Bay is a seasonal fishery that really comes alive in spring when striped bass push in from the south following baitfish up the bay's relatively shallow western shoreline near Plymouth. Bluefish arrive close behind and can show in feeding frenzies over sandy flats through summer. Fluke settle into deeper channel edges and sand-bottom transition zones once water temps climb into the mid-60s. Black sea bass and tautog hold around the rockier structure and scattered ledges further out in the bay. Weakfish and kingfish make occasional appearances in the warmer months, particularly over clean sandy bottom, though both run unpredictably here.

Work the incoming tide along sandy edges and rocky drop-offs — baitfish stack up on the push, and stripers and blues follow tight. Soft plastics like paddle tails and bucktails on a slow retrieve cover the flats well for bass and fluke; live pogies or chunk mackerel will consistently draw aggressive strikes from larger fish. For tautog and sea bass, go to the bottom with green crabs or clams on rocky structure. Pay attention to water temperature — stripers get sluggish once surface temps push above 72 degrees and fishing quality drops fast. Easterly winds muddy the shallows near Plymouth and kill bites, while light southwest winds during a tide change are usually your best window.

Provincetown sits at the very tip of Cape Cod where Cape Cod Bay meets the open Atlantic, and that geography drives everything. Striped bass are the backbone of the fishery, arriving in late spring as water climbs through the low 50s and staying through fall. Bluefish show up close behind and run hard all summer. Fluke move into the shallower sandy areas once water hits the mid-60s, while black sea bass hold on the rocky structure and wrecks scattered offshore. Tautog favor that same rough bottom in spring and again in fall. Weakfish and kingfish appear in warmer months but run unpredictably here near the northern edge of their range.

Provincetown's rips and shoals are the key — stripers and blues stack up where tidal current hits shallow structure, so fish the top two hours and last two hours of the tide hard. For bass, swim large soft plastics or bucktails along the bottom in the rips, or chunk bunker on the incoming tide near drop-offs. Bluefish crush surface poppers in the rips when water temps are warm. Fluke want slow-drifted squid-and-Gulp combos over sandy bottom on a moving tide. Tautog take green crabs worked tight to rocks. Northeast winds push bait into the bay side; southwest winds tend to concentrate fish on the outside beaches.

Buzzards Bay runs warm earlier than most New England waters, which pushes the season ahead of spots to the north. Tautog hold on rocky structure and boulder fields through late spring before the heat backs them off. Striped bass move through on their migration and stack up around the Elizabeth Islands and deeper channel edges. As water temps climb into the low 70s, fluke scatter across sandy bottom flats and bluefish bust bait aggressively throughout the bay. Black sea bass crowd onto any hard structure they can find in summer. Weakfish and kingfish show up opportunistically, particularly over softer bottom near inlets and back edges.

Work the tide changes hard here — moving water is everything. Stripers and blues respond to fast current around the island passages, while fluke prefer slower drifts over clean sandy bottom with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or strip bait. Tautog demand patience with green crab fished tight to bottom on rocky ledges. For kingfish and weakfish, focus on softer substrate with small rigs baited with bloodworm or clam near channel drop-offs. Southwest wind pushes warmer water in and activates surface feeding. When the bay runs murky, downsize lures and slow your presentation — clear water lets you go bigger and faster.

Narragansett Bay fishes like a textbook estuary — species stack up in a predictable sequence as water warms. Tautog and black sea bass hold on rocky structure year-round, with tog fishing toughest in summer heat and best in shoulder seasons. Striped bass push into the bay in spring chasing herring and mullet, then disperse to the surf beaches and breachways through summer. Fluke settle onto sandy bottom from late spring through early fall. Bluefish show up when bait is thick and can be anywhere. Weakfish and kingfish are intermittent — kingfish run the surf beaches on incoming tides in warmer months, while weakfish are never a sure thing but do appear in quieter estuary sections.

Fish moving tides hard — stripers and blues stack on the downcurrent side of rocky points and jetty ends during outgoing water. For tog and sea bass, chunk green crab or asian crab worked tight to the rocks on lighter sinker rigs. Fluke respond best to bucktail tipped with a Gulp strip drifted with the tide across sandy transitions near channel edges. Work surf beaches for stripers with soft plastics or bucktails on incoming tides, especially when wind is pushing water onto structure. Water temps below 55 degrees favor tog; above 65 means fluke are active. Clear water calls for lighter leaders.

Fishers Island Sound is a genuinely productive piece of Connecticut water. Striped bass move through early in the season as water temperatures climb past fifty degrees, staging on rocky structure before pushing inshore to feed aggressively. Bluefish arrive close behind, often tearing up the surface in the rips by midsummer. Fluke settle into the sandy patches and channel edges through the warmer months, while black sea bass and tautog hold tight to the rocky reefs and lobster-pot territory year-round. Weakfish and kingfish make occasional appearances in warmer summers, usually in shallower, calmer areas near eelgrass edges.

Work the current seams where rip lines form over submerged ledges and rocky points — that moving water concentrates bait and puts fish in a feeding posture. On a falling tide, stripers and blues push into the rips hard; slack water is the time to slow down and bottom-fish for tautog with green crab or fluke with a bucktail tipped with a strip bait. When water temperature rises into the low seventies, fluke fishing peaks and drifting sandy bottom with the wind behind you pays off. Northeast winds push bait and fish toward protected structure, while strong southwest winds can dirty up the shallower water and push fish deeper.

Niantic Bay and the lower Niantic River offer a true four-season mixed bag. Striped bass show up in spring as water temperatures climb through the mid-40s into the 50s, pushing bait into the river mouth and along the rocky shoreline. Bluefish arrive close behind in early summer and can be thick through the bay. Fluke move in once bottom temps hit the low 60s and hold through summer on the sandy flats inside the bay. Black sea bass and tautog work the rocky structure year-round, with tog fishing peaking in fall and early spring. Weakfish and kingfish appear more sporadically but show up in the river and bay shallows during warmer months.

Work the river mouth on a dropping tide when baitfish funnel out into the bay — that transition zone consistently holds stripers and blues. Fluke respond well to bucktail and Gulp combinations drifted across the sandy bottom on a moving tide; keep your drift slow and stay in contact with the bottom. For tog and black sea bass, crab baits fished tight to the rocky ledges and jetty structure produce best. Onshore winds that push warmer surface water into the bay can trigger bluefish surface action. In summer, early morning low-light windows before boat traffic picks up are worth prioritizing for stripers near the river mouth and along the western shoreline.

Greenport sits at the heart of some of the most productive mixed-species fishing on Long Island's East End. Spring brings the first striped bass pushing through the North Fork's rocky points and tidal rips as water temps climb through the 50s, with weakfish showing up in the Peconics not long after — a species worth targeting here since this bay system holds one of their last reliable strongholds. Summer fluke dominate the shallow sand flats and channel edges of Peconic Bay, while bluefish churn the surface almost anywhere bait is present. By late summer, black sea bass stack on any hard structure you can find. Fall is prime time, with big stripers migrating through and tautog — locally called tog — settling hard onto rock piles and mussel beds as the water cools.

For fluke, drift sandy bottom with bucktails tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strip, targeting the transitions between the channel edges and the flats — the Peconic system has plenty of these ambush zones. Tautog and black sea bass want crabs and jigs fished tight to rock structure; don't waste time drifting open sand for them. Stripers respond well to swimming plugs and soft plastics worked through the rips and current seams that form off the North Fork's points on a strong moving tide. Wind matters here — an easterly wind pushes bait into sheltered western pockets, concentrating feeding fish. Water temps dropping through the low 60s in fall signal the best striper action, while the low 50s push fluke and sea bass offshore.

Sheepshead Bay sits at the gateway to Jamaica Bay and the Atlantic, giving you access to a remarkable range of species as the seasons rotate. Spring pushes striped bass through the bay's channels and bridge pilings, often with bluefish hot on their heels by late spring into summer. Fluke arrive when water temperatures climb into the low 60s and concentrate along the sandy flats and channel edges inside Jamaica Bay and just outside the inlets. Black sea bass show on the nearshore wrecks and hard structure offshore. Tautog anchor to the same rocky structure in fall and early spring when most other species have moved on. Weakfish and kingfish appear as warm-season bonuses in the bay's calmer back areas.

Work the falling tide at the inlet mouths where baitfish funnel through — stripers and blues stack up to ambush there, and bucktails or swimming plugs in the four to six inch range are hard to beat. For fluke inside the bay, drift the channel edges with a Gulp on a simple high-low rig and keep your drift slower than you think you need to by adjusting weight to current. Northeast wind generally muddies Jamaica Bay and kills the bite fast, so prioritize calm or southwest conditions. Once surface temps push into the low 70s, fluke bite best on the ocean side while the bay holds weakfish and kingfish on small hooks baited with bloodworms or sand eels near grassy shallows.

Freeport sits at the heart of some of Long Island's most productive inshore water. Spring kicks off with striped bass moving through the back bays and along the oceanfront as water temperatures climb through the 50s, followed by the first bluefish showing up slashing baitfish near the inlets. By summer, fluke dominate the bay bottom while black sea bass stack up on nearshore wrecks and hard structure just offshore. Weakfish and kingfish slip into the shallower grass flats and channel edges in warmer months, though weakfish have been sparse in recent years. Come fall, stripers and blues surge again, often feeding aggressively, before tautog claim the rocky structure and jetties through the cooler months.

In the back bays, fluke stack on channel edges and dropoffs — slow-drifting a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip of fresh squid along the bottom is the standard and it works. Work the jetty rocks and inlet structure with soft plastics or chunk bait for stripers and blues on moving tides, especially the last two hours of the outgoing when bait concentrates in the current. Tautog want green crabs fished tight to the bottom near structure, period. Incoming tide pushes clean ocean water into the bays and generally improves clarity and feeding activity. Once water temps push above 72 degrees, focus earlier and later in the day when fish are more active and closer to the surface.

Captree sits right at the mouth of Fire Island Inlet, which makes it a serious striper spot during spring and fall runs when bass follow baitfish through the rip. As water temperatures climb into the mid-60s, fluke move into the bay shallows and the inlet edges, and bluefish show up slashing bait on the surface. Summer also brings black sea bass on nearshore structure just outside the inlet. Weakfish and kingfish work the bay grass edges and sandy runs through warmer months, though weakfish have thinned considerably in recent years. Come fall, the bass fishing gets serious again, and tautog become the target for anglers working jetty and wreck structure with colder water.

The inlet rip is your anchor point for stripers and blues — work surface plugs and bucktails through the current seams on the outgoing tide when baitfish concentrate at the mouth. For fluke, drift the sandy bay bottom east of the inlet with bucktail and Gulp combinations, keeping contact with the bottom in 10 to 20 feet. Tautog and black sea bass want crabs or green crabs bounced slowly on structure. A strong northwest wind drops visibility and pushes cleaner water out; a southwest sea breeze typically muddies the bay shallows and slows the fluke bite. Incoming tide stacks fish tighter at the inlet. Watch for bird activity and breaking fish — when bunker are pushed against the surface near the inlet mouth, everything feeds.

Annapolis sits near the middle Bay, which puts you in productive water year-round. Spring kicks off with white perch flooding the creeks and river mouths to spawn — they're one of the first reliable bites of the year. Striped bass, or rockfish as locals call them, run through on their spring migration, then scatter to cooler, deeper structure through summer. Fall is the crown jewel: rockfish push baitfish against the surface and bluefish join the chaos, making for some of the most exciting fishing the Bay offers. Winter slows things down, but patient anglers targeting deep channel edges can still find rockfish stacked up.

Watch your tides closely — moving water is everything here. Rockfish ambush bait around bridge pilings, channel edges, and points where current accelerates, so position your boat to work lures or live spot into the current seam. Bucktail jigs tipped with soft plastics or a live-lined spot are go-to presentations for rockfish. For bluefish, wire-leader rigs with metal spoons or poppers get the job done when they're up and slashing. White perch respond well to small jigs and bloodworms near shallow structure. Water temps in the low 60s are a sweet spot that tends to activate all three species. Favor east or northeast winds — they push water and bait productively across this stretch of Bay.

Solomons sits where the Patuxent meets the Bay, giving you access to a surprisingly diverse fishery year-round. Spring brings striped bass staging on the shallow flats and channel edges as water temps climb through the 50s, with bluefish pushing in behind them. Summer shifts the focus to fluke drifting the deeper basin edges and the mouth of the Patuxent, black sea bass holding on any hard bottom or structure offshore, and scattered weakfish and kingfish working the sandy shallows after dark. Tautog claim the rockpiles and bridge rubble from fall well into winter, and keeper stripers return heavy once water cools back below 60 degrees.

Fish the Patuxent's channel ledges on an outgoing tide when cooler, cleaner water pulls bait out of the river — that's when stripers and blues stack up. For fluke, slow-drift sandy bottom transitions with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait, and work faster when you find current. Black sea bass and tautog demand you stay tight to structure; green crabs and fiddlers outfish everything for tog. Wind from the south stirs up the water and pushes bait shallow, which is worth watching. When surface temps spike into the low 80s, go early, go deep, or go home.

Kent Island sits right where the Chester and Wye rivers empty into the Bay's main channel, which makes it a natural funnel for migrating fish. Spring striped bass fishing kicks off as water temps climb past 50°F, with fish pushing up from the lower Bay. Bluefish arrive in earnest by late spring and stay aggressive through summer. Fluke show up once surface temps hit the low 60s and hold through early fall around sandy transition bottoms. Black sea bass and tautog work the hard structure throughout the warmer months. Weakfish and kingfish are more of a late-spring through summer fishery here, often overlooked but worth targeting in the shallow grass edges.

For stripers, work the channel edges and rock piles on the outgoing tide with white or chartreuse bucktails tipped with soft plastics — fish often stack just off the current break. Fluke want a drifting bottom rig with a Gulp or strip bait over the sand-shell mix where depth transitions from eight to fifteen feet. Tautog hold tight to any riprap or submerged structure; go heavy with green crab on a knocker rig and be patient. Bluefish will blow up topwater poppers on a wind-chop surface. In summer, fish early morning before heat pushes water temps above 80°F, when stripers especially go lethargic and move deep or offshore.

Tangier Sound fishes differently than the open Bay — it's shallower, grass-edged, and tidal, which concentrates fish in predictable ways. Striped bass push through in spring and again in fall, often mixing with bluefish when bait schools stack up near channel edges. Summertime belongs to fluke working the sandy bottom along deeper channel margins, and black sea bass holding on any hard structure or shell hash you can find. Weakfish and kingfish show up in warmer months too, favoring softer bottom near grass. Once water cools into fall and winter, tautog become the main target around any hard bottom or riprap.

Position matters more than gear here. Fluke producers fish bucktail-and-grub combos along channel drop-offs with a slow drag-and-pause retrieve, while black sea bass eat cut squid or crab near bottom structure. Stripers respond well to live spot or chunk bunker fished on moving tides — the first two hours of incoming or outgoing water are almost always the most productive in this shallow system. Bluefish will blow up on topwater plugs when conditions align. Keep an eye on water clarity; after hard northeast winds push murky water in, bite quality usually drops until it flushes back out.

Delaware Bay and the Lewes Canal are transition fisheries, meaning the action shifts dramatically as water temperatures move. Flounder arrive in the bay shallows and canal edges as water climbs through the mid-50s into summer, holding through August before pushing back offshore in fall. Striped bass show up in spring and again in fall, with the fall run often producing the best action as fish stage in the bay and stack up along the canal current seams. Tautog are a cold-water species here — target them seriously in spring before things warm up and again in fall as temperatures drop back down, when they bite aggressively around hard structure.

For flounder in the canal, drift bucktails tipped with Gulp! or spearing along the bottom through the current, slowing your drift on the downtide side of bridges and pilings where fish park. Stripers in the bay respond well to topwater at dawn and bucktails or paddle tails worked through rips when bait is present. Tautog want crabs fished tight to rocks, jetty structure, and riprap with virtually no slack — you need to feel them. Tide is everything in the canal: fish the moving water, not the slack. Outgoing tide in particular pushes bait through predictably, and the fish know it.

Indian River Inlet fishes differently than most Mid-Atlantic spots because that bridge channel is a genuine tidal funnel — current rips hard, and species pile up accordingly. Spring brings the first striped bass push as fish migrate through, with weakfish mixing in during warmer stretches, though weakfish numbers have been inconsistent for years. Fluke move into the inlet and nearby surf once water climbs into the low 60s, staying through summer alongside bluefish that can show up in aggressive feeding frenzies. Fall is prime time — stripers bulk up here, bluefish go on a tear, and tautog claim the rock jetties. Black sea bass work the structure too. Kingfish run the surf during warmer months, often underrated but worth targeting.

Fish the inlet rocks and jetty bases hard during moving tides, especially the last two hours of outgoing when baitfish get pushed through the cut — stripers and blues stack up waiting. For fluke, drift the inlet channel with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip of squid, keeping bottom contact through the current seam. Tautog respond to green crabs worked tight against the riprap. Surf kingfish prefer fresh clam or bloodworm on a high-low rig. Cold water below 50 degrees slows fluke and weakfish but activates tautog. Offshore wind flattens the surf, improving conditions; onshore chop stirs baitfish and can trigger striper blitzes along the beach on either side of the inlet mouth.

Chincoteague's mix of ocean surf, tidal channels, and shallow bay flats means you're chasing a rotating cast of species year-round. Striped bass move through the surf and inlet in spring and again hard in fall, while weakfish show up in the back bays during warmer months, though their numbers have thinned considerably over the years. Summer is fluke and bluefish time — both hit the surf cuts and channel edges with aggression once water temps climb into the mid-60s. Tautog and black sea bass hold on any hard structure you can find, with tog peaking in spring and fall. Kingfish are an underrated summer target in the surf, showing up in the wash right behind breaking waves.

In the surf, work the troughs and cuts that form between sandbars — that's where stripers and bluefish pin baitfish on a dropping tide. Bucktail jigs tipped with a soft-plastic trailer are versatile enough to cover the flats and channels for fluke, while fresh cut bunker or mullet on the bottom handles stripers and kingfish. In the back bay, a moving tide is everything — fish tend to feed aggressively during the first two hours of an incoming or outgoing tide on the channel edges and marsh drains. Overcast days with a light southwest wind tend to fire up surface action. Cold water below 50°F pushes most species offshore or into deep channel holes, so adjust accordingly.

Wachapreague's seaside marshes, inlets, and barrier island channels offer year-round action if you know what's running. Striped bass push through during spring and again in fall, using the deeper cuts between the marsh islands as travel corridors. Fluke move into the shallower grassy edges and sandy pockets from late spring through summer, while bluefish often show alongside them, slashing bait in the inlets. Weakfish and kingfish work the softer sandy bottom inside the inlets on summer nights and early mornings. Black sea bass and tautog are found on nearshore structure, with tog best in cooler water during spring and fall.

Tides are everything here — fish the last two hours of outgoing and first hour of incoming when bait flushes through the cuts. Fluke stack on the downcurrent side of channel edges, so drift bucktails tipped with Gulp or strip bait along the bottom. For stripers and blues, work surface plugs and spoons through the inlets on a moving tide. Weakfish respond well to small jigs and shrimp under low-light conditions. Water temperature around 55-65 degrees activates the best striper and weakfish bites; once surface temps climb into the mid-70s, go early or target deeper water.

Hampton Roads is one of the most diverse inshore fisheries on the mid-Atlantic coast. Striped bass are the anchor species, staging near the bay mouth in fall and spring as they migrate, with fish pushing into the Roads during cold months to feed near warm-water discharges. Fluke move in from offshore once water temperatures climb into the mid-60s, dominating summer structure fishing. Bluefish show up in blitzing schools spring through fall. Weakfish and kingfish are warm-weather targets often overlooked by visiting anglers but well worth chasing on sandy bottom. Tautog haunt hard structure year-round with the best action in cooler months, while black sea bass peak in spring and fall around the same rock and wreck structure.

Tide movement is everything here — fish the outgoing tide where channel edges meet flats, as predators stack on current seams to ambush bait. For fluke, drift sandy bottom with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strips along the deeper channel shoulders. Stripers respond to chunk bunker and jigging during peak migrations, especially when water temperature drops into the low 50s and bait schools concentrate. Work bridge and pier pilings for tautog using green crab fished tight to structure. Kingfish and weakfish prefer a moving tide over sandy bottom with bloodworms or light rigs. Avoid fishing slack tide in this heavy current water — those windows typically produce very little.

The Bay Bridge-Tunnel and Hampton Roads harbor fish year-round, but the character shifts dramatically with the seasons. Spring brings striped bass staging in the channel edges as water temps climb through the 50s, followed by weakfish moving into the shallower harbor reaches. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the sandy pockets around the tunnel islands and bluefish slashing through baitfish schools near the pilings. Black sea bass and tautog hold on the rockpile structure around the tunnel spans through summer into fall. As water cools below 60 degrees, stripers return in force and kingfish show up in the surf wash near the islands. Deep winter is tautog time on the hard structure.

Position yourself on the upcurrent side of the tunnel islands and let the tide do the work. Fluke respond to bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or live minnows drifted along bottom transitions where sand meets shell. Tautog and sea bass want green crabs or fiddlers worked tight to the pilings. Stripers key on current seams at the island corners, especially on moving tides during low-light windows, with soft plastics, bucktails, or live spot getting consistent results. Bluefish will announce themselves at the surface. Dirty water after hard southwest winds slows nearly everything, so prioritize clean water on the east-facing sides of the structures.

Atlantic Beach sits at the heart of the Crystal Coast, where Bogue Sound meets Beaufort Inlet, and the mix of inshore shallows, inlet structure, and nearshore ledges keeps something biting year-round. Spring brings striped bass working the inlet and sound edges on the run-out tide, while weakfish show up in the sound grass beds from late spring through early summer. Fluke move into the inlet and nearshore shoals as water warms into the sixties, staying active through summer. Bluefish school up in fall, slashing through baitfish along the beaches and inlet mouth. Winter belongs to tautog on nearshore rock piles and black sea bass on structure, with kingfish making good surf catches whenever the water stays mild.

Read the tides carefully here — falling water pushes baitfish out of Bogue Sound through the inlet, stacking stripers and blues at the mouth where structure breaks current. For fluke, drift the inlet channel edges and shoal drop-offs with live mud minnows or small bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp. Tautog and black sea bass respond to green crab or fiddlers fished tight to bottom structure on calm days with minimal drift. Weakfish prefer low-light periods in moderate current over sandy grass-bottom shallows — soft plastic shrimp imitations work well. Water temperature under fifty degrees signals the shift to winter species and slower, more deliberate bottom presentations. Northeast wind muddies the surf and kills visibility, so target those days inside the sound or wait for southwest winds to clear the water.

Murrells Inlet fishes differently than most South Carolina inlets because of its mix of marsh creek structure, jetty rock, and access to nearshore ledges within a short run. Striped bass push through in late fall and winter, working the inlet's tidal creeks and jetty edges when water cools below 60 degrees. Spring brings weakfish into the shallower marsh drains after dark, while fluke move in as water warms and hold through summer on sandy bottom transitions near channel edges. Bluefish show seasonally in choppy surface water, kingfish root along sandy nearshore bottom in warmer months, and black sea bass and tautog stay glued to hard structure year-round.

Work the outgoing tide hard here — it flushes baitfish and crabs out of the marsh, and predators stack at channel mouths and rocky transitions waiting on it. Jigging bucktails tipped with Gulp or cut squid covers fluke, sea bass, and tautog efficiently over nearshore structure. Live finger mullet or mud minnows under a popping cork pull weakfish from creek mouths on calm, low-light tides. For stripers, slow-rolled swimbaits along the jetty rocks on a dropping tide after a cold front outperform everything else. Watch water temperature closely — a sharp drop below 50 degrees pushes most species offshore, while a warming trend in late winter activates tautog and early weakfish before most anglers expect them.

Winyah Bay sits at the confluence of the Black, Pee Dee, Sampit, and Waccamaw rivers, and that mix of fresh and salt makes it one of the more interesting estuaries on the South Carolina coast. Striped bass are the marquee fish here, with the best action in late fall through early spring when cooler water pushes them into the bay and up into the river channels. Summer brings fluke working the sandy shoals near the bay mouth, along with bluefish crashing baitfish on the surface. Tautog and black sea bass show up around any hard structure near the inlet, particularly in cooler months. Weakfish and kingfish make seasonal runs through the shallower grass edges when water temps settle in the mid-60s to low 70s.

Fish the moving tide religiously here — stripers and weakfish stack on current breaks where the river channels pinch down or where creek mouths dump into the bay. On the incoming tide, fluke slide up onto sand flats and drop-offs; fish bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip of fresh mullet along the bottom. For stripers, chunked menhaden fished on the bottom in deeper river bends produces reliably, but live eels or swimbaits worked along riprap and dock pilings at night can be exceptional. Wind out of the northeast tends to dirty the upper bay, so shift toward the cleaner water near the inlet. Tautog want fiddler crabs or green crabs dropped tight to any hard structure — do not work that bait far from the bottom.

Beaufort's tidal creeks, grass flats, and sounds fish differently than most Mid-Atlantic estuaries because the water temperature swings hard and the tides run strong. Striped bass move through in fall and again in late winter as water cools, staging along deeper channel edges. Spring and early summer bring weakfish into the grass lines at dusk, and fluke settle onto sandy creek mouths and sound bottoms through summer. Bluefish show unpredictably, often crashing bait on the flats during tide changes. Tautog and black sea bass hold on the nearshore hard structure just offshore. Kingfish work the sandy bottom year-round but are most active in cooler months.

Fish the outgoing tide hard here — falling water pushes bait out of the marshes and concentrates predators at creek mouths and channel drops. For stripers and weakfish, soft plastics on quarter-ounce jigheads worked slowly along grass edges at low light are hard to beat. Fluke want a slow drift with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait across sandy transitions. Bluefish hit anything fast near the surface. Watch water temperature closely — once it climbs above 80 degrees, fish deep and early. Light southeast winds keep the flats fishable; hard southwest winds muddy shallow water quickly.

The Savannah River mouth and Tybee surf fish hard year-round if you know what to expect. Spring pushes striped bass through the river channel as they follow bait migrations, and bluefish show up slashing through mullet schools along the bars. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the inlet edges and nearshore structure, while black sea bass stack on any hard bottom you can find offshore. Weakfish work the surf and channel margins at night during warmer months. Fall is the most electric season here, with bluefish, stripers, and kingfish all feeding aggressively before the water cools. Tautog move onto jetty rocks and nearshore wrecks once water temperatures drop into the low 60s and hold there through winter.

Read the tides religiously on this water. The Savannah River dumps enormous volumes on the outgoing, flushing bait through the channel edges and along the rip lines that form off the north and south jetties — that moving water concentrates every predator on the list. Fluke want a slow drift with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait along the channel drop-offs. Stripers and blues respond to topwaters and swimbaits worked through rip current seams on the last two hours of outgoing tide. Kingfish hit small fish-finder rigs with fresh shrimp or sand fleas in the near-shore surf troughs. Tautog take green crabs bounced tight to jetty rocks. Avoid dirty water after heavy rain — the river runs brown fast and shuts fishing down until clarity returns.

The Golden Isles sounds — Jekyll, St. Simons, Altamaha, and the tidal creeks threading between them — offer year-round action if you know what to chase. Redfish and spotted seatrout dominate local talk, but plenty of visiting species deserve attention. Bluefish push through hard in fall and again in spring, often schooling visibly on the surface near sound mouths. Fluke settle into the deeper sound channels through summer, while weakfish and kingfish work the shallower grass edges in warmer months. Black sea bass and tautog hold on nearshore structure through cooler seasons, and striped bass show up in the sounds and lower river systems during winter's cold snaps.

Tides run strong here — fish the first two hours of an incoming tide along marsh edges and creek mouths where bait gets flushed out of the grass, and drop jigs or bucktails into deeper channel bends on the outgoing. For fluke, slow-drag gulp-style soft plastics or live finger mullet along sandy channel floors. Bluefish want fast-retrieved metal spoons or poppers. Target black sea bass and tautog on cut crab or clam around shell bottom and dock pilings. Water temperature below 55°F pushes fish deeper and slows presentations considerably. Wind-driven muddy water kills visibility — wait for clearing water on the back side of a blow.

Amelia Island's inlet and surrounding waters fish differently than most of Florida's Atlantic coast. Striped bass push through during cooler months, following baitfish concentrations near the inlet mouth and Nassau Sound. Winter and early spring also bring tautog onto hard structure and rock piles, while weakfish ghost through the marsh creeks and grass edges when water temperatures dip into the low 60s. Come late spring, bluefish flood the inlet with serious aggression, and fluke move in along sandy transitions and channel edges through summer. Black sea bass stack on any offshore relief you can find. Kingfish run tight to the beach in surf conditions during fall and spring.

Work the strong tidal flow through the inlet on a falling tide, which flushes baitfish and triggers feeding along current seams and drop-offs. Fluke respond well to bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or live finger mullet, drifted slowly across sandy bottom near channel edges. For bluefish and stripers, match the bait schools with spoons, jigs, or topwater lures during low-light hours. Tautog want fiddler crabs or green crabs bounced right on structure. Dirty water following wind events slows most bites here, so target clearer water near the inlet mouth after a blow. Clear, moving water in the 58 to 72 degree range is your sweet spot for most species.

The Halifax River is a tidal estuary, not open coast, so expect an inshore mix rather than a striped bass or tautog fishery — those species don't reliably show here. What you will find are redfish, flounder including summer flounder that push into the river through warmer months, bluefish that make seasonal runs through the inlet and along the surf, kingfish working the sandy surf bottom year-round with peaks in spring and fall, weakfish staging around structure during cooler months, and black sea bass holding on nearshore hard bottom just offshore. Surf fishing picks up significantly in fall as baitfish migrations concentrate predators along the beach.

On the river, work deeper channel edges and dock pilings on outgoing tide when baitfish flush out of grass flats — that's when flounder and weakfish ambush feeding lanes. In the surf, kingfish hit best on fresh shrimp or sand fleas right in the wash during incoming tide on lower-wind mornings when the water runs clearer. For bluefish, cast metal spoons or fast-retrieved plugs near the inlet mouth. Water temperature below 65 degrees slows the flat's flounder bite considerably, so cold fronts push action toward deeper river structure rather than shallow grass edges.

Port Canaveral fishes differently than most of Florida's inshore coast because the deep shipping channel cuts almost to the beach, giving you access to offshore-grade species without running far. Spring and fall are the money seasons for king mackerel, when they stack up near the jetty tips and along the channel edges chasing baitfish migrations. Redfish and snook hold in the port basin and along the rock piles year-round, though snook get sluggish in winter cold snaps and push tighter to structure. Mangrove snapper are reliably present around the jetty rocks and any submerged concrete throughout the warmer months.

Work the outgoing tide hard — it flushes baitfish out of the basin and through the jetties, and that's when snook and redfish ambush at current seams along the rocks. For kings, slow-troll a live blue runner or threadfin on a wire rig along the channel edge. Snook and redfish respond well to DOA shrimp, white paddle-tail swimbaits, and live finger mullet fished tight to the jetty granite on a light jighead. Snapper want small live shrimp or cut squid bounced on bottom near the rocks. When east winds push in warm, clear blue water close to the jetties, kings and snapper fishing typically improves noticeably.

Fort Pierce Inlet and the Indian River Lagoon fish differently than most Florida waters because the inlet acts as a funnel, pulling cold-water species down from the north during winter. Bluefish and weakfish move through the inlet in fall and early winter, chasing bait on dropping water temperatures. Black sea bass and tautog work the inlet's rocky structure in cooler months. Warmer months shift action into the lagoon, where fluke bury up on sandy-shell bottom and snook dominate the dock and bridge lights. Striped bass appear seasonally near the inlet during winter cold snaps, while kingfish roam nearshore just outside the mouth in spring and summer.

Tides are everything here. An outgoing tide flushes baitfish through the inlet's channel edges, which is where weakfish, bluefish, and fluke stack up tight to the bottom. Work jigs tipped with gulp or live finger mullet along those current seams. For flounder, slow-drag a paddletail along sandy transition edges inside the lagoon on light wind days when water clarity is decent. Bluefish want fast-moving metals or spoons in the inlet current. When water temps drop below the low 60s, shift to tautog and black sea bass on the inlet's rock piles using fiddler crabs or cut crab fished right on bottom.

Palm Beach sits right on the edge of the Gulf Stream, which keeps water temps warmer year-round than anglers farther north expect. Kingfish run the nearshore reefs and inlet edges during winter and early spring, while bluefish show up in big schools through the inlet on outgoing tides almost any cool-weather month. Warmer months bring blackfin tuna and mahi just offshore in the Stream, but the inlet and inshore reefs hold black sea bass year-round with peak action in cooler water. Weakfish and fluke push into the inlet during spring and fall transitions when water temps swing through the mid-60s. Tautog are rare here, and striped bass are occasional cold-front visitors, not reliable targets in South Florida.

For Gulf Stream edge fishing, watch for color changes where blue water meets greener inshore water and troll rigged ballyhoo or pitch live pilchards around weedlines. Inside the inlet, kingfish and bluefish respond well to fast-moving spoons and cut threadfin herring fished near the bottom on strong outgoing tides when current scours bait off the rocks. Black sea bass stack on any hard structure and hit squid strips or small jigs readily. Work the inlet mouth on the first two hours of outgoing tide in winter for the most consistent action across species. Southerly winds push warmer bluer water close to the inlet; northerly winds dirty things up and slow fishing noticeably.

The Big Pine Key backcountry is a world of shallow grass flats, mangrove-lined creeks, and sandy potholes — and the species that thrive here are almost entirely different from what mid-Atlantic anglers chase up north. Permit, bonefish, tarpon, and snook are the stars of this fishery, with redfish and spotted seatrout rounding out most guides' target lists. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish simply don't inhabit these subtropical flats in any meaningful way. Honest advice: if those are your target species, the lower Keys backcountry isn't the right destination. Tarpon flood the backcountry channels in spring, snook stack under mangroves through summer, and tailing permit and bonefish work the flats whenever water temperatures stay in the upper 70s to low 80s.

To fish this water effectively, focus on moving tides rather than slack water — bonefish and permit feed aggressively on an incoming tide as it pushes over shallow grass, and snook ambush baitfish on the outgoing near mangrove points. Light southeast winds keep the flats fishable and clear; strong north winds in winter dirty the water and push fish deeper. Sight-fishing with 8- to 10-weight fly rods and crab or shrimp patterns is the premier technique, but light spinning gear with live shrimp or small jigs works well for anglers newer to the flats. Read the water by watching for tailing fish, nervous water, and muds.

Homosassa's springs and grass flats are built around a handful of core species, and the calendar drives everything. Redfish and spotted seatrout dominate year-round, but winter draws snook tight into the warm spring vents alongside manatees, making them accessible even in cold snaps. Tarpon roll through the flats from late spring into summer, and that's when things get serious. The species list you'd chase on an Atlantic estuary — striped bass, fluke, bluefish, weakfish, tautog, black sea bass, kingfish — simply don't belong here. This is Gulf Coast spring-fed water, and fishing it honestly means targeting the animals that actually live here.

On the flats, moving tides push baitfish and crabs along grassbed edges, and that's where trout and reds set up to ambush. Work popping corks over submerged grass on incoming tide, or free-line live pinfish and pigfish near spring boils in cooler months. Soft plastics on light jig heads — paddletails and shrimp imitations in natural colors — are workhorses. When water temps drop below 60 degrees, fish compress into deeper spring-fed channels and go lethargic; slow down your presentation dramatically. Northeast winds flatten the bays and push fish shallow. Watch for nervous water and mullet jumping — that usually means predators underneath.

Steinhatchee's Big Bend flats are defined by their vast grass beds, oyster bars, and tidal creeks cutting through shallow mud bottom — structure that draws redfish and spotted seatrout year-round but fishes very differently by season. Spring brings trout onto the flats as water warms into the mid-60s, and they'll stack on the edges of deeper potholes. Summer shifts focus: trout move to deeper grass and channel edges during heat, while reds cruise the shallower flats in loose schools. Summer also opens scallop season, and wading for scallops often puts you right in prime redfish territory. Fall is the sweet spot — cooling water concentrates both reds and trout aggressively feeding before winter. Cold fronts push fish into creeks and deeper cuts.

Read the tides carefully here because the Big Bend has a strong tidal range that moves fish dramatically. On a falling tide, reds push off flooded marsh grass onto the flat edges and funnel through oyster bar drains — position yourself at those choke points. Rising tides let you follow fish back into shallow water under a foot or less. For trout over grass, a popping cork with a live shrimp or a soft plastic paddle tail works consistently; vary the pause until you find the cadence. For reds, weedless gold spoons and DOA shrimp-style soft plastics sight-casted ahead of tailing fish are hard to beat. Wind above 15 knots muddies the shallows fast here, so prioritize leeward shorelines and creeks on rough days.

Cedar Key's Big Bend backcountry is primarily redfish, trout, and flounder country — not striped bass, bluefish, or tautog water. That said, the seasonality here is distinct. Warmer months push spotted seatrout onto shallow grass flats and oyster bars, while redfish school in tidal creeks and along mangrove edges. As water cools into fall and winter, trout move deeper into channels and cuts, and flounder stage near creek mouths before their offshore migration. Sheepshead and black drum become reliable cold-weather targets around structure.

Fish moving tides hard — incoming water pushes baitfish and shrimp onto the flats, and predators follow. A falling tide concentrates fish at creek mouths and deeper potholes. Soft plastics on light jigheads, weedless gold spoons, and live shrimp all produce here. Watch water temperature closely — trout and reds feed aggressively in the mid-60s to low-70s Fahrenheit range. Persistent wind out of the north muddies the shallow flats quickly, so seek leeward shorelines and deeper protected drains on those days.

Apalachicola Bay and the barrier islands — St. George, St. Vincent, Dog Island — fish differently than most Florida destinations because the Apalachicola River pushes enormous volumes of fresh water and nutrients into a relatively shallow estuary, creating habitat that draws species you rarely associate with the Gulf. Redfish, speckled trout, and flounder are the bread-and-butter targets year-round, but the deeper cuts along the barrier island passes and the bay's oyster-bar edges also hold black sea bass on structure through cooler months. Bluefish show up in the passes and nearshore Gulf in fall and winter when water temps drop into the low 60s, often crashing baitfish at the surface near the island cuts. Weakfish — locally called gray trout — turn up in the deeper bay channels in cooler weather and are underappreciated here.

Work falling tides hard, especially where marsh drains and oyster bars funnel baitfish out of the shallows into deeper adjacent water — fish stack at those transition edges waiting. For flounder, slow-drag a live finger mullet or a paddle-tail soft plastic along sandy bottom pockets adjacent to grass and shell; they ambush rather than chase. Black sea bass and the occasional big sheepshead hold tight to bridge rubble and submerged structure, so drop a fiddler crab or small jig directly on the structure. Bluefish and weakfish respond well to a fast-retrieved spoon or jerkbait through current rips in the passes. In cold snaps, avoid open shallow flats — fish go deep and slow your presentation accordingly.

Dauphin Island sits at the mouth of Mobile Bay, where warm Gulf water pushes against cooler, productive bay outflow — and that mixing zone drives everything here. Speckled trout and redfish get most of the local attention, but the pass and nearshore Gulf structure hold a solid variety of traveling species. Bluefish show up in fall and occasionally late winter, moving through in aggressive pods. Fluke work the sandy bay-mouth flats from late spring into summer, sitting tight to structure and current edges. Black sea bass and kingfish are reliable nearshore targets once water temps climb into the low 70s. Weakfish and striped bass appear here, though inconsistently, mostly tied to cooler transitional periods in spring and fall. Tautog are uncommon but show on hard bottom during winter.

For flounder, slow-drag a mud minnow or paddle-tail swimbait along shell-bottom transitions in the pass on a moving tide — they stack where current breaks near drop-offs. Bluefish push bait to the surface in open water; watch for diving birds and cover ground with metal spoons or fast-retrieved topwaters. Black sea bass and kingfish respond well to cut squid or live shrimp fished on bottom around nearshore reefs and rocks. An outgoing tide concentrates fish at the pass mouth as baitfish funnel through — this is almost always your most productive window here. In summer, fish early before the Gulf calms and warms; a slight chop and cooler morning temps keep fish feeding longer on the surface and in the shallows.

The Mississippi Sound is a shallow, brackish estuary, and the fish you'll reliably target shift hard with the seasons. Speckled trout and redfish dominate most conversations, but the Sound also holds solid flounder runs, with summer flounder pushing into the shallower grass flats and channel edges from late spring through early fall. Bluefish move through in good numbers during cooler months, blitzing baitfish along the open sound. Black sea bass hold around nearshore structure, though you'll need to push a bit south toward reef systems to target them consistently. Weakfish and kingfish make seasonal appearances, and while true striped bass and tautog aren't resident Sound fish in significant numbers, structure near the barrier islands occasionally surprises you.

Read the Sound by watching water clarity, tidal movement, and temperature first. Flounder stack in ambush along channel drop-offs and shell bottom where current funnels bait — drift live mud minnows or finger mullet along those edges during moving tides, keeping your presentation tight to the bottom. For bluefish, work surface plugs and spoons when you see diving birds or busting bait. Water temperatures below 60 degrees push most shallow species deeper or off the flats entirely, so shift toward nearshore structure then. An outgoing tide draining the grass flats concentrates bait and predators alike at creek mouths and channel intersections — those transitions are almost always your most productive windows.

Calcasieu Lake — locals call it the Cal — is one of the premier estuaries on the Gulf Coast, and it fishes differently by season in ways that matter. Spring brings speckled trout shallow as water warms into the mid-60s, often over grass and shell. Summer pushes specks deeper to the ledges and channels to escape heat, while redfish scatter across the flats and work marsh drains on moving water. Fall is prime time — trout stack up and redfish school visibly, making it the season most guides live for. Winter concentrates everything in deeper holes, where patient anglers still catch quality fish on slow presentations.

Tides are your most important variable here. A falling tide drains the marsh and pulls baitfish — and the reds and flounder waiting to ambush them — toward channel edges and points. Work those transitions with a paddletail swimbait or a live shrimp under a popping cork for specks, and drag a soft-plastic on a jighead slowly along bottom structure for flounder. Wind out of the north cools things fast and pushes water out; southeast wind warms and floods the flats, which activates redfish. Read the mullet — when they're nervous and scattering, something predatory is moving underneath them.

Terrebonne marsh out of Cocodrie is redfish and speckled trout country at its core, and those two species drive most of what you'll plan around. Spring and fall are prime, with trout schooling on shell edges and redfish tailing shallow in the ponds. Summers get brutal and push fish deep into shaded bayou cuts during midday. Winters concentrate big bull reds in the deeper passes. The species you named — striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish — are not realistic targets in this marsh system. This is Gulf-influenced Louisiana estuary, not Mid-Atlantic or Northeast coastal water, and chasing those species here would mean a very long, fishless day.

For actual Terrebonne success, work the marsh pond edges and oyster reefs on a falling tide, which flushes bait out of the grass and stacks fish at drain points. Soft plastics on quarter-ounce jigheads in chartreuse or white cover water efficiently, while weedless gold spoons are deadly for reds pushing the shoreline grass. Water temperature below 50°F slows trout dramatically — slow your retrieve and drop to a suspending lure or live shrimp under a popping cork. Incoming tides with two to four knots of southeast wind push cleaner water into the interior ponds and noticeably improve both visibility and bite activity.

Rockport's bays and back lakes are built around speckled trout and redfish, the bread-and-butter targets year-round. Flounder — what visitors sometimes call fluke or summer flounder — show up strong in warmer months, stacking along bay edges and draining cuts as water temps climb into the upper 70s. Fall brings some of the best mixed-bag fishing as redfish school heavily before cooler weather. Bluefish push through the bays in fall and can be surprisingly aggressive in the Aransas area. Species like striped bass, tautog, black sea bass, weakfish, and kingfish are not resident targets here — this is a different ecosystem entirely, and chasing those species will put you on the wrong water.

Work your tides hard. Moving water activates everything, especially around spartina grass edges, oyster reefs, and the mouths of back lake cuts. On outgoing tides, flounder and reds stage where drains empty into larger bays — easy ambush geometry. Wind-driven dirty water pushes fish shallow; clear water on calm days means working deeper grass edges with lighter tackle. Gold spoons, soft-plastic shrimp on light jig heads, and topwaters at dawn cover most situations. Live shrimp under a popping cork remains deadly when fish are finicky. In summer heat, fish early and target shaded shorelines or deeper holes mid-day.

Matagorda fishes differently than most Texas coast, and knowing the calendar matters. Redfish and speckled trout anchor the bay and surf year-round, but the mix shifts with water temperature. Cooler months push black drum into the surf troughs and channel edges, while warmer months bring flounder staging near jetty bases and pass mouths. Spanish mackerel and jack crevalle run the surf hard in late spring and summer, and kingfish show up in the suds when clean green water pushes in. Bluefish make seasonal passes through the surf, blitzing baitfish near the jetties in fall. Weakfish are present but less predictable, typically showing during mild transitional weather.

Work the Colorado River mouth area when tidal flow is moving, as current concentrates baitfish and predators stage tight to structure. On the jetties, fish the shadow lines and current seams with live shrimp, cut mullet, or soft plastics worked slowly near the bottom for flounder and drum. In the surf, target the second or third bar where wave action cuts defined troughs, especially during an incoming tide with light southeast wind pushing warm, slightly stained water. When water temps drop below 60 degrees, slow your presentation dramatically and go heavier on natural bait. Clear water calls for natural colors; stained water rewards chartreuse and loud rattles.

Freeport's jetties and nearshore rigs fish differently than most Texas coast, partly because the Brazos River influence and the Bryan Mound and Freeport area platforms create structure that holds a wider mix than you'd expect this far south. Spring through early summer is prime time for kingfish working the jetty wash, while bluefish show up in good numbers when cooler water pushes through. Weakfish move through in spring, often underrated and overlooked. Fluke aren't a heavy target here the way they are up the East Coast, and tautog, striped bass, and black sea bass are genuinely limited in these waters compared to their home range.

For jetty fishing, work the down-current side during an outgoing tide when water clarity is reasonable and temps are in the mid-60s to low 70s. Kingfish respond well to fresh shrimp or cut mullet bounced along the rock base. When bluefish are running, wire-leader spoons and fast-retrieved jigs get bit quickly. On nearshore rigs, drop shrimp-tipped jigs to the structure bottom during the last two hours of outgoing tide. Avoid fishing hard after heavy rain flushes muddy Brazos water into the pass, as dirty water kills bite activity fast.

Half Moon Bay holds a solid lineup of nearshore species, though anglers here should know the fishery skews heavily Pacific — so temper expectations on Atlantic species like fluke, bluefish, weakfish, tautog, and kingfish, which simply don't exist in these waters. What you will find is excellent striped bass action, especially in late spring through fall as baitfish push into the harbor mouth and along Pillar Point's rocky structure. Lingcod, rockfish, and halibut round out the offshore reef fishing, with halibut best worked in shallower sandy zones adjacent to structure.

For stripers in the harbor and along the outer reefs, focus on moving tides — the first two hours of an incoming tide concentrates fish near channel edges and rocky points. Surface water temps in the 54 to 58 degree range tend to activate feeding. Live anchovies are the local standard, though swimbaits and topwater plugs draw aggressive strikes in low-light conditions. Offshore, jigging with iron or drop-shotting soft plastics keeps baits in the strike zone over rocky bottom. Northwest wind above 15 knots pushes swells into a nasty chop off the point, so plan morning departures before the afternoon breeze builds.

Santa Cruz Bay and the wharf fish very differently than East Coast waters, so a quick reality check helps: striped bass are the real local star here, migrating through the bay from late spring into fall and holding near structure and kelp edges. Species like bluefish, fluke, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are Atlantic fish not typically found in Monterey Bay, so set those expectations aside. Black sea bass do exist in California but are a protected rockfish relative, off-limits to harvest. What you will find alongside stripers includes lingcod, cabezon, various rockfish, jacksmelt, and halibut — a genuinely productive mixed bag.

For stripers, focus on the wharf pilings, the surf edges, and the sandy transition zones where baitfish concentrate. Fish moving tides — the hour before and after the turn produces best. Anchovies and sardines fished live or cut are consistently effective, while swimbaits and Berkley Gulp curly tails work well for halibut on the bottom. Cold upwelling suppresses surface activity, so when water temps drop, go deeper and slow your presentation. Onshore winds push bait into the bay and trigger feeding, making those days worth prioritizing.

Ventura Harbor and the Channel Islands are Southern California rockfish and pelagic country — the core targets here are calico bass, sand bass, yellowtail, white seabass, and halibut, not the East Coast species in your list. Striped bass, bluefish, fluke, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are Atlantic and Gulf Coast fish that simply don't live in these waters. Striped bass do exist in California, but they're a Central Valley Delta and San Francisco Bay fishery, rarely showing in Ventura. Writing a report treating those species as Ventura targets would steer you badly wrong.

What I can tell you honestly: Ventura harbor holds legal-size California halibut on sandy bottom year-round, peaking spring through fall. The Channel Islands light up with yellowtail and white seabass when water temperatures climb into the mid-60s. Live squid is the single most effective bait across nearly every species here, and fishing the incoming tide in lower-light hours consistently outperforms midday high-sun conditions.

Long Beach harbor holds a solid mix of species through the year, though the lineup here skews more toward Pacific targets than the Atlantic species list you might be thinking of. If you're planning a trip expecting striped bass, bluefish, fluke, weakfish, tautog, black sea bass, or kingfish, those are East Coast and Gulf species that simply don't live in Southern California waters. The striped bass here is the Pacific strain, and it fishes well in the harbor and outer bay, especially in cooler months when fish push into the channel edges and deeper structure.

For Pacific stripers in the harbor, target current seams near jetty rocks and bridge pilings on moving tides, particularly the last two hours of outgoing. Swimbaits, paddle tails, and live anchovies are the go-to presentations. Cooler water in the 58 to 65 degree range tends to concentrate fish in tighter, more predictable spots. Offshore from Long Beach, yellowtail, calico bass, and halibut dominate depending on season. Read the wind carefully — a stiff westerly pushes bait schools and the predators follow, but it also makes the outer grounds rougher than the short distances suggest.

Santa Monica Bay is solid Southern California water, but let me be straight with you: striped bass are the marquee species here, and the rest of that list — fluke, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, kingfish — those are East Coast fish that simply don't swim these waters. Stripers are your main target, showing best in cooler months when water temps drop into the low 60s and bait schools concentrate near the bay's edges. Halibut replace flounder as the flatfish quarry, while calico bass, barracuda, and bonito round out warm-season action from late spring through fall.

For stripers, work the deeper channel edges and the areas where baitfish pile against structure. Live anchovies are the gold standard, but swimbaits in sardine patterns draw savage strikes. Incoming tides push bait into the bay, concentrating fish near drop-offs — that's your prime window. Light northwest winds lay the surface down and improve bite consistency. When water temps climb past 68 degrees, shift your attention toward calico bass around the kelp edges and rocky outcroppings, dropping live squid or soft plastics along the bottom.

Newport Beach harbor holds a solid year-round fishery, though the mix shifts noticeably with water temperature. Striped bass are the backbone here, moving through the back bay and channel edges spring into early summer before warm water pushes them deeper or northward. Calico bass dominate structure fishing through summer and fall. Offshore, the deeper banks and canyon edges draw yellowtail, white seabass, and halibut as surface temps climb into the mid-60s. Worth noting: the East Coast species listed — fluke, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish — are not native to Southern California and simply do not occur in Newport Beach waters.

For the species that actually live here, focus striper efforts near harbor channel edges and eelgrass flats on incoming tides, especially low-light periods. Swimbaits, paddle tails, and live anchovies produce well. Halibut stack on sandy transitions between structure and open bottom — drift live anchovies or small swimbaits slowly along these seams. Offshore, watch for surface water in the 62–68°F range with good color and bait marks on the sounder; yellowtail respond well to iron jigs and live mackerel. Afternoon sea breezes typically build chop by midday, so plan offshore runs early.

Humboldt Bay and its tributary rivers — the Eel, Mad, and Van Duzen — are best known for salmon and steelhead, and those are the fish that define this fishery through the seasons. Chinook salmon push into the bay and river mouths from late summer through fall, with steelhead following into the rivers through winter and into early spring. Rockfish and lingcod are year-round options in the bay's deeper channels. Halibut move into the shallower flats as water warms in late spring and summer, making them a primary warm-season target. Dungeness crab are also a major draw when seasons allow.

Tides are everything here. An incoming tide pushes baitfish and nutrients into the bay, and halibut stack on the sandy flats near channel edges waiting to ambush them — drift a whole anchovy or a paddle-tail swimbait slowly along the bottom during that moving water. For salmon near the river mouths, fish the tide transitions when current slows and salmon stage before committing to the freshwater push. Rivers run gin-clear in low summer flows, requiring lighter leaders and more subtle presentations; after fall rains color the water, salmon and steelhead become more aggressive and easier to approach. Wind matters most when ocean-bar conditions affect bay access — incoming swells stack up dangerously on the bay entrance bar, so watch the marine forecast carefully before crossing.

Yaquina Bay is Oregon coast salmon and bottomfish country, not mid-Atlantic estuary territory — so striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish simply don't live here. Giving you a report built around those species for Newport would be making things up, and that gets anglers skunked or worse. What Yaquina Bay actually holds is worth knowing: Chinook and coho salmon move through on seasonal runs, Dungeness crab are a major local draw, bay and ocean perch hold around structure, and cabezon along with other rockfish species are available nearshore and offshore. Halibut show up on the continental shelf in summer.

If you're heading to Newport, I'm glad to write you a straight report on what's actually biting — salmon timing in the bay and off the bar, halibut season on the shelf, bottomfish around nearshore reefs, or crabbing the bay channels. Just say the word and I'll give you real, useful information for the water you're actually fishing rather than a report that'll send you hunting for fish that don't exist here.

Depoe Bay's rocky reefs and kelp-fringed structure hold a solid lineup year-round, though the mix shifts with the seasons. Black rockfish and cabezon are the backbone here, biting through most of the year, while lingcod ramp up in late winter and spring when they move shallow to spawn. Halibut show up as waters warm in late spring and carry through summer — that's your flounder-style target on the central coast. Nearshore reefs also hold vermilion and canary rockfish as the season progresses. If you're chasing something with more fight in open water, albacore tuna push inshore during warm summers, often within 20 miles of the bay.

Position matters more than anything here. Fish the upcurrent edge of reef structure and kelp lines — rockfish and halibut both stack where current breaks and baitfish concentrate. For lingcod and blacks, swimbaits and heavy leadheads worked just above bottom are hard to beat. Herring and sardine strips on spreader bars produce well for halibut drifted slowly across sandy transition zones adjacent to reef. Fish the last two hours of an outgoing tide for the strongest bite — current activates the structure. Avoid northwest swells above 8 feet, and watch surface temperature closely in summer; a jump above 58°F often signals albacore opportunity offshore.

Tillamook Bay is primarily a Chinook and coho salmon fishery, with strong runs of Dungeness crab and sturgeon rounding out the action through the seasons. Spring brings the first Chinook push as fish stage near the bay mouth before working upriver, while fall sees the heaviest coho traffic. Perch and flounder — true Pacific species like starry flounder, not fluke or summer flounder — keep light-tackle anglers busy year-round along sandy shallows. Striped bass, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, black sea bass, and kingfish are East Coast and mid-Atlantic species that do not naturally occur in Tillamook Bay, and any report claiming otherwise would be steering you wrong.

For real results here, fish incoming tides as salmon and perch push into the bay's shallower channels and eelgrass edges. Sturgeon hold in the deeper holes and troughs — cut herring or smelt on bottom rigs near channel edges produces well on slower moving tides. For Chinook, back-trolling herring or cured roe near the bay mouth on a strong incoming flood is a proven local approach. Water temps in the low 50s Fahrenheit signal prime salmon activity. Wind out of the southwest can dirty the water fast near creek mouths, so clear green water is always your best visual cue to stay put.

The Columbia River mouth at Ilwaco draws anglers chasing Chinook and coho salmon through summer and fall, with the Buoy 10 fishery being one of the most celebrated salmon runs on the West Coast. Sturgeon are present year-round in the lower river, with spring and winter producing the most consistent action. Sea-run cutthroat trout work the estuary edges in late summer. It's worth noting that striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are East Coast and mid-Atlantic species that do not naturally occur in Pacific Northwest waters, so anglers planning a Columbia River mouth trip should focus their expectations on Pacific salmon, white sturgeon, and coastal bottomfish like lingcod and rockfish.

For salmon at Buoy 10, anchor or back-troll herring and sardine-wrapped plugs in the main channel during outgoing tides, when fish funnel through the shipping lane edges. Incoming tides push fish shallower toward the Washington shoreline, so adjust positioning accordingly. Water temperature through late summer guides fish depth — cooler upwellings concentrate Chinook near the bottom. Watch for wind-driven chop building against an outgoing tide, which creates standing waves that disorient bait and stack salmon underneath. Sturgeon respond well to smelt and sand shrimp fished on the bottom in current seams behind channel bends, particularly during slower tidal windows.

Neah Bay sits at the mouth of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and what you target shifts dramatically with the season. Chinook salmon are the backbone of the fishery, staging near the rocky points and kelp edges from late spring through summer as they push toward their home rivers. Coho arrive later in the season and run shallower, often right in the rip lines. Halibut show up on the sandy flats and gravel humps offshore as water temps climb through spring and summer, then thin out considerably by fall. Lingcod hold structure year-round — rocky reefs, pinnacles, and steep drop-offs — and the biggest fish tend to concentrate in deeper water during winter.

Tide movement is everything out here. The Strait generates serious current, and fish stack on the edges of rips where baitfish congregate. Target the first two hours of an ebbing tide near prominent points for salmon, trolling hoochies or cut-plug herring behind flashers at depths where your sonar shows bait.
