For halibut, anchor or slow-drift sandy transitions adjacent to structure and drop large circle-hook rigs baited with herring or squid. Lingcod hit heavy metal jigs worked tight to bottom on vertical drops. Northwest winds can build ugly chop fast, so watch the forecast closely and run early when it's calm.

The San Juan Islands are a Pacific Northwest fishery, so the species mix here is chinook, coho, pink, and sockeye salmon, along with lingcod, rockfish, halibut, and Dungeness crab — not the Atlantic species you listed. Since you asked me to weave in striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish, I have to be straight with you: none of those fish live in these waters. Writing a report that pretends otherwise would send you out with the wrong gear, wrong expectations, and wasted days on the water. That's not something I'm willing to do to a fellow angler.

What I can tell you is that the San Juans offer genuinely world-class fishing for what actually lives here. Chinook salmon hold near strong tidal rips and kelp edges, lingcod stack on rocky structure in 60 to 120 feet, and halibut show up on sandy flats in the warmer months. If you want a real, honest report covering those species, tactics, and how to read the currents and tides in this particular archipelago, just ask. I'll give you everything I know.

The Inside Passage around Juneau is salmon country at its core — king salmon move through early in the season, followed by coho, pink, and chum runs that carry well into fall. Halibut are the other major draw, holding in deep channel edges and soft-bottom flats year-round but most accessible in summer. Rockfish, Dolly Varden, and cutthroat round out the options. None of the mid-Atlantic species you mentioned — striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish — are present in Southeast Alaska waters, so planning around them here would be a wasted trip.

For kings and coho, troll herring or large spoons along current seams near kelp edges and underwater points on an incoming tide. Halibut stack in 150 to 400 feet on muddy bottom near structure — drop whole herring or large cut bait rigs and work bottom contact. Cold glacial melt keeps water temperatures in the low to mid-50s even in summer, so fish metabolisms stay measured; slow your presentations. Wind funnels hard through the channels, so fish early mornings when surface chop settles and baitfish congregate in protected coves.

Ketchikan sits at the crossroads of the Inside Passage and open Pacific, giving anglers a rare shot at multiple fisheries in a single day. Kings push into the straits and tidal rips first, typically arriving in late spring, with the bigger ocean-bright fish caught along the outer coast before they stage near creek mouths. Silvers follow in midsummer through early fall, often boiling right at the surface in protected inlets and feeding heavily on baitfish pushed against kelp lines. Halibut are available most of the season across both inside and outside grounds, with the largest fish generally found in deeper outside water.

Tide movement is everything here. Halibut stack on the upcurrent side of rocky points and underwater shelves where tidal flow concentrates needlefish and herring, so dropping large cut plug herring or rubber swimbaits straight down on a moving tide outperforms slack water almost every time. For kings, troll brined herring in a slow roll at depth near structure on incoming tides. Silvers come up aggressive on anchovy-pattern spoons or surface poppers when water temperatures dip into the mid-fifties and bait is visibly breaking the surface. Avoid dead-calm, flat-light conditions on the outer coast, and watch for diving birds to mark the schools.

Kodiak's inshore bays come alive in late spring when king salmon push into the protected waters ahead of the summer surge. Silvers follow through late summer and into fall, often stacking tight to creek mouths draining into the larger bays. Halibut are present year-round on sandy and mixed-bottom flats, but they concentrate in fishable depths through summer when water temps climb into the mid-40s to low 50s Fahrenheit. Rockfish fill up the reef structure and kelp edges throughout the season and make excellent targets on slower days or when weather pins you closer to shore.

Work halibut on the slack between tidal exchanges when bait settles naturally — whole herring or circle-hooked squid on bottom rigs fished in 60 to 200 feet covers most productive ground. For salmon, troll or cast spinners and spoons near the mouths of drainages on an incoming tide, which pushes fish shallower and more aggressive. Rockfish come readily on jigged plastics or metal jigs worked just above reef structure. Watch the wind direction carefully here — a building southeast swell can make outer-coast water unfishable fast, so keep an eye on bay entrances and have a fallback spot in mind.

Prince William Sound offers a rich seasonal calendar centered on Pacific salmon runs and bottom fish. Silver salmon arrive in late summer and push hard through early fall, making them the marquee inshore target for most visiting anglers. Halibut are present much of the open season, with larger fish often showing up as water temperatures climb through summer before cooling again in fall. Kings and pinks round out the salmon picture in earlier months, but silvers and halibut together form the core of a productive late-season trip.

For silvers, troll hoochies or spoons near the surface along kelp edges and rocky points where baitfish school up on incoming tides — silvers chase feed aggressively in moving water. Halibut hold on soft-bottom shelves and near underwater structure; fish herring or large jigs tight to bottom on the slack before a tide change, when they feed most predictably. Avoid fishing exposed water during southeast winds, which build quickly here and dirty the shallower bays. When surface temps drop into the low 50s, both species become less aggressive, so slow your presentations down.

Resurrection Bay is a cold, deep glacial fjord in southcentral Alaska, and the honest truth is that it holds no striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish — those are temperate Atlantic and Gulf Coast species that simply don't exist in these waters. Putting that list into a Seward report would steer you badly wrong and waste your trip. What Resurrection Bay actually produces, and produces exceptionally well, is silver and king salmon, halibut, lingcod, rockfish, and Dolly Varden, with runs and timing driven by snowmelt, baitfish cycles, and the bay's dramatic tidal exchange.

If you're planning a Seward trip, I'd strongly encourage you to reach back out with the correct location or the correct species list. A genuine Resurrection Bay report — covering where halibut stack on structure, how salmon move with the tides, which rockfish hold on kelp edges versus deep ledges, and how glacial runoff affects water clarity and fish behavior — would actually serve you. I'd rather give you nothing than give you wrong information that costs you a trip.

Lake Michigan off Chicago keeps anglers busy year-round. Chinook salmon are the marquee target, staging near the surface in warmer months before pushing deeper as summer heat stratifies the water column. Coho show up in good numbers during spring and fall runs, often closer to shore. Lake trout hold in colder, deeper water through summer and become more accessible once surface temps drop in autumn. Smallmouth bass work the rocky nearshore structure — breakwaters, piers, and riprap — from late spring through early fall when water warms into the mid-50s and above.

For salmon and lake trout, trolling with spoons, stick baits, and flasher-fly rigs at depths matching the thermocline is your bread and butter — watch your sonar for the temperature break and concentrate there. Downriggers let you target specific depths precisely. In spring and fall, coho and Chinook push shallower and can be reached with planer boards and shorter lead lengths. For smallmouth, work the concrete and rock structure with tube jigs and drop-shot rigs, especially where current from harbors and river mouths creates baitfish concentrations.

Waukegan Harbor draws a diverse mix of species across the calendar. Smallmouth bass are the bread-and-butter target, holding along the harbor's riprap walls and rubble reefs from late spring through fall. Largemouth show up in calmer, shallower backwater areas near any vegetation or dock structure inside the harbor. Coho and chinook salmon push through on spring and fall runs, while lake trout and brown trout cruise the deeper reef edges year-round. Walleye are present but less predictable, typically showing during low-light windows in spring and fall. Channel catfish work the harbor bottom through summer. Panfish, especially yellow perch, school along the breakwall and can be exceptional during fall.

Smallmouth stack on the outside riprap where current from harbor mouth flow meets warmer near-shore water — watch the thermal break, especially in spring when that 50-to-55-degree surface temperature triggers the first real feeding push. Tube jigs and finesse drop-shots in green pumpkin or watermelon work the rocky substrate hard. For trout and walleye near the reefs, troll or cast stick baits and spoons parallel to structure rather than across it. Catfish and perch respond well to cut bait or emerald shiners fished on bottom near current seams. When northwest winds push cold offshore water in, fishing slows dramatically — that's your cue to move tighter into the harbor and work slower presentations.

Milwaukee's Lake Michigan shoreline gives you a legitimate shot at three of the Great Lakes' best sport fish. Brown trout are your earliest opportunity, moving shallow along the breakwalls and piers as soon as winter ice clears and water temps creep into the low 40s. Coho push close to shore through spring and tend to suspend higher in the water column. Chinook salmon are the main summer event, staging offshore then moving toward tributary mouths as water cools into fall, when both browns and coho also make aggressive nearshore runs.

For spring browns and coho, work the pier heads and along the breakwalls with spoons, stick baits, or live emerald shiners near the surface. Once summer arrives, downriggers are the standard setup for Chinook, targeting the thermocline where cold and warm water meet, typically somewhere between 40 and 55 feet down depending on surface temps. In fall, watch for temperature breaks and bait concentrations on your graph near river mouths, and switch to flasher-fly rigs or larger spoons to match the aggressive mood of staging fish.

Sheboygan's Lake Michigan water is the main draw, and the big three here are chinook, coho, and lake-run brown trout. Spring is prime time for browns and coho stacking near the surface in cooler water, typically 45–55°F, as they stage close to shore before baitfish push offshore. Chinooks dominate midsummer in deeper structure as surface temps climb past 65°F and the thermocline locks salmon down. Fall brings another brown trout push nearshore. While Lake Michigan is the headliner, the Sheboygan River corridor and nearby backwaters do hold smallmouth bass, walleye, channel catfish, and panfish — with smallmouth responding well to rocky current breaks in early summer.

On the big water, watch your fish finder for that thermocline — a dramatic temperature break, often 50–80 feet down by midsummer, is where kings suspend. Run spoons, flies, or meat rigs on downriggers set to that depth. Dipsy divers with J-plug or flasher-fly combos produce when fish are spread horizontally. Browns in spring are more forgiving — crank stickbaits in chartreuse or natural shad patterns in the top 20 feet near tributary mouths when the lake is still cool and fish are chasing smelt. River walleye respond to jig-and-crawler presentations in current seams during low-light windows.

Kenosha sits on a stretch of Lake Michigan where the lake's open water meets nearshore structure, and the fishery shifts dramatically through the seasons. Spring through early summer, Chinook and coho salmon stage offshore while lake trout and brown trout cruise the shallower nearshore zones, often within casting distance of the piers and breakwaters. Smallmouth bass own the rocky structure through summer and into fall, while panfish like yellow perch hold in deeper basin areas seasonally. Walleye show up in the nearshore mix but are secondary here compared to true inland waters. Chain pickerel, largemouth bass, and catfish are honest options in the warmer backwater and harbor areas where weed edges and slower current collect them.

For trout and salmon along the piers, surface and subsurface temperatures matter enormously — fish stack at thermal breaks, so when you see sharp temperature changes in the upper water column, work that zone with stick baits, spoons, or inline spinners. Smallmouth along the breakwater respond well to drop-shot rigs and tube jigs bounced on the bottom in 8 to 20 feet. Perch stack in deeper water through late summer and fall — small jigging spoons tipped with emerald shiner or minnow catch them consistently. In the harbor, slower presentations like slip-floats with live bait or soft plastics near current seams and deeper holes produce catfish and the occasional largemouth around dock structure.

Sturgeon Bay sits at the intersection of Green Bay and Lake Michigan's Door County shoreline, giving you a remarkable mix of fisheries in tight proximity. Smallmouth bass dominate the rocky points and boulder fields along the Door County peninsula from late spring through fall, with fishing peaking when water temps climb into the mid-60s. Walleye run strong through Green Bay's shallower, murkier water, especially during the spring turnover and again in fall when baitfish stack up near transition zones. Chinook and coho salmon patrol the deeper Lake Michigan side in summer before pushing toward structure as water temperatures cool in August and September.

For smallmouth, work tube jigs and drop-shot rigs tight to submerged boulders and limestone ledges, focusing on the windswept sides of points where crayfish get pushed around. Green Bay walleye respond well to jig-and-minnow presentations along soft-bottom flats adjacent to hard-bottom transitions, especially during low-light periods. Salmon fishing out of the bay mouth rewards trollers running spoons and meat rigs at varying depths until you locate the thermocline. Pay attention to surface temperature breaks, as gamefish stack along temperature edges rather than spreading evenly throughout the water column.

Green Bay offers a diverse fishery that shifts dramatically with the calendar. Walleye are the marquee species, running hard through the shallower northern reaches in spring as water temps climb into the low 50s, then pushing deeper and scattering across the mid-bay flats through summer. Smallmouth bass stack on the rocky shoreline structure along both the Door Peninsula and the western shore once temps hit the mid-60s and stay active well into fall. Musky roam the weedy bays and transition zones throughout summer and peak in activity during the cooler weeks of September and October when big females feed aggressively before winter.

For walleye, work bottom bouncers with crawler harnesses over sandy and gravel transitions, or cast jig-and-minnow combos near current seams where tributary rivers meet the bay. Smallmouth respond well to tubes, drop-shots, and crayfish-imitating crankbaits fished tight to submerged rock and riprap. Musky demand patience here — large glidebaits, bucktail spinners, and topwater lures worked over weedbed edges during low-light periods produce the best shots. Pay attention to water clarity, which fluctuates with wind and wave action on this shallow lake; dirty water pushes fish shallower and makes them less spooky, while a clear, calm bay rewards finesse presentations.

Grand Traverse Bay offers a genuine three-season fishery built around distinct runs and migrations. Chinook and coho salmon stage in the deeper water of the main bay through late summer before pushing toward tributary mouths in fall, drawing serious trollers from late July onward. Lake trout hold in the cold, oxygenated depths year-round, with spring and early winter being the most productive windows when they move shallower to feed. Come warmer water, smallmouth bass own the rocky shorelines and boulder fields in both the East and West arms, fishing best from late spring through early fall.

For salmon and lake trout, downrigger trolling with spoons, stick baits, and meat rigs in the 60-to-120-foot range covers the most ground. Watch your surface temperature — salmon prefer the thermocline edge, typically where 55-to-62-degree water breaks sharply. Lake trout respond well to jigging tube baits and Swedish Pimples over hard bottom in 80-plus feet. Smallmouth concentrate around submerged rock piles and gravel points; tube jigs, drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics, and topwater walking baits early morning produce well when surface temps reach the mid-60s.

Ludington sits at the mouth of the Pere Marquette River, one of Michigan's finest steelhead and salmon corridors, and that combination of big lake and cold tributary defines your fishing calendar. Chinook salmon stage offshore in Lake Michigan through summer, chasing bait schools in the thermocline, then pour into the PM in fall on their spawning run. Steelhead follow in waves through late fall and again in spring, with some fish pushing in all winter during mild flows. Brown trout haunt the lower river and the nearshore lake shallows year-round, peaking in activity during fall and early spring when water cools.

In the lake, troll spoons and meat rigs at the depth where you find 52 to 58 degree water on your temperature gauge during summer. Once fish enter the PM, concentrate on the slower inside seams of bends and the soft water behind midstream boulders. For steelhead and late-run Chinook, dead-drifted spawn sacks under a float or swung wet flies through the tail-outs are the local go-to presentations. Rising river flows after rain pull fresh fish upriver fast, so time your river trips to hit the day or two after a good rain when visibility clears to a foot or two.

Manistee sits at the mouth of one of Michigan's best tributary rivers, and that geography shapes everything. In late summer and fall, king salmon stage offshore in Lake Michigan before pushing into the river, followed by coho. Winter and spring belong to steelhead, which run the Manistee in waves tied loosely to water temperature and flow pulses after rain or snowmelt. Brown trout and walleye round out the river, but salmon and steelhead draw most serious anglers here.

On the lake, troll spoons and meat rigs on downriggers over the thermal break where warmer surface water meets cold deep water. Once fish enter the river, focus on the deep runs and seams below gravel riffles where current slows. Swing egg patterns or soft plastics through holding water, and drift spawn sacks near bottom. Rising river levels after rain almost always trigger steelhead movement, so watch the gauge and plan accordingly.

Muskegon Lake connects to Lake Michigan through a channel, and that dynamic shapes everything here. Walleye move through the channel and stage near the lake's deeper basin, especially during spring and fall transitions. Smallmouth dominate rocky points and the sandy shallows along the south shore, while largemouth hold tight to the weed edges and dock pilings in the calmer back bays. Trout — mostly steelhead and brown trout — run the Muskegon River system and can be intercepted where the river meets the lake. Panfish like crappie and bluegill stack on submerged wood and dock structure throughout summer. Catfish and chain pickerel are underrated here, with pickerel favoring weedy shallows and cats working the deeper soft-bottom areas after dark.

Watch water temperature closely — smallmouth turn on hard once temps hit the mid-50s, and walleye feeding peaks during low-light transitions near the channel. Drift rigs with live crawlers cover the walleye basin effectively, while blade baits and jigging spoons work when fish are deeper in cold water. For bass, swimbaits and drop-shots on rocky structure consistently produce smallmouth, and flipping soft plastics into dock pilings or emerging weed pockets gets largemouth. When the channel is moving with wind-driven Lake Michigan flow, baitfish concentrate near the current seam — that's where predators stack up. Time your trips around that movement.

Grand Haven sits at the confluence of the Grand River and Lake Michigan, and that mix drives everything here. Spring draws trout staging near the river mouth and into the lower Grand, where they chase smelt and emergers. As water warms, walleye move upriver at night, and smallmouth bass claim rocky Lake Michigan structure along the piers and nearshore gravel. Midsummer the river channel holds catfish and panfish — bluegill, crappie, and rock bass — while largemouth and chain pickerel settle into slower backwater stretches with weedy edges upstream. Fall pushes trout and salmon back through, and walleye feed aggressively again before ice-up slows things down.

When lake temps drop below 55 degrees, focus on the pier heads and the river mouth where warmer river outflow concentrates baitfish and predators alike. For walleye, drift live crawlers or work shallow-diving crankbaits along current seams after dark near the river channel edges. Smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and drop-shot rigs on exposed gravel and rock rubble. Catfish hang in deeper river bends — cut sucker or chicken liver fished on bottom does the job. For largemouth and pickerel upriver, slow-rolled swimbaits and weedless frogs near emergent vegetation are reliable. Watch river flow — rising water pushes predators to calmer water along the banks; dropping water concentrates them in the main channel.

Saginaw Bay is one of the Great Lakes' most productive walleye fisheries, and that reputation is well earned. Spring draws walleye into the shallower western basin as water temperatures climb through the 40s and 50s, with fish staging near river mouths and rocky shoreline transitions before dispersing into deeper mid-bay structure through summer. Smallmouth bass follow a similar rhythm, moving onto gravel and cobble flats once temps push into the low 60s and holding there through fall before retreating to deeper basin water.

For walleye, trolling crawler harnesses and stick baits over sandy humps and mud-to-gravel transitions covers the most water efficiently, while jigging with paddle tails works well once you dial in the depth. Smallmouth respond well to drop-shot rigs and tube jigs worked along rock edges. Watch your surface temperature gauge — walleye tend to suspend and feed most aggressively in the 58-68 degree range, and fall cooling pushes both species shallower again, making the western bay rocky areas productive well into October.

The Detroit River and Lake St. Clair form one of the most productive freshwater fisheries in North America, drawing anglers chasing walleye, smallmouth bass, and musky year-round. Spring triggers the biggest walleye push as fish move upriver from Lake Erie to spawn in the swift current near the islands and rocky shoals. Smallmouth come alive on St. Clair's massive flats through summer and into fall, while musky follow the same shallow weed edges and transition points. Come late fall, walleye return to the river as water cools and baitfish concentrate.

On the river, walleye stack in current seams behind structure and bottom transitions — vertical jigging with quarter- to half-ounce heads tipped with soft plastics or live crawlers does consistent work. Watch water temperature closely: walleye feed aggressively when river temps hit the mid-40s to low 50s. On St. Clair, smallmouth relate to the sandy humps and weedline edges; drop-shot rigs and tube jigs excel when fish go finicky. For musky, work large bucktails and glide baits along weed transitions during low-light periods in fall when cooling water pushes them shallow and active.

Lake Erie near Erie, PA is a year-round fishery built around three marquee species. Walleye dominate attention from late winter through spring as fish stage in the shallower eastern basin before moving offshore in summer heat. Steelhead run the tributary streams that drain into the lake — think Walnut, Elk, and Fourmile creeks — peaking in fall and again in early spring when water temps climb back above 40 degrees. Smallmouth bass own the rocky reefs and boulder fields around Presque Isle Bay through summer, then scatter to deeper structure as water cools into fall.

For walleye, trolling worm harnesses and stick baits along depth contours between 20 and 35 feet consistently produces, especially when surface temps are transitioning. Work the drop-offs on the east side of Presque Isle Peninsula where bottom composition shifts from sand to gravel. Steelhead in the tribs respond to drifted egg sacs, wax worms, and small jigs in chartreuse or pink — present them naturally at the bottom of the water column in pools below riffles. Smallmouth stack on visible rocky points during the pre-spawn in late spring; drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics or crawfish-colored crankbaits worked slowly along the bottom get bites when fish are finicky.

Lake Erie and the Niagara River offer a serious year-round fishery built around walleye, smallmouth bass, and steelhead. Spring walleye runs concentrate near the eastern basin as fish move shallow to spawn, while summer shifts action to deeper structure and the river mouth. Smallmouth dominate Erie's rocky nearshore areas through summer and fall, becoming more aggressive as water cools into October. Steelhead enter the Niagara corridor in fall, run through winter, and peak again in early spring when tributaries warm slightly and fish stack before moving upstream.

For walleye, troll harnesses and stick baits along defined depth breaks, paying close attention to thermocline depth as summer stratifies the water. Smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and drop-shot rigs worked over submerged rock and gravel points. Steelhead in the Niagara hold in current seams behind mid-river boulders and along slack-water edges — drift spawn sacs or beads under a float, or swing streamers through the deeper runs. Watch river flow levels closely, as rising water pushes steelhead tight to softer edges while dropping flows concentrate fish in predictable slots.

Olcott sits at the mouth of Eighteen Mile Creek, and that tributary influence shapes the fishing calendar more than anything else. Spring brings steelhead stacking at the creek mouth and along the nearshore structure as water warms into the low 40s — these fish are aggressive and often shallow. Summer transitions to open-water trolling for Chinook salmon that follow the thermocline out into cooler, deeper water as surface temps climb. By late summer and fall, both Chinooks and browns push back toward shore, staging near the creek mouth before their upstream runs, and a second wave of steelhead follows close behind into late autumn.

For salmon in summer, run spoons and stick baits off downriggers targeting the 50 to 65-degree temperature band, often 40 to 80 feet down. Browns and steelhead in spring and fall respond well to shallow stick baits and flies worked near the creek outflow, especially when creek flow is elevated and stained water meets clear lake water — fish hold tight to that color edge. In fall, watch for baitfish concentrations near the surface at dawn; Chinooks and browns will push them against the breakwall, making casting spoons or swimbaits surprisingly effective from the pier.

Rochester's Lake Ontario fishery runs on salmon first. Spring brings staging brown trout tight to the river mouth as water temperatures climb through the 40s, with fish stacking where the warmer Genesee discharge meets the cold lake. Chinook and coho salmon dominate late summer through fall as mature fish push toward the river to spawn, creating some of the most intense shore and boat action on the Great Lakes. Walleye are a year-round option, peaking in spring near the river mouth and again in fall as they follow baitfish concentrations along the south shore.

Trolling spoons and stick baits on planer boards works the lake's temperature breaks for browns and salmon, targeting the thermocline where baitfish concentrate. In the Genesee, reading current seams is everything — salmon and browns hold in softer water behind boulders and along ledge edges. Spawn sacks, streamers, and egg patterns produce in the river during fall runs, while jigging blade baits along rocky bottom structure near the mouth will pull walleye when lake temperatures drop into the low 50s and fish tighten to deeper structure.

Oswego sits at the mouth of the Oswego River where it drains into Lake Ontario's eastern basin, making it a genuine crossroads for three serious fisheries. In spring, brown trout stage near the river mouth and along rocky nearshore structure before water temps climb. Come late summer, the action shifts to open-water trolling for Chinook and Coho salmon as they begin their pre-spawn staging miles offshore, then progressively push toward the river as fall approaches. Walleye remain a year-round option but peak in spring and fall when they concentrate near river current and transitional bottom structure.

For salmon, trolling spoons and stick baits off planer boards in the 50-to-100-foot range is standard, with depth dictated by where baitfish are suspended on the fish finder. Brown trout often respond to smaller spoons worked shallower, especially when surface temps are in the mid-50s. Walleye hold along current seams near the river mouth and over gravel-to-sand transitions — night jigging and bottom-bouncing with soft plastics or live bait produces well when daytime pressure is high. Watching water temperature breaks and the direction of river flow will consistently put you on fish more reliably than any single lure choice.

The Salmon River is a true four-season fishery. Chinook salmon push in hard during early fall, running big numbers through the lower and middle sections before coho follow a few weeks behind, typically smaller but scrappy and willing to bite. Once the salmon runs wind down and water cools, steelhead take center stage and carry the fishery clear through winter and into spring — these fish are the backbone of what keeps guides busy during the coldest months. Brown trout inhabit the system year-round, staging near salmon redds in fall to feed on loose eggs, then holding in deeper runs and pools through winter.

For salmon, concentrate on the deeper slots and tail-outs of pools where fish rest during their upstream push. Egg sacs, beads, and bright spoons or spinners all produce, with skein patterns working well on fresh-run fish. Steelhead favor faster seams and the edges of current breaks — swing soft hackles and Woolly Buggers or dead-drift natural-colored egg patterns under a float. Watch the USGS gauge closely: flows between roughly 300 and 600 cfs typically fish best, giving you manageable wading and fish that aren't blowing through. Cold snaps that drop water temperature into the low 40s will slow steelhead metabolism, so slow your presentation down and get it deep.

Lake Erie's central basin out of Cleveland is one of the best inland fisheries in the country, and it stays productive across seasons if you follow the fish. Spring kicks off with walleye running shallow along the nearshore reefs and rock structures as water temps climb through the 40s and 50s — these fish are aggressive and staging after the spawn. Summer pushes walleye deeper into the thermocline, often 25 to 40 feet over open basin flats, while yellow perch school up over soft bottom and smallmouth bass absolutely light up the rocky structure and boulder fields closer to shore. Fall brings a second walleye push shallow as temps drop again.

For walleye, trolling stick baits and deep-diving crankbaits along temperature breaks is the workhorse approach all season; watch your sonar for the thermocline and troll just above the fish. When walleye stack on specific reefs, casting jigs tipped with paddle tails or jigging vertically at anchor produces well. Yellow perch respond to small jigging spoons and live minnows fished close to bottom — locate a school and stay tight to them. Smallmouth on Erie's central basin love rocky points and underwater ledges; tube jigs and drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics in clear water are your best bets.

Toledo sits at the western basin of Lake Erie, one of the most productive walleye fisheries in North America, and the Maumee River feeding it draws some of the largest walleye runs in the Midwest every spring. When water temps climb into the low 40s, walleye flood the Maumee in enormous numbers to spawn over the rocky shoals. White bass follow closely behind on a similar thermal trigger, often staging near the river mouth before pushing upriver themselves. Summer shifts fishing back to open-water Erie, where suspended walleye roam offshore, and white bass school aggressively around structure and baitfish concentrations.

For spring Maumee walleye, wading the rocky shallows and casting quarter-ounce jigs tipped with curl-tail grubs or live minnows into the current seams is the standard approach. Work downstream edges of boulders where fish hold out of the main push. As the river drops and clears post-spawn, fish move toward the mouth. Summer Erie walleye respond well to trolled crankbaits and spinner rigs pulled over humps and transition lines between 18 and 30 feet. White bass pile onto breaking baitfish schools and hit small swimbaits and inline spinners retrieved quickly near the surface.

Lake Superior and the Duluth harbor offer a genuine mixed bag depending on the season. Lake trout are available year-round in the cold, deep water off the breakwalls and along the rocky structure that drops sharply just outside the harbor mouth. Salmon — primarily coho and chinook — push into the harbor and nearby river mouths during fall staging runs, making late summer through October some of the most exciting fishing of the year. Walleye tend to concentrate in the harbor itself, especially near current breaks and the channel edges where warmer, shallower water meets the main lake.

For lake trout, work deep with jigging spoons or tube jigs tipped with a smelt strip when the thermocline drops in summer, targeting 80 to 150 feet. Salmon respond well to trolling spoons and stick baits along temperature breaks — watch for that 50 to 55 degree surface layer and fish the edges hard. Walleye in the harbor bite best at dawn and dusk; slow-roll a paddle-tail swimbait or drift a live shiner along deeper channel edges and near any structure that creates current seams. Dropping water temperatures in fall consistently trigger the best bites across all three species.

Lake Superior off Marquette offers a genuine mixed bag through the year. Lake trout are the backbone of the fishery and hold year-round in the cold, deep water Superior is known for — think 80 to 150 feet once summer sets in. Chinook and coho salmon show up as surface temperatures drop in late summer into fall, staging near river mouths before pushing toward tributary streams. Smallmouth bass are the surprise for many visitors, moving into the rocky nearshore structure through summer and fishing well until water temperatures slide below 50 degrees in autumn.

For lakers, deep jigging with tube jigs or swimbaits in natural smelt and cisco colors produces consistently — vertical presentation matters more than horizontal here. When salmon are active near the surface, spoons and stick baits trolled in the upper water column around thermal breaks and current edges will find fish. Smallmouth congregate around the abundant cobble and boulder fields close to shore, and a simple drop-shot or finesse jig worked slowly through that structure is hard to beat. Pay attention to surface temperature when trolling — baitfish and the salmon chasing them bunch up along temperature breaks, so a basic thermometer or fish finder with temp readout earns its keep on this water.

Lake Lanier is a deep, clear highland reservoir on the upper Chattahoochee, and that clarity shapes everything. Spotted bass dominate the mid-lake structure year-round, while largemouth push shallower into creek arm pockets during spring prespawn and again in fall. Striped bass are the big draw — Lanier's open-water stripers school aggressively and chase threadfin and gizzard shad on the main lake, peaking in spring and again when surface temps drop into the low 60s in fall. Crappie stack on submerged timber and dock pilings in the creek arms, most reliably in spring and late fall when they move shallow to feed.

For spots and largemouth, finesse tactics earn bites in Lanier's gin-clear water — drop shots, shaky heads, and small swimbaits fished on main-lake points and humps in 15 to 30 feet cover most situations. When surface temps push above 80 degrees in summer, fish go deep and the bite tightens; a swimbait or umbrella rig worked over submerged creek channels finds both bass and roaming stripers. Live shad under a balloon or heavy jigging spoons worked vertically over baitfish schools on the graph are the most consistent striper producers. For crappie, small tube jigs or live minnows around dock posts in 8 to 15 feet are reliable whenever you find fish stacked on the graph.

Lake Hartwell sits on the Georgia-South Carolina border and runs cool and clear with significant depth swings, which drives very different seasonal patterns depending on what you're chasing. Largemouth and spotted bass both thrive here, but the spots tend to push deeper and relate tighter to main-lake structure, especially in summer heat. Striped bass follow shad schools through the main lake channel and the Savannah River and Tugaloo River arms, running aggressive in spring and fall when water temps sit between 58 and 68 degrees. Crappie gang up on brush piles and submerged timber in late winter through early spring, making them very catchable before bass season heats up.

For bass, target the rocky points, submerged roadbeds, and clay banks with shaky heads, drop shots, and swimbaits when water clarity is high, and switch to spinnerbaits or crankbaits around docks and shallow flats during the spring spawn. Striper anglers should troll umbrella rigs or large swimbaits along the main river channels and watch the thermocline on a graph, keeping presentations above it in summer. Crappie fishing is a vertical game, working small jigs or minnows tight to submerged structure in 10 to 20 feet. As water temperature rises past 75 degrees, bass and crappie both go deeper, so let your electronics lead the way.

Lake Marion is one of the Southeast's most productive shallow-water fisheries, built around a flooded timber and stump-field ecosystem that suits multiple species year-round. Largemouth bass draw serious pressure from late winter through spring spawn, when fish push onto flooded cypress flats and staghorn structure in water as shallow as two feet. Crappie stack in the standing timber during the same pre-spawn window, making spring a two-species opportunity. Catfish, particularly blue and channel cats, fish well through summer heat when bass and crappie slow, then blue cats feed aggressively again in fall as baitfish school up.

For bass, work spinnerbaits and soft-plastic crawfish through cypress knees and laydown timber in the upper lake's murky, tannic water. When water temps climb into the mid-60s, topwater around emergent stumps at first light produces well. Crappie hold tight to submerged timber — a jig-and-minnow combo fished vertically into the canopy, not beside it, is the difference-maker here. Watch flow from the Santee Canal tailrace: increased current pulls catfish and bass into creek-channel edges, and a temperature drop of even a few degrees in fall triggers feeding flurries across all three species.

Lake Murray is a large Midlands reservoir where largemouth bass, striped bass, and crappie are the primary draws. Largemouth fishing peaks in spring when fish move shallow to spawn around coves, points, and flooded timber along the upper lake arms. Stripers stack up in deeper water during summer's heat and push bait to the surface in fall — those topwater blitzes are worth timing your trip around. Crappie fishing is strong through winter and early spring when fish suspend near structure in 12 to 20 feet of water.

Come summer, watch your surface temperature gauge and target stripers in the thermocline, typically 20 to 35 feet down, using live herring or umbrella rigs near main-lake humps and the dam area. For largemouth, work laydowns and dock edges with swimbaits or Texas-rigged plastics as water warms. Crappie respond well to small jigs and minnows fished vertically around bridge pilings and standing timber. In fall, follow the shad migrations toward the upper creek arms — both largemouth and stripers will be close behind.

Lake Norman is a large piedmont reservoir on the Catawba River, and that river-channel backbone shapes everything. Largemouth bass dominate the shallow coves and shoreline structure, while spotted bass tend to run deeper along main-lake points and channel edges. Striped bass thrive here thanks to stocked populations and the lake's depth, chasing threadfin and gizzard shad year-round. Spring pushes all three species shallow as water climbs through the mid-50s into the 60s. Summer heat drives largemouth into shade and cover at dawn and dusk, sends spots deep, and pulls stripers down to the thermocline. Fall is the prime striper season as shad schools tighten on the surface.

For largemouth, work laydowns, docks, and creek-cove transitions with Texas-rigged plastics and swim jigs. Spotted bass respond well to drop-shots and finesse shaky heads on main-lake points in 15 to 25 feet. Stripers are a shad-matching game — live threadfin under a float when you find them feeding on top, or deep-jigged umbrella rigs when the thermocline pushes them down in summer. Watch surface temperature carefully: once it climbs above 80 degrees, concentrate striper efforts near the deeper river channel where cooler, oxygenated water holds. In fall, follow diving birds to locate breaking stripers.

Kerr Reservoir is a big, sprawling impoundment straddling the Virginia-North Carolina line, and it fishes very differently depending on the season. Spring is the prime window — striped bass stage in the upper arms near the Roanoke River tributaries as water temperatures climb through the 50s, while largemouth move shallow into coves and flooded timber to spawn. Crappie school tight to brush piles and dock pilings during this same warming period and are often the most reliable bite of the year. Summer pushes stripers deep following baitfish schools and cooler thermoclines, while fall triggers aggressive feeding runs as water cools again.

For stripers, watch the surface for baitfish activity and work topwaters or swimbaits early in low-light conditions, then drop jigging spoons down to suspended fish as the sun rises. Largemouth key on submerged timber, laydowns, and chunk-rock points — creature baits and Texas-rigged plastics outperform most everything in warmer months, while lipless crankbaits cover water efficiently in early spring. Crappie here respond well to small jigs tipped with minnows, especially when you slow down and fish vertically in 10 to 20 feet around visible structure. Pay attention to current — when generation at the dam picks up, baitfish concentrate and stripers often turn on.

Smith Mountain Lake is a deep, clear reservoir in the Blue Ridge foothills that holds striped bass, largemouth bass, and crappie as its primary draws. Stripers run big here and follow shad schools throughout the water column, becoming most accessible in spring when they push into shallower creek arms and again in fall when cooling water pulls them toward main-lake points. Largemouth fishing peaks in spring around shallow coves with laydowns and dock structure, then shifts deep through summer. Crappie stack on brush piles and submerged timber in spring and fall, moving to deeper structure during summer's heat.

Water temperature is your most reliable guide on this lake. Stripers are most aggressive when surface temps are in the 58-68 degree range, and live gizzard shad or umbrella rigs worked along main-lake points and channel edges near the dam are consistently productive. For largemouth, target the rocky points and dock pilings with swimbaits or Texas-rigged plastics, working deeper as temperatures climb past 75 degrees. Crappie respond well to slow-rolled jigs or live minnows suspended under a slip-float near any submerged wood you can mark on your sonar.

Chickamauga Lake, a Tennessee River impoundment managed by TVA, is best known for producing trophy largemouth bass along with excellent crappie fishing throughout the year. Spring is the prime season for both — largemouth push shallow into the abundant milfoil, hydrilla, and flooded timber as water temps climb through the 58–68 degree range, while crappie stack on the same shallow brush and dock pilings to spawn. Summer heat pushes both species deeper or into shaded cover, and fall brings a strong second bite as baitfish schools concentrate and bass aggressively feed before winter.

In cooler months, focus crappie efforts on deeper brush piles and channel edges using small jigs or live minnows fished vertically. Spring largemouth respond well to bladed jigs, swimbaits, and soft plastics worked through the hydrilla mats and laydowns that define Chickamauga's character. When TVA is generating heavy flow through the dam, bass often position behind current breaks and points rather than in open flats. Watch water temperature closely — that 60-degree threshold in spring is your trigger to move shallow and stay there.

Pickwick Lake sits on the Tennessee River and draws serious attention because of its diversity. Smallmouth are the headliners, thriving in the rocky shoal areas and ledges that characterize this tailwater system. Largemouth hold more in the back of pockets, coves, and timber. Spring brings both species shallow as water temps climb through the 55-to-65-degree range, triggering pre-spawn staging on main-river ledges and secondary points. Summer pushes fish deep onto current-swept ledges in 15 to 25 feet. Fall pulls them back shallow as shad migrate, and winter concentrates everything on deep structure near the main channel.

For smallmouth, focus on rocky main-lake points and current seams using swimbait, finesse football jigs, and drop shots with crawfish or baitfish profiles. Largemouth respond to soft plastic creature baits worked through wood cover and grass pockets. Watch your electronics for baitfish schools stacked over ledges in summer — that's where you position. Current flow from dam generation matters enormously here; smallmouth especially activate when water moves. Catfish are a legitimate target, particularly flatheads and blues staging below current breaks, where cut shad and live bait fished on the bottom after dark consistently produces.

Old Hickory Lake on the Cumberland River system fishes quite differently depending on the season, and knowing what runs when makes all the difference. Largemouth dominate the shallow creek arms and flooded timber from spring through early summer, while smallmouth set up on rocky points and the harder substrate near the main channel. Summer heat pushes catfish activity into low-light windows, and flatheads stack in deeper holes near current breaks. Fall turnover fires up panfish and walleye along channel edges, and winter brings trout stocked in cooler tailwater sections near the dam face.

Water temperature and Cumberland River flow are your real guides here. When generation is running, baitfish concentrate below current breaks and walleye and smallmouth feed aggressively — crankbaits and swimbaits worked along those seams pay off. Largemouth favor laydowns and dock pilings in the upper creek arms; Texas-rigged plastics and bladed jigs cover both. Chain pickerel lurk in the shallower, brushy backwaters year-round and hit spinnerbaits and soft jerkbaits hard. For catfish, cut shad drifted near channel ledges after dark rarely disappoints. Watch the gauges — rising water moves fish shallower, falling water pulls them back to main-lake structure fast.

Wheeler Lake is a Tennessee River impoundment that draws serious bass anglers, with largemouth dominating the shallower, more vegetated creek arms and smallmouth showing up along the rocky, current-swept main channel structure. Spring is prime time for both species as they stage on points and ledges before moving shallow to spawn. Catfish — channel, blue, and flathead — thrive here year-round, with blue cats especially productive during summer and fall. Panfish like crappie and bluegill load up around brush piles and bridge pilings from spring through early summer. Walleye and chain pickerel exist in the system but are incidental catches rather than reliable targets, and Wheeler does not support a trout fishery in its warm, lowland waters.

For bass, the ledge bite along the main river channel is Wheeler's signature pattern once summer heat pushes fish deep — dragging big football jigs, deep-diving crankbaits, or Carolina-rigged creatures over submerged creek channel intersections consistently produces. Watch your electronics for baitfish suspended over structure in the 15-to-25-foot range. In spring, focus on chunk rock banks and flooded willows with jerkbaits and swimbaits when water temps climb into the low 60s. Catfish anglers work current seams below the dam using cut shad or live bream on the bottom. For crappie, vertical jigging small tube jigs around woody structure in 8 to 15 feet is reliable whenever water clarity improves after rain events settle out.

Beaver Lake is a deep, clear Ozark reservoir on the upper White River system, and that clarity shapes everything. Largemouth hold tight to the rocky bluff transitions and submerged timber in the upper arms, while smallmouth thrive on the main-lake gravel points and chunk-rock banks where the water stays coldest. Striped bass roam the main channel and open water, chasing shad schools heavily in fall and again in late spring. Spring is the most productive overall season, with all three species moving shallow as water climbs through the 55 to 65 degree range.

For largemouth and smallmouth, work finesse setups like drop shots or ned rigs along rocky transitions in 8 to 20 feet when fish are post-frontal or sluggish. Swimbaits and crankbaits matched to the abundant threadfin shad produce well on points during the fall feeding push. Stripers follow bait on your graph into the main-lake depths mid-summer and respond to live shad or heavy jigging spoons fished vertically. Pay attention to thermocline depth in summer, as both smallmouth and stripers stack just above it rather than scattering throughout the water column.

Grand Lake o' the Cherokees is a big, timber-studded reservoir in northeast Oklahoma that holds solid populations of largemouth and spotted bass along with excellent crappie fishing year-round. Spring is the peak season across the board — bass push shallow to spawn in the coves and along flooded timber edges when water temps climb into the mid-60s, and crappie stack up around brush piles and submerged wood in 8 to 15 feet. Summer heat pushes bass deeper and toward main-lake structure, while crappie suspend near deeper brush. Fall triggers a reliable feeding binge as shad schools move shallow, and winter crappie fishing on vertical structure can be outstanding.

Read the timber. Grand Lake's flooded standing timber and laydowns are the key fish-holding features across all seasons. In spring, work shallow wood with Texas-rigged plastics, jigs, and spinnerbaits for bass. For crappie, slow-roll or spider-rig minnows and small jigs through brush in 10 to 20 feet. In summer, target main-lake points and deeper timber edges with deep-diving crankbaits or drop-shots. Pay attention to water clarity near the Neosho River arm — after heavy rains that arm muddies quickly, pushing fish toward cleaner mid-lake areas where reaction baits like chartreuse crankbaits and spinnerbaits shine.

Lake Texoma is a striper factory, and those fish are the main draw for most serious anglers on this reservoir. Spring through early summer, striped bass chase shad schools aggressively near the surface, making topwater action explosive around points and channel edges. As summer heat sets in, fish move deeper and suspend over main-lake structure, requiring downriggers or deep jigging. Fall triggers another feeding binge as stripers corral shad in open water. Crappie stack on brush piles and flooded timber through spring and again in fall, while catfish — channel and blue — stay productive year-round, peaking in summer near current-washed flats.

For stripers, watch water temperature around 65 to 72 degrees for peak surface activity; live shad is the gold standard, but white bucktail jigs and swimbaits work well over channel drops. Crappie respond to small tube jigs and minnows fished vertically in 10 to 20 feet near submerged structure. When the Red River arm has current pushing through, catfish congregate in transition zones where current slows, and cut shad or fresh chicken liver on the bottom gets bites fast. On calm mornings, birdwork over open water signals feeding stripers worth chasing hard.

Sam Rayburn is one of East Texas's premier fisheries, built around largemouth bass and crappie as the primary draws. Bass fishing peaks in late winter through spring when fish push shallow into the flooded timber, brush, and grass edges to spawn. Summer heat sends bass deep along submerged creek channel ledges and timber lines, where they school and can be located with electronics. Fall brings a second feed when cooling water temps pull both baitfish and bass back shallow. Crappie follow a similar rhythm, concentrating around standing timber in winter and spring before scattering to deeper structure through the heat.

For bass, work lipless crankbaits and swimbaits over submerged grass flats in spring, then transition to deep-diving crankbaits and Carolina rigs along creek channels in summer. Crappie respond well to small jigs and live minnows suspended under floats near standing timber year-round. Rayburn's stained water favors chartreuse, white, and natural shad colors. Watch your depth finder for baitfish concentrations, especially shad, and your fish will be close. During drawdown periods, bass often stack at the mouths of creek channels where moving water concentrates forage.

Lake Conroe is primarily a largemouth bass fishery, and those fish are the main draw year-round. Largemouth push shallow into standing timber and creek arms during the spring spawn, then pull back to deeper brush piles and channel edges through the heat of summer. Catfish — both blues and channels — are abundant and active after dark in warmer months, while crappie and bluegill hold tight to submerged structure nearly all year. Conroe does not support wild trout, walleye, smallmouth bass, or chain pickerel in any meaningful way, so anglers targeting those species should look elsewhere.

For largemouth, focus your time in the creek arms on the lake's upper end, where shallow timber, laydowns, and hydrilla edges concentrate fish. Texas-rigged soft plastics, swim jigs, and spinnerbaits cover water effectively early in the year, while finesse techniques like drop shots and shaky heads produce when fish suspend over deeper brush in summer. Watch water temperature closely — bass activity picks up significantly when surface temps climb into the low 60s in late winter and early spring, triggering the pre-spawn push shoreward. For catfish, cut shad fished on bottom near channel bends after sunset is hard to beat, and crappie stack on submerged brush in 10 to 18 feet.

Lake Minnetonka is a sprawling metro fishery with deep, connected bays that produce quality walleye, largemouth and smallmouth bass, and the occasional musky. Walleye fishing shines in early spring when fish stage on rocky points and gravel transitions before the spawn, then pulls back during summer heat before rebounding on main-lake structure in fall. Largemouth dominate the weedy, shallow bays like those on the north end, peaking in summer over cabbage beds, while smallmouth favor harder bottom and deeper rocky humps. Musky action builds through summer and peaks dramatically in fall when water temps drop into the low 50s.

Work walleye at dawn and dusk with jig-and-minnow combinations along inside weed edges and main-lake mud flats in 18 to 28 feet. Largemouth respond well to flipping heavy Texas-rigged plastics into thick coontail and cabbage, while smallmouth on rock piles take drop-shot rigs and tube jigs. Musky anglers should cover water efficiently with large bucktails and glide baits, focusing on weedy bays in summer and transitioning to open main-lake points as surface temps cool in autumn. Wind-blown shorelines consistently push baitfish and draw active predators.

Leech Lake is one of Minnesota's premier inland fisheries, built around walleye, muskie, and jumbo perch. Walleye are the main draw, with spring post-spawn fish staging on gravel points and rocky shorelines as water temps climb through the low 50s. Summer pushes walleye deeper onto the main-lake humps and mid-depth flats. Muskie follow a similar pattern, hunting weed edges and open-water transitions from summer through the fall cooling period. Perch school tight to deeper soft-bottom basins most of the year, with fall producing some of the biggest fish.

For walleye, slip-sinker rigs with live leeches or crawlers work well over rock and gravel structure, while jig-and-minnow combinations shine in cooler water. Watch for walleye moving shallow during low-light feeding windows on windy, wave-washed points. Muskie respond well to large bucktails and glide baits worked along the outside edges of cabbage weed beds, especially as water temps drop into the low 60s in fall. Perch fishing means anchoring over deeper basin mud and working small jigs or dropper rigs tipped with minnows.

Lake Winnebago is a sprawling, shallow inland sea where walleye, white bass, and lake sturgeon are the main draws. Walleye run hard in early spring when ice clears and water temps climb through the low 40s, then scatter across the basin through summer before tightening back up on structure in fall. White bass go on a feeding frenzy during their spring run up the Fox and Wolf Rivers, and again in late summer when they school aggressively on the surface. Sturgeon are a unique trophy opportunity here, traditionally targeted through the ice in February during the state-regulated spearing season.

For walleye, focus on the hard-bottom reefs and rocky points scattered across the lake, especially at dawn and dusk using jig-and-minnow rigs or shallow-diving cranks in natural shad patterns. When water temps push past 65 degrees, go deeper on structure or fish weed edges after dark. White bass will stack behind current breaks where tributaries push baitfish into the main lake — cast small white jigs or inline spinners and work them fast. Sturgeon during the ice season hold on sandy flats; anglers position decoys near the bottom to lure them into spearing range under darkhouses.

Lake Sakakawea is a massive Missouri River reservoir running through western North Dakota, and the three species worth chasing here are walleye, smallmouth bass, and landlocked chinook salmon. Walleye dominate the fishing from ice-out through early summer and again in fall, when cooling water pulls them shallow onto rocky points and windswept shorelines. Smallmouth bass concentrate around the many rocky arms and boulder fields during summer warmth. Salmon fishing picks up in colder water, particularly in spring and late fall when they run deeper and relate to the thermocline.

For walleye, target windblown rock piles and points with jig-and-minnow rigs or bottom bouncers trailing spinners tipped with nightcrawlers. Smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and crankbaits worked along chunk rock. Salmon run deep and respond to trolled spoons and stick baits pulled behind planer boards once surface temperatures drop into the low fifties or colder. Watch water temperature closely — walleye and smallmouth move shallow as water warms through the fifties into the sixties, then push to deeper adjacent structure during summer peaks. Read current seams near submerged creek channels, which concentrate baitfish and pull all three species into predictable feeding lanes.

Lake Oahe is primarily a walleye fishery, but the Missouri River reservoir also holds strong populations of smallmouth bass and a solid chinook salmon run in its upper reaches near the dam tailwater. Walleye fishing peaks in spring when fish push into the shallower bays and rocky points to spawn, then transitions to deeper structure through summer. Smallmouth follow a similar shallow-to-deep pattern and are most aggressive in late spring and early fall. Salmon stack near the dam during cooler months and respond well to trolling deeper in summer when surface temps climb.

For walleye, jig-and-minnow combinations worked along submerged river channel edges and rocky humps are consistently productive, especially where bottom composition transitions from mud to gravel. Water temperature is your best guide: walleye feed most aggressively in the 50-65 degree range, and salmon push shallower as temps cool into fall. Smallmouth relate tightly to rocky shoreline structure and respond well to tube jigs and crankbaits. Watch for wind-driven current pushing baitfish against points, as both walleye and smallmouth concentrate on the upwind side of structure during those conditions.

Table Rock is a clear Ozark impoundment with dramatic depth changes, and it supports a genuine three-species bass fishery. Largemouth dominate the upper creek arms and shallower flats with timber, while smallmouth favor the main lake's rocky points and gravel transitions, and spotted bass hold in between, often suspending over deep structure near channel ledges. Spring is the prime season as all three species push shallow to spawn on rock and gravel from the mid-lake down toward the dam. Summer stratification pushes fish deeper or into shaded timber during midday. Fall triggers aggressive feeding along baitfish schools on main-lake points before winter slows everything to a crawl on deep channel breaks.

Watch water temperature closely since the upper end warms earlier in spring, meaning spotted and largemouth action starts there weeks before the clearer, slower-warming main lake heats up for smallmouth. Work rocky main-lake points with drop-shot rigs, tube jigs, and shaky heads for smallmouth and spots when temperatures climb into the low 60s. Swimbaits and crankbaits matching shad patterns produce well on ledge structure through summer. In the creek arms, flipping jigs and Texas-rigged creature baits around submerged timber targets largemouth. The lake's clarity demands lighter fluorocarbon and finesse presentations more often than not.

Flaming Gorge is built around three main targets, each with distinct seasonal windows. Lake trout dominate winter and early spring when surface temps drop into the low 40s and lakers cruise the upper water column — this is the best time to find big fish in accessible depths. As summer heat pushes in, lakers drop to 60–120 feet and require serious vertical work. Kokanee are a warm-weather obsession here, typically staging in the 40–60 foot range through summer before their fall spawning run draws crowds. Smallmouth bass offer the most accessible fishing, peaking in late spring and early summer around the rocky canyon arms when water temps hit the mid-50s to low 60s.

For lakers, vertical jigging tube jigs or large swimbaits over submerged points and canyon walls produces well, and trolling deep-diving plugs along thermal breaks is reliable in summer. Kokanee respond best to small dodgers trailing wedding rings or small spindles tipped with shoepeg corn, trolled at precise depth once you mark fish on your sonar — they school tight, so depth matters enormously. Smallmouth hold in the rocky canyon sections, especially near submerged structure where current once carved the old river channel. Work tube jigs and drop shots along steep rocky banks in the morning. Water clarity here is excellent, so lighter line and natural presentations consistently outperform heavier gear.

Clear Lake is one of California's premier bass fisheries, and largemouth are the main draw year-round. Spring brings the best action as bass move shallow into tule margins and rocky points to spawn when water temps climb into the low 60s. Crappie stack up near submerged structure and dock pilings during the same warming period, making spring a two-for-one opportunity. Summer heat pushes catfish into deeper basin areas at night, while bass retreat to shade under floating mats of vegetation. Fall cooling triggers another strong topwater bite for bass before winter slows everything down.

For bass, work the tule edges with frogs and punching rigs through the thick mat cover that defines much of the lake's shoreline. Crappie respond well to small tube jigs and minnows fished vertically around any submerged wood or pier structure. Catfish take cut bait or chicken liver fished on the bottom in deeper water after dark. Watch surface temps closely — once summer pushes past the mid-70s, fish go deep or nocturnal. The lake's clarity varies with algae conditions, so in murky water downsize to slower presentations and use rattles or bright colors to help fish locate your offering.

Shasta Lake is a serious year-round fishery built around spotted bass, largemouth bass, and kokanee-stocked rainbow trout. Spots are the bread-and-butter species here and stay active even through cold months when largemouth slow down. Spring brings both bass species shallow into the coves and rocky points to spawn, making it the most exciting topwater and sight-fishing window. Summer pushes fish deep as surface temps climb into the mid-70s, while fall cooling triggers aggressive feeding and some of the best big-bass action of the year.

Shasta's dramatic canyon arms, submerged timber, and rock bluff walls are your roadmap. In warmer months, target spotted bass along steep rocky banks in 20 to 40 feet using drop shots, shaky heads, or swimbait. Largemouth stack in timber and brush pockets in flatter cove areas — punch matted cover or flip soft plastics tight to structure. Trout suspend in the thermocline; troll flasher-and-worm rigs or spoons in the upper third of that cold layer. When the lake drops and exposes new structure in fall, those freshly submerged points concentrate fish fast.

Lake Berryessa holds a solid mix of largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, and rainbow trout, each following distinct seasonal rhythms shaped by this reservoir's steep canyon arms and dramatic water-level swings. Largemouth dominate the shallows from late winter through spring spawn, then push deeper into summer as surface temps climb into the upper 70s. Smallmouth tend to favor the rockier, more exposed points and transition edges year-round. Trout fishing peaks in the cooler months, roughly fall through early spring, when surface temps drop into the comfortable range and fish roam the upper water column near creek inflows.

For bass, target submerged brush and rocky points with drop shots, swimbaits, or Texas-rigged plastics, working depth transitions where structure meets open water. A temperature gauge helps enormously here because fish compress into narrow depth bands during summer stratification. Trout respond well to trolled flashers paired with nightcrawlers or small spoons along the main lake basin during cool months. When reservoir levels are higher, bass push into flooded vegetation and willows along the coves, so keep moving until you locate active fish rather than anchoring on dead water.

Lake Mead holds striped bass, largemouth bass, and channel catfish, and the fishing shifts dramatically with the desert seasons. Stripers are the heartbeat of this fishery — in spring they school aggressively near canyon walls and points as water temps climb into the mid-60s, making them genuinely easy to locate. Summer pushes largemouth deep into shaded rocky structure or sparse vegetation in the backs of coves, while stripers follow threadfin shad schools into open water. By fall both species feed heavily before cooling temperatures slow metabolism heading into winter, when catfish become more consistent targets along soft muddy flats.

For stripers, watch your sonar for suspended shad schools between 20 and 50 feet and work live threadfin, swimbaits, or blade baits through the column. Largemouth respond well to drop-shots and finesse plastics crawled along rocky transitions and submerged ledges, especially when surface temps spike above 80 degrees and fish go lethargic. Catfish hold in deeper basin areas and near inflows after rains, where cut shad or chicken liver fished on the bottom produces consistently. Water clarity at Mead is typically excellent, so long leaders and natural presentations matter more here than in stained reservoirs.

The Bighorn below Yellowtail Dam is tailwater fishing at its finest, with wild brown and rainbow trout thriving year-round in cold, clear, nutrient-rich flows. Spring brings active feeding as flows stabilize after snowmelt adjustments, summer rewards early-morning and evening sessions when surface temperatures climb, fall triggers aggressive pre-spawn behavior in browns, and winter fishing stays surprisingly productive given the dam-regulated temperature buffer.

Fish hold tight to the weed beds that blanket the Bighorn's flat limestone bottom — these are your primary feeding zones. Small scuds, sowbugs, and midges in natural olive, tan, and gray are essential here; match the hatch precisely because these trout are educated. Watch your flows: when releases increase, fish stack behind structure and gravel ledges. Nymphing under an indicator through seams adjacent to weed edges is consistently productive. Rising fish in fall often respond well to dry-dropper rigs targeting PMD and caddis hatches.

The San Juan below Navajo Dam is tailwater fishery built around trophy rainbow and brown trout, with cold, clear releases keeping fish active year-round. Winter often produces some of the best dry-fly fishing you'll find anywhere, since consistent flows and midge hatches bring big fish to the surface even in cold months. Spring runoff rarely affects this stretch the way it hammers free-stone rivers, so expect reliable conditions. Fall triggers brown trout to move aggressively as spawning instincts kick in, making them more catchable but also more vulnerable — handle them with care.

Focus your effort in the first few miles below the dam where cold water concentration holds the most fish. Midges are the bread-and-butter pattern here year-round — tiny Zebra Midges and RS2s in sizes 22 through 26 consistently produce. Watch for pod-feeding fish in slower seams along current edges and behind submerged boulders. When flows spike, trout push tight to the banks. Match your tippet to the clarity — this water runs gin-clear, so fine tippet and precise presentations matter more than almost anywhere else you'll fish.

Oneida Lake is one of New York's premier walleye fisheries, and that reputation drives most of the traffic here. Walleye are the star attraction, running aggressive feeding patterns in spring as water temps climb through the low 50s, then pulling back to deeper structure and lower-light windows through summer. Smallmouth bass thrive along the rocky reefs and gravel points scattered across the lake, with action peaking in late spring and again in fall. Yellow perch round out the fishery and can be found schooling in shallower bays in spring and over deeper soft-bottom areas as temperatures drop in autumn.

For walleye, work the shallow rock reefs and sandy flats at dawn and dusk using spinner rigs tipped with nightcrawlers or soft plastic paddle tails on jigs. Trolling stick baits along depth transitions between 8 and 18 feet is consistently productive when fish scatter mid-lake in summer. Smallmouth hold tight to rocky points and submerged humps, responding well to tube jigs and drop-shot rigs. Perch concentrate in schools, so if you mark fish on a graph, drop a small jigging spoon or live minnow straight down. Water clarity on Oneida is historically affected by zebra mussels, so expect fish to use structure and depth more than vegetation for cover.

Cayuga Lake runs deep and cold — over 400 feet in places — which makes it prime water for lake trout year-round and landlocked salmon from fall through early spring. Lakers hold in the thermocline during summer, typically suspended between 60 and 100 feet as surface temps climb, then move shallower in fall and again under ice. Smallmouth bass dominate the rocky shoals and points along both shorelines from late spring through early fall, peaking when water temps settle in the 65-72 degree range. Landlocked salmon stack near tributary mouths in autumn as they stage for spawning runs.

For lakers, troll spoons or tube jigs deep along the main basin, watching your sonar for the thermocline edge where baitfish concentrate. Landlocked salmon respond well to trolled streamers and small wobbling spoons fished just above the bait schools in spring and fall. Smallmouth reward a methodical approach — work tube baits, drop-shots, or natural crayfish imitations along cobble and boulder structure, especially where depth transitions from 10 to 25 feet. Pay attention to wind-driven current pushing warm surface water toward a shoreline; that temperature edge often positions actively feeding fish.

Lake George is a cold, clear Adirondack lake that rewards anglers who understand its depth and seasonal rhythm. Lake trout dominate the deep basins year-round, but they're most accessible in early spring and late fall when cold water pulls them into the upper water column. Landlocked salmon run shallower structure in spring and again as surface temps drop in autumn, often competing for the same forage. Smallmouth bass thrive in the rocky shoals and boulder fields throughout the warmer months, peaking in activity from late spring through early fall before retreating to deeper haunts.

For lakers, troll deep with lead core or downriggers using smelt-style spoons and stick baits once temperatures push them below the thermocline in summer. Watch your fishfinder for the thermocline break, typically where lakers and salmon stack. Landlocked salmon respond well to smaller spoons and streamers trolled near points and rock ledges during low-light periods. Smallmouth are suckers for drop-shot rigs, tube jigs, and crayfish-imitating plastics worked along submerged boulders and gravelly points. Reading the clear water here is an advantage — on calm mornings you can spot bass holding in the rocks before you even make a cast.

Lake Winnipesaukee is a big-water fishery with real variety. Smallmouth bass own the rocky points and boulder fields in the shallower bays from late spring through fall, going deep once temperatures drop below 50°F. Lake trout and landlocked salmon share the cold, oxygenated depths throughout summer, typically suspending in the 55 to 60°F thermocline, then becoming more accessible near the surface during spring and fall as the water column mixes.

For smallmouth, work tube jigs and drop-shots around submerged boulders and gravel transitions. In summer, target lakers and landlocks by trolling streamer flies or small spoons on lead-core or downriggers once surface temps climb into the upper 60s. Early and late in the season, landlocked salmon chase smelt near the surface at dawn, making light tackle with live smelt or white streamers particularly productive around rocky shorelines and points where baitfish stage.

Sebago is one of Maine's premier coldwater fisheries, built around landlocked salmon and lake trout with solid smallmouth bass action as a bonus. Ice-out kicks off some of the best fishing of the year — salmon move shallow and aggressive as surface temps climb into the low 40s, often stacking near inlet streams and the mouths of feeder rivers. Lake trout hold deeper through summer, suspending along thermoclines in the 50-60 foot range when surface temps push into the 70s, while smallmouth move onto rocky points and gravel shoals from late spring through fall.

For salmon at ice-out, troll streamers like Gray Ghosts or Nine-Threes on lead core or light wire near the surface along windward shorelines. Summer lake trout respond well to jigging tube baits or trolling deep with spoons and sewn smelt once you locate the thermocline on your sonar — watch for that distinct temperature break, usually 40-50 feet down by midsummer. Smallmouth are suckers for soft plastics and small jigs worked along Sebago's rocky structure. Come fall, salmon feed heavily near the surface again as temps cool, and long-lining light tackle streamers can be deadly.

The Yellowstone below Livingston holds a strong mixed bag of wild brown, rainbow, and cutthroat trout, and the fishing changes dramatically through the year. Runoff typically blows out visibility from late spring into early summer, pushing most serious wading until flows drop and clarity returns. Once the river settles, dry fly action picks up fast — this stretch is known for consistent summer hatches of PMDs, caddis, and golden stoneflies. As water cools in fall, big brown trout move shallow and aggressive ahead of their spawn, offering some of the best streamer fishing of the year.

Focus on seams where fast and slow water meet, tailouts of pools, and boulder pockets — all three species use these features. When flows run higher and off-color, fish the inside edges and slower bankside water with weighted nymphs like hare's ears or stonefly patterns. Once temperatures drop into the low 50s Fahrenheit, switch to articulated streamers swung or stripped along undercut banks to target browns. In summer's warmer afternoons, move to faster oxygenated riffles where rainbows and cutthroat stack up, and watch the surface for rising fish before choosing your approach.

The Missouri River tailwater below Holter Dam is a world-class fishery built around wild brown and rainbow trout that grow large on a steady diet of midge larvae, scuds, and aquatic invertebrates. Rainbows tend to be aggressive and hold in faster riffles and runs, while browns favor slower edges, undercut banks, and deeper pools. Spring brings exceptional dry-fly action as Blue-Winged Olives emerge, summer shifts fishing toward early mornings and evenings to avoid heat, fall triggers aggressive pre-spawn behavior from brown trout, and winter rewards patient anglers with midging fish in slower, deeper water.

Watch the dam releases closely — rising flows push fish tight to banks and seams, while stable low flows concentrate trout in classic feeding lanes.
