Nymphing with scud and midge patterns under an indicator accounts for most fish year-round, but don't overlook dry-dropper rigs during afternoon hatches. In clear, cold water below 45 degrees, slow your drift and downsize your tippet. In warmer summer water above 68 degrees, give stressed fish quick releases and target shaded, oxygenated stretches near the canyon walls.

The Madison River around West Yellowstone holds wild trout year-round, with brown and rainbow trout dominating the system. Spring runoff pushes flows high and off-color, making fishing tough, but as flows drop and clear through early summer, dry fly action picks up and continues strong through fall. Late summer brings lower, warmer water, which stresses fish and concentrates them in faster, oxygenated riffles. Fall is prime time as brown trout stage for their spawn, becoming aggressive and willing to take bigger patterns.

Fish hold in current seams where fast water meets slow, behind boulders, and in the soft edges of deeper runs. When water temperatures climb above 68 degrees, move to faster riffles or fish early and late. Hopper-dropper rigs covering broken water produce well through summer, while streamer fishing with articulated patterns triggers aggressive browns in fall. In slower, flatter stretches, technical dry fly and nymph presentations on longer leaders are often necessary. Match elk hair caddis, PMDs, or blue-winged olives to whatever is hatching, and watch surface activity to guide your approach.

The Gallatin and Yellowstone rivers are home to healthy populations of wild trout, primarily brown and rainbow trout, with some cutthroat mixed in on the Yellowstone drainage. Spring runoff through late May or early June pushes flows high and murky, making fishing tough but not impossible near softer edges. As flows drop and clear into summer, dry fly fishing peaks with prolific salmonfly, PMD, and caddis hatches. Fall brings aggressive pre-spawn brown trout behavior, often the best window for bigger fish. Winter slows things down considerably, but midges and small nymphs still produce on milder days.

Fish hold in predictable lies — seams between fast and slow water, behind mid-channel boulders, and in deeper runs and undercut banks. When flows are high, tight-line nymphing with heavy stonefly or worm patterns near the banks is your best bet. In clearer summer conditions, match whatever hatch is active and look for rising fish in the morning and evening. Water temperature matters here: wild trout feed most actively between roughly 50 and 65 degrees, so midday summer heat can push fish deep and lethargic. Watch streamflows closely — local gauge data will tell you whether conditions are fishable before you drive out.

The Beaverhead and Big Hole are tailwater and freestone systems that demand different approaches. The Beaverhead below Clark Canyon Dam runs cold and clear year-round, making it a consistent trophy brown and rainbow trout fishery even in summer heat. The Big Hole fishes best in late spring before runoff peaks, then again in late summer and fall when flows drop and big browns move shallow to feed aggressively ahead of spawning season.

On the Beaverhead, fish hold tight to undercut banks and deep channel edges — nymphing with sow bugs, midge larvae, and small scuds gets results when nothing is rising. The Big Hole rewards dry-fly fishing during salmonfly and golden stone hatches in early summer. Watch water temperature closely on the Big Hole; when it climbs above 65 degrees, fish stress quickly and smart anglers shift to early mornings or take a break entirely. Fall dropping flows concentrate fish in pools and seams — streamer fishing then can move the biggest browns of the year.

The Snake River through Jackson Hole is classic cutthroat country, home to the native Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat trout — a distinct subspecies shaped by this drainage. Spring runoff typically blows the river out with cold, silty water, making fishing tough until flows drop and clarity improves heading into summer. That mid-summer window through early fall is prime time, when cutthroats are active, well-distributed, and feeding aggressively on the surface. As water cools into autumn, fish feed heavily before winter and can stack up in slower, deeper runs.

Read the seams — cutthroats hold along current edges where fast and slow water meet, near undercut banks, and behind mid-channel boulders. In summer, dry flies shine: large attractor patterns like stimulators and parachute adams draw explosive surface eats. When fish aren't looking up, nymphs drifted through deeper slots produce well. Watch water temperature closely; when it climbs into the upper 60s Fahrenheit, fish stress quickly, so focus on early mornings and consider moving to shaded reaches or higher-elevation tributaries. Drift boats cover water efficiently, but wading anglers can do very well working slower side channels.

The North Fork Shoshone and the Bighorn below Thermopolis both hold wild trout worth traveling for, but they fish very differently by season. On the Shoshone, brown and rainbow trout are the primary targets, with spring runoff from snowmelt pushing flows high and off-color through late spring. Fishing improves significantly once flows drop and clear in early summer. The Bighorn tailwater runs colder and clearer year-round, producing consistent wild trout action even through winter when most Wyoming rivers are locked up or blown out.

On the Shoshone, focus on seams behind larger boulders and deep undercut banks where browns ambush prey. Weighted stonefly nymphs and sculpin patterns produce well in heavier water. The Bighorn rewards midge and scud patterns fished deep and slow near the bottom in winter, transitioning to PMD and caddis hatches in warmer months. Watch water temperature closely — wild trout feed most aggressively between roughly 50 and 65 degrees. When flows spike, abandon midstream presentations and work the slower water tight to the bank.

The North Platte through Saratoga holds a strong population of wild brown and rainbow trout, with fishing shifting notably through the year. Rainbows run aggressive in spring when snowmelt cools flows and insects begin hatching. Midsummer can slow midday as water warms, but browns feed heavily at low light. Fall is prime time for big browns staging pre-spawn, often moving into shallower riffles and taking swings hard.

Watch river flows closely — after runoff settles and clarity improves, dry fly action picks up fast. Fish rainbows in seams behind mid-river boulders and in tailouts. Browns favor undercut banks and deeper runs, especially cottonwood-lined stretches. Streamers stripped through those deeper holes produce well in cooler water. When surface temps climb above 68°F, fish deep and early.

The Green River above Fontenelle and the high lakes scattered across the Wind River foothills offer some of Wyoming's best wild trout fishing. Cutthroat dominate the mountain lakes and upper river, with browns and rainbows mixing in through lower stretches. Spring runoff through late June pushes fish tight to banks and slack water. Once flows drop and clear in midsummer, dry fly fishing peaks. By September, cooling water triggers aggressive pre-winter feeding, making it arguably the best window of the year.

On the river, trout hold in seams where fast water meets slow, behind boulders, and at the heads of pools. High-sticking nymphs through pocket water accounts for most fish during runoff, while elk hair caddis and pale morning duns produce well on calm summer evenings. In the lakes, small woolly buggers stripped along drop-offs early morning outfish most anything else. Watch water temperature — when surface temps push into the upper 60s, fish go deep and slow your presentation accordingly.

The Arkansas River through Salida holds strong populations of wild brown and rainbow trout in a freestone tailwater system that fishes differently as seasons shift. Spring runoff pushes flows high and turbid, making fishing tough but not impossible near calmer edges. Once flows drop and clear through early summer, both species become aggressive. Midsummer heat can stress fish, with rainbows especially retreating to faster, oxygenated riffles. Fall triggers the best dry fly action and pre-spawn activity from brown trout, which move more boldly as water temps cool.

Fish hold behind mid-channel boulders, in seams along faster current, and in tailouts below riffles. During runoff and high water, swing streamers through softer inside bends where trout stack to avoid the push. As flows normalize, dead-drifted nymphs like hare's ears and pheasant tails in size 14-18 produce consistently. When surface temps cool into the 50s, watch for caddis and PMD hatches and match them with appropriate dry flies. Wade carefully and read current seams — the fish are usually right where fast meets slow.

The Roaring Fork and Colorado confluence near Glenwood Springs offers some of western Colorado's most productive wild trout water. Browns and rainbows dominate, with the occasional cutthroat showing up in cleaner stretches of the Fork. Spring runoff typically blows out flows through late May into June, but once clarity returns, summer and fall fishing can be exceptional. Browns become increasingly aggressive heading into their fall spawn, and winter low-water conditions concentrate fish in predictable deep pools.

When flows are high and off-color, drift large stonefly nymphs and egg patterns tight to the bank where fish escape current. As water clears and drops, transition to smaller PMD and caddis imitations. Wild trout in these rivers hold along seams between fast and slow water, behind mid-channel boulders, and in tailouts. Watch water temperature closely — fishing slows when temps push above 65 degrees Fahrenheit in summer, and early morning sessions become essential. In winter, slow your nymphing presentations way down through deeper slots where fish stack up conserving energy.

The Gunnison River is a blue-ribbon tailwater fishery where wild trout — primarily brown and rainbow — are the main draw year-round. Spring runoff from snowmelt can blow flows out through late spring, pushing fish tight to banks and eddies. Summer settles the river into ideal conditions, with evening caddis and PMD hatches producing excellent dry-fly action in the canyon stretch. Fall is prime time as big browns move and become aggressive ahead of their spawn, and winter fishing slows but rewards patient nymphing on milder days.

Fish hold behind mid-channel boulders, in tailouts below riffles, and along undercut banks — especially when flows run high. Nymphing with small mayfly and midge patterns under an indicator covers most situations, while streamer fishing with sculpin and leech patterns draws aggressive strikes from larger browns, particularly in fall. Watch water temperature closely: wild trout feed most actively between roughly 45 and 65 degrees. When flows spike, slow your drift and fish softer inside seams where trout conserve energy.

The South Fork stretch of the Rio Grande holds a solid population of wild trout, primarily brown and rainbow trout, with browns being the dominant catch through most reaches. Spring runoff pushes flows high and off-color from snowmelt, making fishing tough through late spring. Once flows drop and clear — typically by early summer — fishing picks up dramatically. Fall is prime time, as brown trout become aggressive ahead of their spawning season and actively feed throughout the day.

Fish hold behind mid-channel boulders, in seam lines where fast and slow water meet, and in deep outside bends where undercut banks offer cover. During summer, nymphs like hare's ear and pheasant tail fished under an indicator produce consistently, while hoppers and elk hair caddis work well on surface during afternoon hatches. In cooler water, slow down your presentation and target deeper pockets. Watch for water clarity — clearer flows mean spookier fish, so drop to lighter tippet and approach runs from downstream.

Henry's Fork is legendary dry-fly water, and trophy rainbow trout are the main draw for serious anglers making the pilgrimage to Island Park. Spring runoff can blow out flows and push fish tight to slower edges and backwater pockets, while summer drop brings the famous technical dry-fly fishing during prolific PMD, Green Drake, and Trico hatches. Fall sees fish feeding aggressively before winter, and cooler water temperatures concentrate larger fish in deeper runs and tailout seams.

Read the water by focusing on foam lines, current seams, and the edges of weed beds where rainbows sip emergers and surface insects. During heavy hatches match the hatch precisely — these fish are pattern-selective and leader-shy, so long fine tippets and accurate presentations matter more than anywhere else. When flows run high or cold, nymphing deep with Pheasant Tails, Copper Johns, and soft-hackles along the bottom of slower runs produces when dry-fly action is tough.

The upper Salmon River near Stanley runs cold and clear through high mountain terrain, and the fishing shifts dramatically through the year. Resident rainbow and cutthroat trout are the year-round backbone here, feeding actively during summer and early fall when aquatic insect hatches are strongest. As fall arrives, chinook salmon push through on their spawning migration, drawing both anglers and the browns that key on loose salmon eggs drifting downstream. Steelhead follow later into the fall and again in spring, giving dedicated anglers another reason to make the drive into the valley.

Trout and steelhead hold in the predictable seams — tailouts of pools, current edges behind boulders, and the slower water along undercut banks. For trout, dry-fly fishing during caddis and PMD hatches can be exceptional in summer, while nymphing with stonefly or midge patterns produces year-round. Egg patterns and small streamers shine during and after salmon season when browns and steelhead stack up below spawning gravel. Watch water temperature closely — trout feed best in that sweet window between 50 and 65 degrees, and when flows drop and clarity increases, you need to go lighter on tippet and approach with patience.

The Deschutes below Pelton Dam is a year-round redband trout fishery, with these native fish active even through winter cold snaps thanks to the tailwater's relatively stable temperatures. Spring and early summer bring consistent dry fly action as pale morning duns and caddis hatches fire up. Steelhead push into the river from late summer through fall, drawing serious swinging anglers from across the region. Summer trout fishing can slow midday but picks back up as evening caddis activity builds.

Redbands stack in the seams along the basalt ledges and in the broken water behind mid-river boulders — look for the transition between fast and slow current. For trout, dead-drifted nymphs under an indicator work well when fish aren't rising, and elk hair caddis or parachute adams patterns shine during surface activity. Steelhead respond well to swung wet flies and spey presentations through the deeper tailouts and runs. Watch river flow carefully — higher flows push fish tight to softer edges, while dropping water concentrates fish in predictable slots. Cooler water temperatures in fall correlate with the best steelhead aggression.

The Rogue River through the Grants Pass stretch is a year-round fishery built around salmon and steelhead. Fall Chinook are the marquee run, pushing through in late summer into autumn when the river begins to cool. Winter steelhead follow, keeping dedicated guides busy through the cold months, while a summer steelhead run gives anglers something to chase during the warmer season. Both species use this section of the Rogue as a highway, so fish are generally moving rather than staging for long.

Because fish are on the move, focus on current breaks, deep slots behind boulders, and tailouts where running fish pause to rest. Drift fishing with roe or sand shrimp covers water efficiently, while side-drifting and back-bouncing excel from a sled when flows are up and turbid. At lower, clearer flows, swinging flies or casting spinners and spoons through tailouts produces well for steelhead. Watch river temperature closely — steelhead activity picks up noticeably when water drops into the upper 40s to mid-50s Fahrenheit, and aggressive feeding slows in warmer summer flows.

The Yakima River near Ellensburg is classic tailwater dry-fly country, and wild trout — primarily rainbows with some browns mixed in — are what draws anglers here year after year. Spring brings good hatches of Blue-Winged Olives during cool, overcast days, and summer sees evening caddis and PMD activity that can produce explosive surface fishing. Fall is often the most productive season overall, with aggressive pre-winter feeding and the added bonus of large brown trout moving and becoming more territorial.

Focus your attention on seam lines where fast water meets slower current, undercut banks, and deep slots behind mid-river boulders — wild trout in this freestone-influenced tailwater hold tight to structure. Drift a nymph rig with a copper john or hare's ear under an indicator through those deeper runs when surface action is slow. When flows are elevated and water temperature drops below 45 degrees, fish slow down and you need to get your presentation nearly on the bottom. Conversely, rising water temperatures into the mid-50s reliably trigger hatch activity and make the Yakima's wild trout far more willing to look up.

The Middle Provo through Heber Valley holds healthy populations of wild brown and rainbow trout, with browns typically running larger and more territorial. Spring runoff pushes fish tight to banks and into slower eddies as flows spike, making fishing tough until water drops and clears in early summer. Summer offers the most consistent dry-fly action, especially in evening hours. Fall is prime time for big browns as they move and feed aggressively ahead of spawning, and winter nymphing can be surprisingly productive when you find slow, deep slots out of the current.

Focus on seam water where fast current meets slow — that's where both species stack up to intercept food. Small nymphs like pheasant tails and hare's ears fished tight to the bottom account for most fish year-round. When water temps climb into the mid-50s and above, watch for surface activity and match the hatch with elk hair caddis or parachute adams. Elevated flows call for heavier split shot and longer leaders; clear low water means downsizing tippet and slowing your approach considerably.

Spring Creek and Penns Creek are classic central Pennsylvania limestone spring creeks, and wild brown trout are the main attraction on both. Spring Creek fishes well year-round thanks to its consistent temperatures, while Penns Creek shines during the famous Green Drake hatch in late spring and again during autumn when big browns become aggressive ahead of spawning season. Both creeks hold a mix of smaller resident fish and larger trout that push into tighter lies when flows warm or drop.

On both waters, wild browns favor undercut banks, deeper pools below riffles, and shaded runs near overhanging vegetation. Matching the hatch with dry flies pays off during emergence windows, but nymphing with caddis and sulphur patterns covers more fish through the day. When flows are higher and cold, streamers stripped through deeper pools can draw aggressive strikes from larger fish. Watch for surface feeding activity as your primary timing cue, and slow down your presentations in clear, low summer flows.

The Beaverkill and Willowemoc are legendary Catskill freestoners where wild brown trout are the main prize, supplemented by stocked browns and rainbows. Spring runoff brings aggressive pre-spawn and post-stocking feeding, making it the most productive window. Summer low water pushes fish into shaded, oxygen-rich riffles and deeper pools, demanding a delicate approach. Fall triggers territorial browns to slash at large streamers ahead of spawning, while winter finds the hardiest anglers nymphing slow tailouts for sluggish but catchable fish.

Watch flow levels closely — both rivers fish best at moderate, clear flows after spring spates subside. During hatches, match the natural closely; Catskill-style dry flies like Cahills and Hendricksons shine here. When fish aren't rising, dead-drift nymphs through seams behind boulders and along undercut banks. In low summer water, downsize tippets and approach carefully from downstream. Streamers worked through deep pools at dusk are hard to beat for bigger wild browns in fall.

The West Branch Delaware below Cannonsville Reservoir is a tailwater fishery, and that changes everything. The cold, controlled releases keep wild brown trout and rainbow trout active well into summer when most freestone streams go slack. Spring brings aggressive pre-spawn browns stacking in riffles, while early summer sees strong rainbow runs as water warms into the mid-50s. By late summer, fish push toward the coldest seams and deep pools near tributary mouths. Fall is prime time for big browns moving on their spawning instinct — the largest fish of the year become vulnerable during this window.

Fish hold in the bucket behind mid-river boulders and along current seams where fast water meets slow. Drift a nymph rig through those transition zones using Pheasant Tails, Hare's Ear patterns, or small midge larvae. Dry fly fishing peaks during Sulphur and Trico hatches — match the size carefully, the fish here are selective. When flows run higher and off-color, switch to streamers stripped across the current for browns holding tight to undercut banks. Watch your thermometer: below 55°F the fish feed aggressively, above 70°F they stress easily — consider resting the water.

The Battenkill is one of Vermont's most storied wild-trout fisheries, drawing anglers specifically for its self-sustaining population of wild brown trout, with brook trout more common in the smaller feeder tributaries above town. Spring runoff pushes flows high and cold, but as water drops and clarity returns, browns become increasingly catchable. Midsummer heat is the great equalizer here — fish go deep and nocturnal when temps climb. Fall is prime time, as cooling water triggers aggressive feeding and browns move ahead of spawning.

Reading water temperature is critical on the Battenkill — aim for flows between 55 and 65 degrees Fahrenheit for peak activity. Focus on undercut banks, deep bends, and the shaded pools where brown trout stage during bright days. Dry-fly fishing with small mayfly and caddis patterns earns the most respect on this pressured, clear river, but a well-drifted nymph along seams and tail-outs produces consistently. Match hatch size carefully — these wild fish are notoriously selective.

The Au Sable near Grayling is classic Michigan trout water, spring-fed and cold enough to hold fish year-round. Brown trout are the primary quarry throughout the main river corridor, with native brook trout more common in the smaller tributaries and upper reaches where the canopy is dense and temps stay coldest. Spring brings aggressive pre-spawn browns willing to chase streamers, summer fishing slows midday but picks up during evening hatches, and fall triggers the best dry-fly action of the year as browns stage and feed heavily before the spawn.

Fish hold in seams along current breaks, under undercut banks, and in the deeper bends where gravel transitions to silt. When water temps climb above 65°F, trout push into shaded runs and tributary mouths to find cooler water — target those spots at dawn. Elk Hair Caddis and Hex patterns match the river's famous hatches, while small Woolly Buggers and sculpin streamers produce browns in higher flows. Wade quietly, fish upstream, and keep a thermometer handy — cold stable flows in the 55–62°F range signal the most active feeding windows.

The White River below Bull Shoals Dam is tailwater trout fishery, and the cold, clear releases keep trophy brown and rainbow trout active year-round. Spring and fall are prime time when stable generation schedules and moderate flows concentrate fish. Summers can be tough during heavy generation, but low-light windows early and late still produce. Winter slows metabolism but big browns move shallow during spawning runs, and patient anglers often connect with the largest fish of the year.

When generators are off and flows drop, wade the gravel bars and work the seams where fast water meets slow. Marabou jigs fished under a float are the local standard, and natural drift matters more than flash. Sculpin-pattern streamers and small egg flies shine during brown trout spawning. Watch water temperature closely — trout feed most aggressively when it holds in the low to mid fifties. Match your retrieve speed to the current, stay stealthy on clear water, and position yourself upstream of any visible current edge.

The Owens River below Pleasant Valley Reservoir is the centerpiece here, offering a mix of wild browns and rainbows alongside DFW-stocked fish that cycle through regularly. Spring and early summer bring excellent dry-fly fishing as flows stabilize and aquatic insect hatches kick off. Midsummer heat pushes trout into shaded undercuts and deeper runs, slowing midday action considerably. Fall is prime time for larger wild browns as they feed aggressively ahead of the spawn, and winter fishing can be surprisingly productive when crowds thin and fish concentrate in slower, deeper water.

Wild fish stack in undercut banks, behind mid-channel boulders, and in the seam where fast water meets slow. Small nymphs like Zebra Midges and Pheasant Tails fished under an indicator are consistently effective, while dry-dropper rigs shine during caddis and PMD hatches. When water temps climb above 65°F, fish early mornings exclusively and leave fish to recover. Stocked rainbows tend to hold in slower runs near access points, while wild browns are deeper in the system and far less forgiving of sloppy presentations.

Cherokee's Oconaluftee River and the tribal trophy waters hold a solid mix of rainbows, browns, and the occasional native brook trout tucked into the cooler headwater tributaries. Spring runoff brings aggressive feeding as water temperatures climb into the mid-40s to low 50s, and fish spread throughout the water column. Summer pushes brookies and browns toward shaded, oxygen-rich seams while midday heat slows things down. Fall is prime time — cooling temps trigger pre-spawn aggression in browns especially, and the whole river seems to wake up again.

Watch your water temperature closely — trout feed most actively between 45 and 62 degrees. In higher flows, target the soft edges behind boulders and current breaks near undercut banks where browns and rainbows stage without burning energy. Small weighted nymphs like hare's ears or pheasant tails fished dead-drift produce year-round. In lower, clearer conditions, downsize your tippet and switch to dry flies or small inline spinners worked across seams. Worms and PowerBait remain consistent for anglers not fly fishing, particularly in deeper pools. Morning hours consistently outperform midday.

The Farmington River's catch-and-release TMA below Hogback Dam holds some of the finest wild and holdover trout fishing in southern New England. Spring brings aggressive feeding as water temps climb into the mid-40s to low-50s Fahrenheit, with fish staged in seams and tailouts during blue-winged olive hatches. Summer pushes wild browns into deep, shaded runs and spring holes to escape warming flows. Fall is prime time — cool water and pre-winter feeding make trout less selective and more willing.

Wade the broken pocket water and read current edges carefully; fish stack behind boulders and in slow troughs adjacent to fast runs. Nymphing with Pheasant Tails and Hare's Ears under an indicator produces year-round, while surface action rewards patience during evening caddis and olive hatches. When flows run high and off-color, swap to streamers swung through deep runs. Watch the USGS gauge — flows between roughly 150 and 400 cfs are most wadeable and fishable.

The South Holston is a tailwater fishery below South Holston Dam, and it earns its reputation on the strength of its trophy brown and rainbow trout. Browns dominate the conversation, with the river producing genuinely large fish for anglers willing to put in time. Rainbows are abundant throughout. Spring and fall are prime seasons when water temps stabilize in the mid-50s to low 60s, triggering aggressive feeding. Summer fishing depends heavily on generation schedules, and low, clear conditions between generation cycles concentrate fish and demand lighter presentations.

Watch the USGS gauge and TVA generation schedules closely before wading. During low flows, trophy brown and rainbow trout hold in deeper pools and along undercut limestone ledges. Midges and sulfur emergers under an indicator account for most fish. Streamer fishing after generation flow drops is deadly for big browns. In warmer months, fish early mornings in the riffles above deeper pools where oxygen levels stay higher. Match the hatch whenever possible, and downsize tippet in clear, slow-moving stretches.

Lake Taneycomo is a tailwater fishery fed by cold releases from Table Rock Dam, making it one of Missouri's premier destinations for trophy rainbow and brown trout year-round. Rainbows dominate the upper stretches near the dam and respond well through all seasons, while brown trout tend to become more active and aggressive during fall and early winter, staging near structure as cooler water triggers their spawning instincts. Summer heat drives both species deeper or tighter to the dam where water stays coldest.

Flow from the dam dictates everything here. When generation is running high, fish move to slower eddies and seams along current edges behind boulders and submerged structure. During low-flow periods, wade anglers can work shallow flats effectively with small PowerBait, egg patterns, or lightweight inline spinners. Midges and scud imitations on light tippet consistently produce for fly fishers, especially when water clarity is high. Watch the discharge schedule and plan your approach accordingly — both trophy rainbows and browns feed most aggressively when flow stabilizes after a generation cycle ends.

Lake Cumberland is a deep, clear Army Corps reservoir on the Cumberland River, and it holds a genuinely diverse fishery. Striped bass are the marquee draw, running in big schools and growing heavy in the main lake's cold, oxygenated depths. Largemouth fishing heats up as water warms into spring and early summer, with fish pushing into the creek arms and shallow timber. Walleye are present but underappreciated here — they tend to school along rocky main-lake points and channel edges, especially during low-light hours in cooler months when competition from bass slows down.

Stripers follow shad schools and are best located by watching for birdwork or running your graph over deep mid-lake humps and channel bends. Live shad or large swimbaits worked vertically will draw strikes when fish are stacked on structure. Largemouth respond well to Texas-rigged plastics and jigs around submerged brush in the creeks during warming trends. Walleye reward anglers who slow down and fish curly-tail grubs or blade baits along rock transitions after dark or during overcast windows. Water temperature is your compass — striper action peaks when surface temps cool into the mid-60s and below, while largemouth fire up on the climb.

Dale Hollow is one of the clearest, coldest, deepest impoundments in the mid-South, and that character shapes everything. The lake is best known for producing trophy smallmouth bass, with fish growing large and fat in the cool, deep, clear water. Smallmouth are the primary draw for most serious anglers, but walleye quietly thrive here too, particularly in spring and early winter. Spring brings smallmouth shallow to rocky points and gravel banks as water temps climb toward 60 degrees. Summer pushes both species deep into the thermocline. Fall pulls smallmouth back to the mid-depth range, and winter concentrates walleye on main-lake structure.

For smallmouth, target rocky main-lake points and bluff ends with tube baits, drop-shots, or suspending jerkbaits. Depth-find the thermocline in summer, then work just above it. Walleye respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits and live minnows drifted along sloping main-channel banks, especially in low-light periods. Clear water demands lighter line and natural color finesse presentations year-round. Watch your graph for baitfish schools, particularly shad, since smallmouth and walleye stack beneath them. When surface temps cool into the mid-50s, both species become more aggressive and shallower, making fall and early spring your most productive windows.

Center Hill is a deep, clear Corps of Engineers impoundment on the Caney Fork River, and that clarity shapes everything. Smallmouth are the bread-and-butter species, thriving in the rocky main-lake points and ledges the lake is known for. Largemouth favor the shallower creek arms and transition areas where wood and bank cover exist. Walleye, often overlooked by visiting anglers, are a legitimate target here, especially during late winter and early spring when they stage near the dam and along deeper main-channel structure before moving toward spawning shallows.

For smallmouth, work main-lake points and submerged humps with drop-shot rigs, tube jigs, or shaky heads in clear-water colors. Walleye respond well to blade baits and jigging spoons worked vertically along channel edges when water temps drop into the low 40s. Summer pushes both bass species deeper onto ledges in 20 to 35 feet of water, where big swimbaits and Carolina rigs shine. Watch the Caney Fork arm closely after generation starts at the dam, as current pulls baitfish and activates feeding across all three species.

Watts Bar Lake, stretching roughly 39 miles along the Tennessee River system, holds a solid mix of largemouth bass, crappie, and catfish year-round. Spring is prime time across the board — largemouth push shallow into the abundant creek arms and flooded timber as water temps climb into the mid-50s to 60s, while crappie stack on brush piles and dock pilings to spawn. Summer heat pushes fish deeper and more structure-oriented, though catfish stay active through warm nights near channel edges. Fall triggers a feeding binge as baitfish schools move shallow, and winter concentrates crappie and catfish in deep river channel bends.

Work the countless dock-lined coves and submerged creek channels — Watts Bar has plenty of both. Largemouth respond well to Texas-rigged plastics and swimbaits crawled through flooded wood in spring, and deep diving crankbaits along main-lake points in summer. Watch your depth finder for suspended shad schools, because bass and crappie follow them. Crappie fall readily to small jigs and live minnows fished vertically around structure, especially when water temps dip below 60 degrees in fall and early spring. Catfish favor cut shad or chicken liver drifted along channel drops, particularly after generation flows from the upstream dam stir the bottom.

Lake Eufaula on the Chattahoochee River system is primarily a largemouth bass and crappie fishery, with both species following distinct seasonal rhythms tied to this reservoir's fluctuating pool levels and extensive flats. Largemouth move shallow into the grass and flooded timber during spring prespawn as water climbs toward the mid-60s, then retreat to deeper creek channel edges and main-lake points through summer. Crappie stack on submerged structure during winter and early spring, making those colder months surprisingly productive for slab hunters willing to slow down.

Eufaula's abundant hydrilla and milfoil beds are your roadmap for bass year-round. Work Texas-rigged soft plastics and frogs through grass in warmer months, and slow down with jigs and drop shots when water cools. For crappie, vertical jigging small tube jigs or minnows around flooded standing timber and bridge pilings is consistently reliable. Watch water temperature carefully at seasonal transitions, and pay attention to river flow through the system, as rising water pushes fish onto newly flooded structure while falling water concentrates them on main channel edges.

Lake Seminole sits at the confluence of the Flint and Chattahoochee rivers in southwest Georgia, and that river-fed character shapes everything here. Largemouth bass thrive in the sprawling shallow flats, flooded timber, and grass beds — spring spawning pushes them into skinny water near emergent vegetation, while summer heat pushes them deeper into submerged timber and channel edges. Crappie follow their own rhythm, staging near flooded brush and dock pilings through winter and early spring, then scattering to deeper structure as water temperatures climb through summer.

For largemouth, work spinnerbaits and frogs through grass early and late, then drop a Texas-rigged creature bait into timber as the sun rises. Watch water temperature carefully — bass feed most aggressively in the 60s and low 70s. For crappie, vertical jigging with small tube jigs or minnows around submerged brush piles is consistently productive. Flow from the river arms influences bait position, so fish the upstream side of structure when current is running and let bait drift naturally.

Clarks Hill is a big, fluctuating Georgia reservoir where largemouth bass, hybrid bass, and crappie all draw serious attention throughout the year. Largemouth fishing peaks in spring when fish push into the backs of coves and creek arms to spawn, then transitions to deeper main-lake structure through summer heat. Hybrids are the wild card here — these fish roam open water in large schools, especially during fall when they chase shad to the surface in open expanses of the main lake. Crappie fishing holds steady spring and fall around submerged timber and bridge pilings, with winter producing slower but quality fish once you dial in the depth.

For largemouth, target flooded timber, laydowns, and secondary points in creek arms with swim jigs, Texas-rigged plastics, or chatterbaits in spring. When water temperatures push above 80 degrees in summer, move to main-lake humps and ledges in 15 to 25 feet and slow down with deep-diving crankbaits or drop shots. Hybrids demand a completely different approach — watch for birds and surface activity in open water, then meet them with topwater plugs or white swimbaits matched to shad size. Crappie respond well to small jigs and live minnows fished vertically near structure, especially when the lake stabilizes after periods of heavy generation flow from the dam.

Lake Oconee is a Georgia Power reservoir on the Oconee River, and it holds a solid mix of largemouth bass, striped bass, and crappie that follow predictable seasonal swings. Largemouth are the bread-and-butter target year-round, moving shallow to spawn in spring and pulling back to main-lake structure and deeper coves as summer heats up. Striped bass use the river channel and deeper water, becoming most active in cooler months when water temps drop into the 50s and 60s. Crappie stack on submerged timber and dock pilings in late winter and spring, then scatter to deeper brush piles through summer.

Focus largemouth on dock edges, submerged points, and laydowns, throwing Texas-rigged plastics or crankbaits in spring and switching to deep-diving crankbaits or drop shots near channel swings in summer. Stripers respond well to live shad or large swimbaits worked along the river channel, especially in fall and winter when they corral baitfish. For crappie, vertical jigs tipped with minnows around standing timber are hard to beat. Watch surface temperature carefully — largemouth turn aggressive on the way up through the mid-60s, and crappie fishing peaks just before full spawn when temps stabilize in the upper 50s.

Lake Wylie is a Catawba River reservoir straddling the North and South Carolina line, and it fishes like one. Largemouth bass are the main draw year-round, with crappie running a close second, especially for anglers who learn the submerged timber and dock pilings scattered throughout the lake's many coves. Bass action peaks in spring when fish push shallow onto chunk-rock banks and flooded brush to spawn, then pulls deep through summer's heat before reviving again in fall as shad schools concentrate near creek mouths. Crappie follow a similar rhythm, stacking in timber during the pre-spawn warming period and again in autumn.

For bass, work laydowns and dock edges with Texas-rigged soft plastics or shallow-running crankbaits when water temps climb into the low 60s. As summer pushes temps into the upper 70s and 80s, drop-shotting ledges and deeper brush piles in 15 to 25 feet produces well. Crappie respond to slow-drifted minnows or small tube jigs worked vertically through flooded timber, especially where creek channels swing close to shallower flats. Pay attention to wind-driven current in the larger coves — baitfish and feeding fish both stack on the windward side.

Lake Keowee is a deep, clear, piedmont reservoir where spotted bass often steal the spotlight from largemouth. Spots dominate the main-lake points and offshore structure, while largemouth favor the shallower, warmer creek arms with heavier vegetation. Spring brings both species shallow to spawn along the clay-bottom flats and rocky transition banks. Summer pushes fish deep as surface temps climb, and fall pulls them back into the creek arms as baitfish stack up. Winter fishing gets tough but productive on slow, deep presentations targeting suspended fish over main-lake humps.

In summer, graph the main-lake points and long tapering ridges for suspended spotted bass in the 20-30 foot range, then finesse them with drop shots or shaky heads. Spring and fall, work the upper creek arms with moving baits like spinnerbaits and shallow crankbaits along the chunk-rock banks. Keowee's clarity means spotted bass can be line-shy, so drop down to lighter fluorocarbon when the water is calm and bright. Watch water temperature closely around the 55-65 degree range in spring and fall — that window triggers the most reliable feeding activity on this lake.

Lake Gaston is a long, riverine impoundment on the Roanoke River system straddling the Virginia-North Carolina line, and that river-lake character shapes everything here. Largemouth bass dominate the upper, shallower coves and creek arms with heavier cover, while striped bass use the main-lake channel and deeper, cooler water, especially as summer heat sets in. Spring is prime time for both — largemouth move shallow to spawn, and stripers chase shad through the main basin. By midsummer, stripers go deep or stack below the dam where cooler, oxygenated water holds them.

Watch water temperature carefully — stripers become stressed above 75°F and concentrate near thermoclines and the dam tailrace. Swimbaits, umbrella rigs, and live shad work well for stripers trolled along the main channel drop-offs. For largemouth, target the creek mouths, docks, and laydowns in the upper lake arms with Texas-rigged plastics and topwater lures in low-light hours. In fall, both species feed aggressively as water cools — follow the shad schools and you will find the fish.

Lake Travis is a long, canyon-shaped Highland Lakes reservoir on the lower Colorado River, and it holds a solid mix of largemouth, white bass, and striped bass that each peak at different times of year. Largemouth dominate the upper, shallower creek arms and tend to be most active during the spring spawn and again in fall when water cools into the low 60s. White bass and striped bass are the real draw in late winter and early spring when they stage in big schools and push shad toward the surface, often producing fast, aggressive action. Summer stratification pushes stripers deep, and they can be sluggish until temperatures drop again in October.

During the striper and white bass runs, follow diving birds and watch your electronics for suspended shad schools near main-lake points and the deeper river channel. Jigging chrome or silver spoons, swimbaits, and topwater lures through breaking fish is highly effective. For largemouth, work rocky bluff walls and submerged cedar structure in the creek arms with Texas-rigged soft plastics, finesse worms, or jigs. When surface temperatures climb above 85 degrees in summer, shift to early-morning or night fishing and target largemouth tight to shaded docks and deeper brush piles. Let water temperature and baitfish location drive every decision on this lake.

Lake Buchanan is the headwaters reservoir of the Highland Lakes chain on the Colorado River, and its character shifts dramatically with the seasons. Striped bass are the star attraction, drawing serious anglers throughout the year, but spring and fall are peak periods when threadfin and gizzard shad schooling activity pulls big fish toward the surface. Largemouth bass fishing picks up as water temperatures climb into the low 60s in late winter and early spring, with fish staging on rocky points and submerged creek channels before the spawn. Flathead and blue catfish thrive here year-round, benefiting from the deep water and strong river-channel structure that Buchanan's upper end provides.

For stripers, watch for birds working baitfish on the surface early morning and run topwater walk-the-dog plugs or swimbaits through the commotion fast. When fish go deep in summer heat, downrigging or live-lining shad over main-lake structure in 20 to 40 feet produces. Largemouth respond well to soft plastic crawfish and creature baits worked slowly around chunk-rock banks and flooded timber near coves. The upper river arm near the Colorado River inflow concentrates all three species during periods of active current flow following rainfall, as bait stacks up and predators follow. Catfish anglers do well anchoring the deep river channel with cut shad on bottom.

Caddo Lake is a labyrinth of cypress-studded bayous and lily-pad flats straddling the Texas-Louisiana line, and its tangled structure shapes how fish behave year-round. Largemouth bass are the main draw, moving shallow into the pads and cypress knees during the spring spawn, then retreating to deeper channels and submerged timber through the summer heat. Crappie stack tight around flooded timber and brushy structure from late winter through spring, then scatter into cooler, shadier bayou corridors in summer. Channel and flathead catfish cruise the deeper connecting channels and open lake areas, feeding most actively from late spring through early fall.

On Caddo, reading the cypress timber is everything. Bass hold tight to the shady side of trunk clusters and knee fields; pitch a weedless frog or soft-plastic creature bait right to the wood. In summer, slow a swim jig through submerged vegetation edges early and late. For crappie, vertical jig small tube jigs or live minnows directly against standing timber in 8 to 14 feet. Catfish respond well to cut bream or stinkbait fished on the bottom of the deeper connecting bayous and lake pockets. When surface temperatures climb above 85 degrees, focus your bass and crappie efforts during low-light windows and in areas with noticeable current or shade.

Falcon Lake is famous among serious bass anglers as one of the premier trophy largemouth bass fisheries in the country, with fish routinely pushing well into double digits. The reservoir's massive shallow flats, submerged brush, and mesquite-lined coves create ideal habitat. Spring is the peak season, when bass move shallow to spawn on sandy flats near structure and feeding activity is aggressive. Summer pushes fish deeper into creek channels and submerged timber to escape heat. Fall brings renewed shallow feeding, while winter concentrates both bass and catfish in deeper, slower water near the main lake basin.

Work topwaters and swimbaits over shallow flats early spring mornings when water temps climb into the mid-60s. As summer heat builds, drop Carolina rigs and deep-diving crankbaits along submerged channel edges and timber lines. The Rio Salado arm and creek mouths consistently hold fish during transitional seasons. For catfish, cut bait fished on the bottom near deeper channel bends produces well, particularly after water releases increase flow through the reservoir. Watch surface temps and wind-driven current, as bass stack on the upwind side of points when baitfish concentrate there.

Lake Amistad is a big, clear-water reservoir on the Rio Grande, and it produces largemouth and smallmouth bass along with heavy flathead and blue catfish year-round. Spring is the prime season for bass — warming water pushes fish shallow into rocky points, creek arms, and the brush-covered flats on the Mexican and Texas sides alike. Summer heat sends largemouth deep to thermoclines around submerged structure, while smallmouth stay glued to rocky ledges and hard-bottom transitions. Catfish run big in Amistad and feed actively through summer nights when water temps climb into the upper 70s and 80s.

For bass, target transitions between rock and brush using swimbait, drop-shot, and Carolina-rigged plastics when fish are deep, then switch to topwater and shallow crankbaits during spring and fall feeding windows. Amistad's clarity demands lighter line and natural color profiles — green pumpkin and watermelon plastics consistently outperform bright patterns. Catfish respond well to cut carp or shad fished on the bottom near creek channel edges and submerged timber. Watch the Rio Grande inflows after rainfall — stained water pulls feeding fish to the edges of the color change, and that transition zone is often the most productive water on the lake.

Cedar Creek Reservoir draws anglers primarily for largemouth bass, crappie, and catfish, and the fishing shifts noticeably with each season. Bass fishing peaks in spring when fish move shallow into flooded timber and grass flats to spawn, then retreats to deeper structure through the brutal Texas summers. Fall brings a reliable feeding window as shad schools push toward creeks and bass follow aggressively. Crappie stack on submerged brush through winter and early spring, while channel and blue catfish stay active nearly year-round, ramping up in summer heat when bass slow down.

Water temperature is your best guide here. Bass respond well to Texas-rigged soft plastics and swimbaits worked along standing timber edges and submerged points. In summer, fish deep timber with Carolina rigs or drop shots when surface temps exceed 85 degrees. Crappie consistently hold on brush piles in 10 to 20 feet using small jigs or live minnows under a slip float. For catfish, cut shad or punch bait fished on the bottom near creek channel bends produces steadily. Watch for shad activity on the surface to locate feeding bass and catfish simultaneously during fall.

Lake Tawakoni is a proven big-fish reservoir in northeast Texas where largemouth bass, crappie, and catfish all draw serious attention. Bass fishing peaks in late winter through spring when fish move shallow into the abundant standing timber and rocky points to spawn. Crappie stack up in those same submerged trees during the spawn, then pull deeper into brush through the summer heat. Catfish — including some heavy flatheads and blues — feed actively on main-lake humps and creek channel edges nearly year-round, but night fishing through the warmer months consistently puts the biggest fish in the boat.

When surface temps push above 80 degrees, target bass early and late with topwater around the timber edges, then switch to Texas-rigged plastics and deep-diving crankbaits worked along channel drops as midday heat sets in. Crappie respond well to small jigs and live minnows suspended vertically in brush piles, especially when you mark fish on your sonar holding tight to structure. For catfish, cut shad or fresh chicken liver fished on the bottom near creek channel bends and main-lake flats after dark is hard to beat. When water temps cool into the 50s, slow your presentations down considerably — all three species become lethargic and finesse approaches outperform reaction baits.

Norfork Lake is a deep, clear Ozark reservoir where anglers primarily chase striped bass, largemouth bass, and crappie across dramatically different seasonal windows. Stripers are the headline act, staging near the surface in spring and fall when shad push shallow, then retreating to deep thermocline water through summer. Largemouth follow creek-arm flats and laydowns through spring spawning, while crappie stack on submerged timber and dock structure in spring and again in fall. Winter fishing slows but never stops, with stripers still catchable by fishing deep main-lake structure.

Reading water temperature is critical here. When surface temps climb above 80 degrees, find stripers by locating suspended shad schools on your sonar over 30 to 60 feet of water and work live shad or large swimbaits through that zone. Largemouth respond well to Texas-rigged plastics and crankbaits along rocky points and creek channel edges during the pre-spawn and fall feed. Crappie in Norfork reward slow presentations, with small jigs and minnows fished vertically around standing timber producing consistently. Pay attention to the dam generation schedule since current pulls baitfish and triggers feeding across all three species.

Greers Ferry is a clear, deep Ozark impoundment on the Little Red River system, and that clarity shapes everything. Largemouth dominate the shallower, more vegetated upper arms and creek pockets, while smallmouth thrive on the rocky main-lake points and bluff walls the lake is known for. Hybrid bass roam open water and often betray themselves with surface-busting schools, especially in fall and spring when shad push toward the surface. Winter fishing slows but never dies — find largemouth staging near wood in the backs of creeks, and smallmouth hugging deep rocky structure. Spring is prime for both, as smallmouth move onto gravel and chunk-rock to spawn in surprisingly shallow water given the lake's clarity.

For smallmouth, work chunk-rock points and bluff ends with finesse — drop shots, shaky heads, and tube baits in natural crawfish colors account for a lot of fish. Largemouth respond to jigs and soft plastics worked through wood and laydowns in the creek arms. When surface temps push into the mid-60s and above, move faster with reaction baits like crankbaits on main-lake points. Hybrid bass are a different game — watch your graph for suspended shad schools, and when fish are busting, match the hatch with a swimbait or topwater pencil bait. Thermocline depth in summer is critical; most active fish stack just above it.

Lake Ouachita is a deep, clear highland reservoir in the Ouachita Mountains, and that clarity shapes everything. Striped bass are the marquee fish here, thriving in the cold, well-oxygenated depths that this impoundment holds even through summer. Largemouth bass dominate the shallower coves and timber lines, while crappie stack around submerged structure throughout the year. Spring brings the most predictable action, with largemouth moving shallow to spawn in protected coves, stripers corralling shad near points and channel edges, and crappie sliding into brush piles in eight to fifteen feet.

Come summer, chase stripers by watching your sonar for suspended shad schools in the main lake basin and fishing live shad or heavy jigging spoons vertically beneath them. Largemouth push deeper and hold on bluff walls and submerged timber edges, where deep-diving crankbaits and Carolina-rigged plastics produce. Crappie stack tighter to deep brush in twenty-plus feet when surface temps climb. In fall, cooling water triggers aggressive feeding across all three species, and topwater plugs over main lake points can bring explosive striper action at low light. Winter slows things down but concentrates fish predictably on deeper structure.

Truman Lake is a large, shallow Corps of Engineers impoundment on the Osage River system in west-central Missouri, and that flooded timber character shapes everything. Crappie are the star attraction, drawing serious numbers of anglers each spring when fish push into the standing timber and brushy coves to spawn. Largemouth bass follow similar shallow-timber patterns through spring and early fall, while catfish — both channel and flathead — thrive in the deeper creek channels and flats year-round, peaking in summer activity.

For crappie, slow-roll a small jig or minnow tight to standing timber at whatever depth matches water temperature — shallower as temps climb toward 60 degrees in spring, deeper and slower during summer heat. Bass respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits and Texas-rigged plastics worked through submerged wood. Read the creek arm mouths carefully; when the Osage arm flows are elevated and slightly stained, baitfish stack near current breaks and bass follow. Catfish hold in deeper outside bends of old river channels; cut shad and live bream fished on the bottom produce consistently after dark in warm months.

Lake of the Woods is a walleye and sauger factory, with northern pike providing aggressive action throughout the year. Spring brings walleye shallow onto hard-bottom reefs and rocky points as water temps climb into the upper 40s and low 50s, particularly in the south basin near the Rainy River inlet. Summer pushes fish deeper onto mid-lake humps and saddles in 18 to 28 feet. Sauger become especially important in fall and winter, holding tight to river-connected structure and mud-to-gravel transitions. Pike roam weed edges year-round but stack up in shallow bays during ice-out and again in fall.

Jigging a half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce paddle-tail or minnow-style jig tipped with a live or frozen shiner is the backbone presentation here, especially vertically over confirmed marks. Slow-death rigs with a single hook and half a nightcrawler work well during summer's warmer surface temps when walleye go lethargic. Sauger favor slightly heavier jigs to stay bottom-focused in deeper current-influenced zones. For pike, flashy spinnerbaits and large white or chartreuse swimbaits along reed edges before ice-up produce hard. Watch your sonar for that classic suspended walleye arch just off bottom, and adjust depth as afternoon light fades and fish rise.

Rainy Lake is a vast, border-water system with a rocky Canadian Shield character that shapes how fish behave across seasons. Walleye are the primary draw and are most aggressive during the post-spawn period when water temps climb through the mid-40s into the low 50s Fahrenheit, pushing fish onto windswept rocky points and the lips of deeper reefs. As summer progresses, walleye suspend over basin edges and move shallower at low-light periods. Smallmouth bass thrive around the countless rocky islands and cobble shorelines, peaking mid-summer. Northern pike lurk in the weedy bays and narrows year-round, becoming especially active during cool spring and fall windows.

For walleye, live-bait rigs with leeches or crawlers worked along rock transitions and mid-lake humps are consistently productive, while jigging with a quarter-ounce leadhead in stained water earns strikes when walleye are tight to structure. Watch water temps carefully — smallmouth feed aggressively on crayfish-imitating crankbaits once surface temps reach the mid-60s, especially around island clusters with mixed gravel and boulders. Pike respond well to large spinnerbaits or suspending jerkbaits worked through shallow vegetated bays early and late in the season. Wind-driven current concentrates baitfish on specific reef edges, and those are the spots to prioritize.

Upper Red Lake is a sprawling, shallow prairie lake where walleye and crappie dominate angler attention. Walleye fishing peaks in spring shortly after ice-out when fish stage on the sandy shoals and rocky transition areas along the south basin. Summer pushes walleye deeper toward the basin edges and submerged structure as water warms, while crappie school around any emergent vegetation and timber in the shallower northern reaches. Come fall, both species feed aggressively before ice sets up, and ice fishing produces consistently once the lake locks over hard.

Because Upper Red is so shallow overall, subtle depth changes matter enormously. Walleye respond well to jigs tipped with minnows or leeches drifted slowly across sandy flats and weed edges, while crappie hit small tube jigs and live minnows suspended under a slip bobber near weed lines. Watch water temperature closely — walleye activity peaks when temps sit in the mid-50s to low 60s Fahrenheit. In summer, fish early morning and evening low-light windows when walleye push into shallower feeding zones.

Lake Vermilion is a sprawling, island-studded Minnesota border lake where walleye, smallmouth bass, and muskie are the primary draws. Walleye fishing peaks during the post-spawn period when fish push onto rocky points and gravel shorelines, then transitions to deeper structure through summer before moving shallower again in fall. Smallmouth thrive in Vermilion's clear, rocky habitat and provide aggressive action from late spring through early fall. Muskie fishing builds through summer and hits its stride in autumn when big fish feed aggressively ahead of ice-up.

For walleye, work rocky points and mid-lake humps with live leeches or crawlers on jigs in the 10-18 foot range, going deeper on bright days. Smallmouth stack around boulders and rocky shorelines — tube jigs and drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics consistently produce in Vermilion's clear water. Target muskie along weed edges and rocky structure using large bucktails and glide baits; figure-eight every cast religiously. Water clarity here means downsizing presentations matters, and evening low-light windows often trigger the best action across all three species.

Lake Winnibigoshish is best known as a walleye factory, but the massive shallow flats also hold exceptional yellow perch, especially through the ice and into early open water. Walleye fishing peaks in late spring as fish scatter off spawning areas onto the vast mid-lake humps and rocky points, then again in fall when cooling water pushes them shallow and aggressive. Perch stack in deeper basin edges come winter, making Winnie a legitimate two-species destination across all seasons.

Walleye here respond well to live leeches and crawlers on lindy rigs dragged along the gradual 8-to-14-foot breaks connecting the flats to deeper water. Jig-and-minnow setups shine during cold fronts when fish tighten to bottom. Watch water temperature transitions in the mid-50s to low-60s Fahrenheit range for the most active walleye movement. Perch concentrate over sandy and mixed-bottom flats, particularly where cabbage weeds begin to establish, and small tungsten jigs tipped with waxworms or wigglers consistently produce during hard-water season.

Lake McConaughy is Nebraska's largest reservoir, and it fishes differently depending on what time of year you show up. Walleye are the primary draw, most active in spring when they move shallow to spawn along the sandy north shore flats and rocky points near the dam. White bass and wipers surge into feeding frenzies through late spring and summer, often busting shad on the surface in open water — some of the most exciting fishing the lake offers. By midsummer, all three species push deeper as surface temps climb, and fall brings them back shallower as water cools and shad schools bunch up.

For walleye, work spinner rigs and nightcrawlers along the transition zones where sand meets rock, or troll shallow-diving crankbaits parallel to the north shoreline during spring. Once summer heat sets in, jigging blade baits and swimbaits in 20 to 35 feet near the dam structure becomes more reliable. For wipers and white bass, watch the surface for diving birds — those birds are marking shad, and the fish are right underneath. Match the hatch with small chrome or white jigging spoons and lipless crankbaits. Water temperature in the low 60s triggers the most consistent walleye action; once it climbs past 75, go deeper or fish early morning.

Lake Francis Case, formed by Fort Randall Dam on the Missouri River, is a walleye fishery at heart, with smallmouth bass offering a strong secondary bite that most visiting anglers underestimate. Walleye action peaks in early spring as fish stage near rocky points and wind-blown shorelines before and after the spawn, then again in fall when cooling water pushes them shallow to feed aggressively. Smallmouth thrive around the lake's abundant riprap, rocky bluffs, and boulder-strewn flats, with their best action running from late spring through early fall.

For walleye, slow-trolling live crawlers on bottom bouncers along sloping rock transitions is a proven producer, especially when surface temps drop into the mid-50s or below. Target depth breaks where current-influenced areas meet calmer water near the dam tailwaters or main-lake points. Smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and drop-shots worked tight to submerged rock structure. Pay attention to wind direction — sustained northwest winds concentrate baitfish and predators alike on the windward shores, and that's often where both species stack up.

Fort Peck is a massive Missouri River reservoir in northeastern Montana, and the sheer size of it means you need to think in terms of sections rather than treating it as one body of water. Walleye are the bread-and-butter species here and draw the most attention, running hard in spring as water temperatures climb into the upper 40s and low 50s, then pulling deeper onto main-lake structure through summer heat. Lake trout hold in the deeper, colder basins year-round and become more accessible as surface temps cool in fall. Northern pike dominate the shallower upper arms and backwater bays, most aggressively in spring and again in early fall when they stage near emergent vegetation.

For walleye, work wind-blown points and rocky shoreline transitions with jig-and-minnow combos or bottom-bouncer rigs pulling spinner harnesses — depth often matters more than location, so experiment between 15 and 35 feet until you mark fish on your electronics. Lake trout respond well to jigging heavy spoons or swimbaits vertically over deep structure, particularly where the old river channel cuts through basin floors. Pike will crush large spinnerbaits, flashy spoons, or live suckers fished near weed edges and flooded timber in the upper reservoir arms. Pay attention to water temperature transitions; walleye especially stack near thermoclines during summer, and a good graph will put you on fish faster than covering water blind.

Flathead Lake holds a solid fishery built around lake trout as the primary deep-water target, with mountain whitefish offering bonus action in shallower rocky areas and tributary mouths. Spring and early summer bring lakers up into the water column as surface temps stay cold, making them more accessible. By midsummer they push deep, suspending over the basin's significant depths. Fall is prime time as cooling water pulls lakers shallower again and whitefish stage near rocky points ahead of spawning.

For lakers, vertical jigging tube jigs or swimbaits in 80 to 150 feet produces when they're deep, while trolling with lead core or downriggers covers the water column efficiently. Target steep rocky structure and points dropping into deep water. Whitefish respond well to small jigs and spawn sacks near rocky shallows. Watch surface temperature carefully in spring and fall, as that 50 to 55 degree range tends to concentrate both species at fishable depths.

Chautauqua Lake has a well-earned reputation as one of the premier muskellunge fisheries in the northeast, and that fish drives serious anglers here season after season. Spring brings walleye onto shallow gravel and sand flats as water temperatures climb through the low 50s, making this a productive early window before the crowds arrive. Largemouth and smallmouth bass light up as temps push into the 60s, with the weedy upper lake holding largemouth and the cleaner, harder bottom of the lower basin favoring smallmouth. By midsummer, muskie activity peaks and trollers work the basin edges hard through fall until turnover.

Position yourself along the distinct weed edges that define this lake, particularly where cabbage and coontail give way to open water. Walleye respond well to jig-and-minnow presentations worked slowly near those transitions at dawn and dusk. For bass, pitching soft plastics tight to emergent vegetation and dock edges produces consistently. Muskie anglers should throw large bucktails and glide baits along weed lines, focusing figure-eight presentations at boatside, where a surprising number of strikes occur on this water. Watch surface temperatures carefully as fall approaches, since the cooling mid-50s window reliably triggers aggressive muskie feeding before the season winds down.

Seneca Lake runs cold and deep — over 600 feet in the main basin — which makes it prime year-round habitat for lake trout and landlocked salmon. Lakers are the backbone of the fishery, holding near the thermocline in summer and moving shallower as surface temperatures drop in fall. Landlocked salmon favor the upper water column and tend to be most active in spring and again in late fall when temps cool into the low 50s. Smallmouth bass work the rocky shorelines and shale points from late spring through fall, particularly in the northern end where structure concentrates fish.

For lakers, trolling spoons and stick baits on leadcore or downriggers along the depth breaks between 60 and 120 feet covers the most productive summer water. Watch your surface temperature — once it drops below 55 degrees, fish push shallower and jigging tube baits or Swedish Pimples near bottom structure becomes effective. Landlocked salmon respond well to smaller spoons and squids trolled faster and higher in the column. For smallmouth, work rocky shoreline transitions with drop-shot rigs or swimbaits, focusing on where shale meets deeper water.

The St. Lawrence River through the Thousand Islands holds a legitimate shot at four serious predators across the season. Smallmouth bass own the rocky shoals and current edges from late spring through early fall, and the fishing here ranks among the best in the Northeast. Walleye run strong in faster current seams and deeper channel edges, particularly in spring and again as water cools in fall. Northern pike lurk in weedy back bays and slower eddies year-round. Muskellunge are resident throughout the archipelago, with peak activity in early summer and again in fall when big fish feed aggressively before ice-up.

Match your target to water temperature and position in the river. Smallmouth stack on submerged rock points and ledges in six to fifteen feet of water — tube jigs, drop-shots, and finesse swimbaits work well in clear conditions. Walleye prefer low-light periods and respond to jig-and-minnow rigs drifted through current breaks and channel drop-offs. Pike ambush from cabbage weed edges; large spinnerbaits and flashy swimbaits pulled parallel to vegetation draw strikes. Muskellunge require patience and dedication — figure-eight your retrieve beside structure, use large glide baits or bucktails, and target periods when surface temps drop into the low sixties.

Cave Run Lake in eastern Kentucky is one of the finest muskellunge fisheries in the Southeast, drawing dedicated muskie hunters alongside bass and crappie anglers year-round. Spring brings all three species shallow as water temperatures climb through the 50s and 60s — crappie push into coves and flooded timber to spawn, largemouth stack along rocky points and transition banks, and muskies cruise shallow flats and creek arms after their own spawn. Summer heat pushes fish deeper or into shaded structure, while fall triggers aggressive feeding as temperatures drop and forage concentrates near creek channel mouths and submerged timber edges.

For muskies, work large bucktails and glide baits along weed edges and rocky shoreline transitions during low-light periods, burning through likely water and varying your retrieve. Largemouth respond well to Texas-rigged soft plastics and jigs worked along bluff walls and laydown timber, especially where depth changes abruptly. Crappie hold tight to standing timber and submerged brush — vertical jigging small tube jigs or live minnows under a slip float in 10 to 18 feet produces consistently outside the spawn. Watch water temperature closely; a sustained drop in fall triggers some of the best muskie and bass action the lake offers.

Lake Barkley sits in western Kentucky connected to Kentucky Lake through a canal, and that relationship with moving water shapes everything here. Largemouth dominate the shallow backwater bays and flooded timber, while smallmouth gravitate toward the rockier main-lake points and channel edges. Crappie stack deep on submerged structure through summer heat, then push into the flooded willows and laydowns in spring to spawn. Catfish — both channel and blue — run heavy in the deeper river bends and below the dam tailwaters, particularly active after spring rains push current through the system.

Water temperature is your calendar on Barkley. Once surface temps climb into the low 60s, bass and crappie move shallow and become predictable. Target largemouth with Texas-rigged soft plastics and shallow crankbaits around submerged timber and secondary points. Small jigs and live minnows suspended under slip floats produce crappie on brush piles in 10 to 18 feet. When current pulls through from the canal, smallmouth set up on downstream edges of rocky points — a swimbait or finesse jig worked slowly is hard to beat. For catfish, fresh cut shad fished on bottom in deeper channel bends stays consistently productive.

Pyramid Lake is home to the iconic Lahontan cutthroat trout, a large, hard-fighting native strain that draws serious trout anglers from across the West. Fall through early spring is the prime window, when cooler water temperatures bring fish into the shallows along the tufa-lined shoreline. Summer heat pushes Lahontans deeper and slows surface activity considerably, making shoulder-season fishing far more productive.

Wading anglers work the rocky, gradually sloping shoreline from ladders or stepladders, which are the traditional and most effective way to get flies and lures out past the shallow shelf to where fish cruise. Intermediate and sinking fly lines with large Woolly Buggers, Leeches, or custom Cui-ui-style streamers in olive and black consistently draw strikes. Spin anglers do well with heavy spoons and swimbaits retrieved slow and deep. Watch water temps — when surface temps drop into the mid-40s to low 50s Fahrenheit, Lahontans move predictably close to shore and feed aggressively.

Lake Oroville is a big, deep reservoir on the Feather River system that holds spotted bass, largemouth bass, and a run of king salmon that push up from the Sacramento system. Spotted bass are the real bread-and-butter here, thriving in the rocky, canyon-country structure that dominates the main arms. Largemouth concentrate more in the shallower, brushy coves and the warmer back-ends of the arms. Bass fishing is most consistent spring through fall, with the spawn pulling fish shallow in late spring. King salmon enter the system seasonally and attract a dedicated crowd of trollers targeting them in deeper, cooler water during their upstream push.

Spotted bass stack on submerged points, ledges, and rocky bluffs, especially where water temperature stratifies and baitfish suspend along the thermocline in summer. Finesse tactics like drop shots and shaky heads in the 20-to-50-foot zone consistently produce when bass go deep in summer heat. In spring and early fall, swimbaits and crankbaits worked along main-lake structure are productive. For kings, trollers run flashers and meat rigs or large spoons at depth, watching surface temperature and working cooler water near canyon necks and the upper arms. When reservoir levels drop significantly, fish relocate off newly exposed structure, so watch how flow and drawdown affect where the bottom transitions.

Folsom Lake's main quarry are largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, and rainbow trout, and the fishery shifts dramatically with the reservoir's notorious water-level swings. Largemouth dominate the shallower, brushy coves of the American River arms in spring when water climbs into the mid-50s and they push into flooded timber and tule edges to spawn. Smallmouth, which thrive in the rockier main-lake points and canyon walls, peak through late spring and early summer. Trout fishing is strongest in cooler months, particularly winter and early spring, when fish suspend in the upper water column rather than diving to deeper, colder thermal layers.

When the lake is dropping, focus smallmouth on exposed rocky shelves and submerged points using finesse techniques like drop-shot rigs with small profile plastics, or swimbaits matched to the local shad and minnow forage. Largemouth respond well to flipping soft plastics and jigs into any remaining flooded cover along the North and South Forks. Trout anglers should troll inline spinners or small spoons at depths where water temperature sits between 52 and 58 degrees, adjusting based on your surface temperature and thermocline feel. Rising water years concentrate fish near newly submerged structure, while drought years compress both bass and trout into deeper, harder-to-find zones, so reading the current pool elevation before you launch shapes your whole game plan.

New Melones is primarily a spotted bass fishery, with largemouth mixed in at the upper end where the Stanislaus arm flattens into shallower, warmer water with more vegetation. Spots dominate the steep main-lake structure and rocky points that define much of this canyon reservoir. Rainbow trout are stocked and provide solid action in cooler months, particularly in the upper arms and near inflows when water temperatures drop into the mid-50s and below. Spring brings aggressive pre-spawn bass shallow, summer pushes them deep onto ledges and submerged timber, fall triggers a reliable shad-chasing feeding spree, and winter fishing slows but rewards patient anglers working the thermocline.

Watch your electronics for submerged creek channels and standing timber, which hold spotted bass year-round at varying depths depending on temperature and bait position. During warmer months, target spots on main-lake points and rockpiles in 20 to 45 feet using drop shots with finesse worms, or swimbaits matching the abundant shad. Topwater walking baits shine during early morning low-light windows in fall when bass are pinning shad against the surface near points. For trout, slow-troll flasher and nightcrawler rigs along the thermocline in cooler months, or cast small spoons near inflow areas when cool water is flowing in and concentrating fish.

Castaic Lake is a Southern California powerhouse for both largemouth and striped bass, and the two fisheries fish very differently by season. Largemouth dominate the upper lake's shallow coves and tule edges, peaking in spring when water temps climb into the mid-50s and fish push shallow to spawn.
