Stripers are a year-round draw but shine hardest in late fall and winter when they school up and chase threadfin shad aggressively near the main lake basin and the lagoon area below the dam.

For largemouth, work rocky points and brushy coves with swimbaits, drop-shots, or shaky heads as temps stabilize in spring. Stripers respond well to live mackerel or large swimbaits trolled or cast near baitfish schools — watch your sonar for suspended bait clouds and target the edges. Summer heat pushes both species deep, so downsize and slow down, fishing shaded canyon walls early and late. Water clarity here runs clean, so finesse presentations and natural colors consistently outperform.

Lake Roosevelt, the reservoir behind Grand Coulee Dam, offers a diverse fishery that shifts significantly through the year. Walleye are the bread-and-butter species, drawing serious anglers from across the region. Kokanee run strong through summer and into fall, staging near deeper, cooler water as temperatures climb. Rainbow trout are most active in spring and again in fall when surface temps cool into that productive 50-65 degree range, and they can be surprisingly large given the forage base this impoundment provides.

For walleye, target rocky points, submerged structure, and transition edges where gravel meets soft bottom, using jig-and-minnow combinations or bottom bouncers with crawler harnesses — dawn and dusk bites are most reliable. Kokanee respond well to small dodger-and-wedding-ring setups trolled at depth; find the thermocline and you find the fish. Trout cruise shallower during cooler months and can be intercepted with spinners or bait near tributary inflows, especially when spring runoff draws them to feeding lanes.

Potholes Reservoir is a desert impoundment where walleye, largemouth bass, and crappie all thrive, but each species demands different timing. Spring is prime time overall — walleye move shallow to spawn as water climbs into the low 50s, crappie stack tight to flooded brush and emergent vegetation once temps push into the 60s, and largemouth become increasingly aggressive as summer approaches. Midsummer heat pushes walleye deep into the cooler basin water while bass hold near the thick aquatic weed growth Potholes is famous for. Fall triggers a second feeding window as cooling water draws fish back toward mid-depth structure.

For walleye, troll or drift nightcrawler harnesses and stick baits along sandy flats and rocky transitions in 8 to 18 feet. Crappie respond well to small tube jigs and minnows suspended under a bobber near the standing timber and tule edges scattered throughout the reservoir. Bass love the dense milfoil and cattail margins — pitch soft plastics and jigs tight to that vegetation. Watch surface temperature; once it climbs above 75 degrees, move deeper or target low-light periods at dawn and dusk when walleye especially feed aggressively in the shallows.

Lake Pend Oreille is one of Idaho's deepest lakes, and that depth shapes everything. Rainbow trout are targeted year-round, with the best surface action in spring and fall when cooler temperatures push fish shallow into creek mouths and rocky points. Kokanee, the landlocked sockeye, run deep through summer and draw serious attention from trollers, then stage shallower and become aggressive as fall spawning instinct kicks in. Winter fishing quiets down but determined anglers still find rainbows near thermal breaks.

For kokanee, troll Wedding Ring spinners or small dodger-and-hoochie rigs with white corn, watching your fishfinder for tight schools suspended in the thermocline. Rainbows hang near the same depth transitions but also cruise structure and inlet currents. Matching depth to water temperature matters more here than anywhere — when surface temps drop into the mid-50s Fahrenheit, expect both species to move up and bite windows to open.

Bear Lake sits high on the Utah-Idaho border and runs cold and extraordinarily clear, which shapes everything about fishing it. Cutthroat trout are the main draw year-round, but the real spectacle is the January cisco spawn, when these native forage fish swarm into the shallows along the shoreline and draw both predators and anglers in numbers you rarely see at other times. Summer cutthroat fishing slows as surface temperatures climb and fish push deep, while late fall and early spring offer the most consistent nearshore action as water cools and trout move up to feed aggressively.

Cutthroat in Bear Lake relate strongly to the cisco population, so match-the-hatch thinking pays off — slender silver spoons, small swimbaits, and white or chrome jigging spoons that mimic cisco profile outperform most other offerings. During the cisco spawn, fish the shallow gravel and sand margins where baitfish concentrate; a simple hook baited with a fresh cisco or a small jig worked just beneath the surface school can be deadly. In summer, downrigging or trolling with lead core gets lures into the thermocline where cutthroat suspend. Watch surface temperature — once it drops below 55 degrees, trout move shallow and fishing picks up noticeably along rocky points and sandy drop-offs.

Strawberry Reservoir is Utah's premier trophy trout fishery, holding cutthroat, rainbow, and kokanee salmon that all behave differently through the year. Cutthroat tend to be most active in early season just after ice-out, cruising the shallows as water temps climb into the low 50s. Rainbows spread across mid-depth structure through summer before pushing deeper during peak heat. Kokanee school tight and go on aggressive feeding runs through late spring and early summer, then move deeper and suspend as temperatures peak, making them a different game entirely once midsummer arrives.

For cutthroat and rainbows, focus on points, submerged humps, and the transitions between shallow flats and deeper basins. Trolling Rapalas, Needlefish, or small spoons along these depth breaks produces consistently. Kokanee respond well to small Wedding Ring spinners tipped with shoepeg corn, trolled slowly through suspended schools once you locate them on a fishfinder. Shore anglers targeting cutthroat do well with PowerBait or night crawlers fished on the bottom near channel edges. Watch your surface temps — when they push above 65 degrees, shift your trolling depth down and slow your presentation.

Elephant Butte is a big, desert-canyon reservoir where the fishing shifts dramatically with the seasons. Largemouth bass dominate the rocky points and cove shallows from late winter through spring, moving into spawning flats when water temps climb into the mid-50s. White bass run in massive schools and are often the most consistent action, especially during spring migrations up the Rio Grande arm. Walleye are an underrated trophy here — they thrive in Elephant Butte's clear, open water and tend to be most catchable in cooler months when they push shallower at dawn and dusk.

For largemouth, work bluff walls and submerged brush with Texas-rigged plastics or swim jigs. White bass stack on main-lake points and suspended baitfish schools — a white or chartreuse swimbait or curly-tail grub on a quarter-ounce head gets bit fast. Walleye respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits and live or cut shad fished along transitional bottom near channel edges. Watch your surface temp — when it drops below 60 degrees, fish compress into deeper structure and slow presentations outperform reaction baits.

Navajo Lake sits at roughly 6,000 feet in the San Juan Basin, and that elevation shapes everything. Smallmouth bass are the real prize here — they thrive in the clear, rocky canyon arms and hit hard from late spring through early fall. Largemouth show up in the shallower, warmer coves near brushy structure but are less dominant than the smallmouth. Kokanee salmon draw dedicated trollers, peaking in summer when schools suspend in the thermocline, then staging near inlet areas as fall approaches and water cools.

For smallmouth, work rocky points and submerged ledges with tube jigs, small swimbaits, or drop-shot rigs in natural crayfish and green pumpkin colors. Kokanee respond well to trolled small spoons and spinners tipped with white shoepeg corn, run at the depth where your electronics show temperature breaks and baitfish marks — typically 30 to 60 feet in summer. Watch for wind-driven current pushing baitfish into canyon pockets; smallmouth stack on the windward side. As surface temps drop into the low 50s in autumn, both bass species move shallower and feed aggressively before retreating to deeper structure for winter.

Lake Pleasant is a desert reservoir northwest of Phoenix fed by the Agua Fria River and Central Arizona Project canal water, and that blended inflow shapes the fishery in important ways. Largemouth bass dominate structure fishing year-round, with the best action in spring when fish push shallow to spawn along rocky points and cove pockets. White bass school aggressively in open water and tend to run the mid-lake and upper river arm, especially when threadfin shad are balling near the surface. Stripers grow large here and follow shad schools throughout the water column, peaking in fall and winter when cooler temps concentrate baitfish.

When surface temps drop into the low 60s, stripers stack near the river channel and main lake basin — vertical jigging white swimbaits or live shad produces well. Largemouth hold tight to submerged brush, boulder fields, and dock structure; Texas-rigged soft plastics and football jigs work best when fish are sluggish in summer heat or winter cold. Watch for diving birds marking striper and white bass blitzes on open water and burn a swimbait or topwater through the mayhem. In summer, fish very early or after dark when largemouth move shallow to escape triple-digit surface temps.

Roosevelt Lake is a big, sprawling desert reservoir on the Salt River, and the fishing revolves around largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, and crappie through most of the year. Largemouth dominate the creek arms and brushy flats, especially when spring warming pulls them shallow to spawn. Smallmouth favor the rockier main-lake points and canyon walls. Crappie school heavily in timber and submerged structure, peaking in spring but holding in deeper brush through summer.

Water temperature is your primary guide here. When surface temps climb into the upper 80s during Arizona summers, bass push deep or go nocturnal — fish main-lake points from 15 to 30 feet with drop-shots and shaky heads. In spring, shallow swimbaits and jigs along grass edges and flooded brush produce big largemouth. Crappie respond well to small jigs and live minnows suspended under a float near standing timber. Fall cooling triggers aggressive feeding on rocky transitions — moving baits like crankbaits covering water quickly will locate active smallmouth.

Lake Mohave runs long and canyon-cut between Hoover and Davis Dams, and that Colorado River corridor character shapes everything about the fishing. Striped bass are the main draw and they run in schools that shift dramatically with season — pushed shallow and surface-feeding in summer mornings, then suspending deep in the canyon midsection once heat locks in. Largemouth hold tighter to structure year-round and tend to stack in the warmer coves along the Nevada and Arizona shorelines. Rainbow and brown trout thrive in the cold, clear water near the Hoover Dam end, where deeper temperatures suit them best in warm months and they move shallower as water cools in fall and winter.

For stripers, watch for surface schooling activity at dawn and run topwater plugs or swimbaits when you find it — when they go deep, drop heavy jigging spoons vertically over the main channel. Largemouth respond well to soft plastics and crankbaits worked along rocky points, submerged ledges, and any chunk of shade-producing structure. Trout near the upper end take inline spinners and small spoons, or bait fished near the thermocline. Water temperature is your key variable — stripers become more predictable feeders once surface temps drop into the upper 60s, and trout activity shuts down if you chase them in warm surface water rather than finding that cold-water zone.

The Kenai River below Soldotna runs king salmon through late spring into midsummer, drawing serious combat-fishing pressure as these fish stack in the deeper holes. Once kings taper off, silver salmon push in through late summer and into fall, offering some of the most reliable action of the year. Rainbow trout are present year-round, but fishing picks up considerably in fall when spent salmon carcasses concentrate protein in the system and big rainbows move shallow to feed aggressively.

For kings, back-trolling plugs or drifting cured roe through the deep outside bends where current breaks against the bank is the standard approach. Silvers respond well to spinners and flies swung through the shallower tailouts, especially in cooler water below about 55 degrees. Rainbows hold in seams behind boulders and in soft water adjacent to fast current — dead-drifting beads or flesh patterns along the bottom puts fish in the net when flows are moderate and the water carries that characteristic glacial green clarity.

Ship Creek and lower Cook Inlet offer one of the most unusual urban fisheries in Alaska. King salmon push into Ship Creek through early summer, drawing shoulder-to-shoulder crowds right downtown. Silvers follow later in summer and run well into fall, often providing more fishable windows than kings. Cook Inlet also holds Dolly Varden and occasional chum salmon, but kings and silvers are the headliners most visiting anglers build their trips around.

On Ship Creek, fish hold in the deeper slots and pools just below the dam and near current seams — kings especially stack in slower water adjacent to faster flow. Incoming tides push fish up the creek, so plan your session around the flood, not the slack. For kings, heavy spinners and cured eggs fished on the bottom produce consistently. Silvers respond better to brighter spoons, pink or chartreuse, worked with an erratic retrieve. Water clarity matters in Cook Inlet given glacial silt — fish by feel and time your efforts around tidal movement rather than sight-fishing conditions.

Petersburg sits in the heart of the Inside Passage, where the target species are king salmon, coho, pink and chum salmon, halibut, rockfish, and Dungeness crab. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are not found in these waters. Kings show first in late spring around deep structure and current seams, coho arrive through summer into fall, halibut are available most of the season, and rockfish hold year-round on rocky bottom.

For halibut, work deep mud and sand flats on the flood tide with heavy jigs or herring fished near bottom. Salmon concentrate along rip lines and kelp edges where baitfish stack up. Troll flasher-and-hoochie rigs or cut plug herring for kings and coho. Cooler, cleaner water following slack tide on a falling current often produces better bites than muddy surge. Wind-protected channels give you better boat control and keep presentations where fish are holding.

The Copper River Delta draws serious anglers because the fishery shifts dramatically through the season. Sockeye and Chinook salmon push through the sloughs and braided channels in late spring and early summer, followed by pinks and silvers into fall. The delta's maze of shallow distributary channels concentrates fish as they stage before heading upriver, making timing your visit around the salmon runs critical. Halibut are less the focus here than offshore near the Sound, but deeper tidal cuts near the delta mouth hold fish worth targeting, especially midsummer.

For salmon in the channels, drift natural roe or work pink and chartreuse spinners through current seams behind gravel bars where fish rest between pushes. Read the tides carefully — incoming tides pull salmon into the sloughs, while outgoing tides concentrate them in deeper holding water near channel bends. Cold, turbid glacial runoff from the Copper River stays murky most of the season, so bright or UV-treated lures and flies outperform natural-finish presentations. Wind off the Gulf can make the outer delta unworkable fast, so plan halibut runs on calm mornings.

Prince William Sound out of Whittier is primarily a Pacific fishery, so you won't find striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish in these waters — those are Atlantic coast species. What you will find is world-class salmon fishing for king, silver, pink, and chum salmon, along with halibut, rockfish, Dolly Varden, and occasionally lingcod. Kings show first in late spring, silvers peak late summer into fall, and halibut are available throughout the open season. Pinks flood the system in massive numbers during odd years, making for nonstop action near creek mouths and shallow bays.

For halibut, fish deep structure and muddy bottom transitions on the leading edge of an incoming tide, using large herring, octopus, or heavy jigs bounced near bottom. Salmon stack in protected bays and near glacial outflows, especially on tide changes — outgoing tides push baitfish and concentrate fish near points and narrows. Water temperature matters here; cooler, cleaner water away from heavy glacial melt often holds fish better during summer. Wind in PWS can build fast, so plan morning departures and watch for afternoon williwaws funneling through mountain passes.

Oceanside Harbor and its adjacent kelp edges and sandy flats fish differently than most Southern California spots because the harbor mouth funnels bait and predators in predictable ways. Calico bass and yellowtail dominate warm-water months when the Southern California Bight heats up, while bonito push through spring into fall chasing anchovies. Halibut hold on sandy bottom year-round but bite most reliably in spring and early summer. Rockfish and sheephead stay on structure offshore through cooler months when surface action slows. Worth noting: species like striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are Atlantic and Gulf Coast fish that do not naturally occur in Oceanside waters.

For harbor halibut, drift live anchovies or swim a swimbait slowly along the channel edges on a moving tide, keeping contact with the bottom. Yellowtail and bonito respond to iron jigs worked fast near the harbor mouth and kelp paddies offshore when surface temps climb above 65 degrees. Morning incoming tides concentrate bait inside the harbor and draw calico bass tight to the jetty rocks. Offshore, watch for temperature breaks on your sonar — those edges hold pelagics. Light northwest winds make for manageable conditions; anything above 15 knots pushes fish deeper and makes reading the water harder.

Dana Point's offshore banks and kelp beds target a very different mix than what most East Coast anglers expect. Yellowtail, white seabass, calico bass, halibut, and bluefin tuna dominate here depending on season. If you're coming from the Atlantic side hoping to target striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish, understand those are not species you'll encounter in Southern California waters. Spring brings white seabass into the kelp as water warms past the mid-50s. Summer and fall push yellowtail and pelagics onto the 9-Mile and 43-Fathom banks. Winter slows things down but calico bass hold in the kelp year-round.

Work kelp edges on the tide changes, particularly the last two hours of an outgoing. Calico bass and white seabass stage where current sweeps baitfish past kelp margins. Live sardines or mackerel are your most reliable offerings. For yellowtail, a scrambled live bait on a flat line or an iron jig worked fast in the mid-column produces well when fish are actively feeding. Watch for water temperature breaks around 60 to 65 degrees — that thermal edge concentrates bait and draws predators. Light morning wind is ideal; afternoon westerlies chop the surface and push fish deeper, so plan your drift accordingly.

Morro Bay holds strong populations of striped bass year-round, with the best action coming on incoming tides as fish push through the channel and up into the back bay shallows. Spring and early summer bring the most aggressive striper feeding, often coinciding with warmer water pulling baitfish into the estuary. The nearshore reefs outside the bay entrance hold black sea bass, which move shallower as water temperatures climb into summer. Rockfish dominate those same reefs through fall and winter. Note that several species in your list, including fluke, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish, are primarily Atlantic coast fish and are not present in Morro Bay or California waters.

For stripers inside the bay, focus on the main channel edges and eelgrass flats on incoming tide, especially early morning. Swimbaits, paddle-tail plastics, and live anchovies are consistently productive. Water temperature matters enormously here; stripers become lethargic when bay temps drop below the low 50s or spike above the low 70s. For reef fish outside the bay, watch the wind carefully. Anything over 15 knots from the northwest makes the entrance rough and the reefs uncomfortable. On calm days, dropper loops with squid near structure in 40 to 80 feet put black sea bass in the box reliably.

Fort Bragg's offshore waters hold rockfish year-round, with canary, vermilion, and black rockfish stacking up along the rocky reef structure that defines this stretch of the Mendocino coast. Lingcod move shallower through late winter and spring to spawn on those same reefs, making them more aggressive and accessible from roughly midwinter into early spring. Salmon are the seasonal headline, with chinook pushing through from spring into early summer as they follow bait schools along the nearshore upwelling zone, then again in fall as fish stage before heading into coastal rivers.

For rockfish and lingcod, target the kelp edges and rocky pinnacles in 60 to 150 feet. Swimbaits, heavy jigs, and live or cut squid all produce well, and lingcod will key on large profile baits worked slowly near bottom. Watch the tides closely — moving water activates feeding, while slack tides often go quiet. Northwest wind is the enemy here; calm mornings are your window before the afternoon wind builds. For salmon, troll the green-water edge where upwelled cold water meets warmer surface water. Water temps in the upper 50s Fahrenheit consistently hold bait and draw kings tight to the surface zone.

The Chetco River and Brookings south coast are built around chinook and coho salmon, winter and summer steelhead, and bottom fish like lingcod and rockfish nearshore. Salmon fishing peaks in fall as fish stack at the river mouth waiting for rain to lift the Chetco, then push upstream through the lower drift water. Summer steelhead arrive earlier and offer a longer window, while winter steelhead follow heavy December through February rains. Offshore, anglers target halibut during calmer summer swells, and rockfish are available most of the year when bar conditions allow crossing.

On the Chetco, fish hold in the deep green slots behind gravel bars and along cut banks during low clear flows. Side-drifting roe or casting spinners gets more attention when water runs off-color after rain. Watch the bar crossing carefully — the Chetco mouth is notorious for dangerous surf when swell and outgoing tide oppose each other. Cooler water temperatures in fall concentrate salmon near the surface and make them more aggressive. Incoming tides push bait and fish into the lower estuary, so timing your drift to coincide with that push improves contact significantly.

Coos Bay's resident chinook and coho salmon, along with trophy striped bass, draw the most attention, but the bay also holds healthy populations of black rockfish, lingcod along the jetties, and excellent crabbing year-round. Striped bass are the glamour target from late spring through fall, with larger fish pushing into the upper bay and tidal sloughs as water warms. Perch, greenling, and cabezon round out the cooler months when salmon seasons close. Note that species like fluke, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are not naturally present in Coos Bay — this is Pacific Northwest water, and honest advice means saying so rather than sending you after fish that don't swim here.

For striped bass, focus on outgoing tides near channel edges, eelgrass flats, and the deeper holes where the bay narrows toward the upper reaches. Anchovies, herring, and sand shrimp fished on the bottom or drifted under a float are consistent producers. Swimbaits and topwater plugs draw aggressive strikes during the low-light windows at dawn and dusk. At the north and south jetties, work rocky structure on the incoming tide for black rockfish and greenling using leadhead jigs or crab-tipped rigs. Avoid fishing in strong westerly winds that push dirty ocean water into the bay and cloud visibility — clear, greener water moving on a moderate incoming tide is your best window.

The Siuslaw River and Florence coast are primarily salmon and steelhead water, with chinook and coho running the river seasonally and surf perch, rockfish, and dungeness crab drawing anglers to the beaches and jetties year-round. Species like striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are East Coast and Mid-Atlantic fish that simply do not inhabit Oregon's Siuslaw system or its adjacent Pacific waters. Recommending tactics for those species here would be genuinely misleading and useless to you.

If you want a report I can actually stand behind, I'm happy to break down the Siuslaw's fall chinook timing, winter steelhead runs, jetty rockfishing, or surf perch tactics along the dune beaches south of the river mouth. Those are the fisheries that will actually put fish on the bank for you when you arrive in Florence.

Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are Atlantic Coast species. Writing them into a Port Angeles report as if they're legitimate targets here would give you genuinely bad information and could lead to a wasted trip. The San Juan Islands are Pacific Northwest water, so the honest answer is that striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish simply do not live here. Nantucket Sound draws a solid mix of species as water temperatures swing through the seasons. Striped bass move through first in spring, often thin but worth targeting in the rips and shoals as bait schools concentrate. By early summer, fluke settle onto sandy bottom throughout the Sound, and bluefish show up with real aggression when bunker push in close. Midsummer the Sound fills out — black sea bass hold tight to any hard structure, weakfish show sporadically around eelgrass and soft bottom, and kingfish turn up in the surf and shallower reaches. Tautog are a fall staple once the crowds thin out, hanging on mussel beds and rocky bottom into late season.

Work the tide changes hard here — the Sound has strong tidal flow through its rips, and fish tend to stack on the downtide edge of shoals and bars rather than fight current in the main flow. For fluke, drifting with bucktail jigs tipped with squid strips or Gulp over sandy bottom near dropoffs produces consistently. Stripers respond well to soft plastic swimbaits and clam-soaked rigs in the rips. Bluefish will slash topwater poppers when surface conditions allow. For black sea bass and tautog, drop green crabs or fresh clams straight down on structure. Watch water temperature — when it climbs above 70, weakfish and stripers often push deeper or move at dawn and dusk. Wind direction matters because southwest chop can muddy shallower flats and push bait off the bars.

Point Judith is one of the most productive stretches of southern New England water, and the seasons here turn fast. Striped bass show first in spring, pushing through the rips as water temps climb through the mid-50s, chasing sand eels and bunker along the current edges. Bluefish arrive close behind and can blow up bait schools on the surface through summer. Fluke pile into the softer-bottom pockets inside the Sound and along the channel edges from late spring through early fall. Black sea bass stack up on the rougher structure and wrecks through summer, while tautog hold that same rocky ground in spring and fall. Weakfish and kingfish are the quieter players, often taken incidentally in calmer backwater edges and sandy shallows.

The rips here fish best on a moving tide, especially the last two hours of the outgoing, when current accelerates and concentrates baitfish. Stripers and blues work the down-tide side of rip edges, so position upcurrent and work bucktails, soft plastics, or live bunker back through the wash. Fluke want a slow drift with a bucktail tipped with squid or a Gulp strip across sandy transitions. Tautog and sea bass respond to green crab or Asian crab fished tight to bottom on structure. Wind opposing the tide steepens the rips and puts fish on edge, sometimes literally boiling the surface. When water temperatures drop into the low 60s in fall, the striper bite often peaks before fish push south.

Carolina Beach is a year-round fishery with real seasonal rhythm. Winter and early spring belong to tautog around jetty rocks and bridge rubble, with weakfish occasionally mixing in during mild stretches. As water temps climb through spring, striped bass move through the surf and inlet on their way north, giving way to hard-pulling bluefish by late spring and early summer. Fluke take over the warm months, dominating the inlet and nearshore sloughs, while kingfish keep surf anglers busy all summer long. Black sea bass appear on structure in cooler water, peaking fall and spring. Bluefish return heavy in fall before things cycle back to tog.

Work the Carolina Beach Inlet on the moving tide, especially the last two hours of the outgoing when bait concentrates at the mouth. Fluke stack along the channel edges and sand transitions — drag a bucktail tipped with a Gulp swimming mullet along the bottom and slow down through every depth change. Surf kingfish and bluefish respond to cut mullet or fresh shrimp fished just behind the first trough. For striped bass, work the wash at dawn with swimbaits or chunk bunker near the inlet jetties. Avoid fishing warm, flat, clear water — a little color after a northeast blow, combined with a moving tide, puts everything in play.

Pawleys Island's tidal creeks and nearshore surf fish differently than much of the Carolina coast because of the mix of marsh habitat, sandy bottom, and structure. Spring brings the best weakfish action in the creeks on moving tides, while striped bass push through the inlets and creek mouths during cooler months chasing bait. Summer heats up with fluke holding on sandy edges near creek mouths and along the surf troughs, and bluefish show up in the wash tearing into anything that moves. Fall cools things down and black sea bass and tautog become worthwhile targets around any hard bottom or structure you can find offshore or near inlets. Kingfish run the surf from spring through fall and are often overlooked.

Work the first two hours of an incoming tide in the creeks — fish funnel through the mouths, especially where current bends around marsh points. For fluke, drag a Gulp or live finger mullet slowly along the sandy drop-off at creek edges. Stripers and weakfish respond to suspending plugs and soft plastics worked with a slow twitch. Bluefish in the surf want fast-moving metal or cut bait. For kingfish, fish the trough closest to shore with fresh shrimp or sand fleas on a small hook. Water temperature below 60 degrees pushes most creek species out to deeper holes near the inlet, so adjust accordingly.

Long Beach Island's surf, inlets, and back-bay waters fish differently by season, and knowing the rotation matters. Striped bass kick things off in spring and return hard in fall, with the October-November run through Barnegat Inlet being one of the most reliable on the Jersey coast. Fluke move into the bay and nearshore ocean as water climbs through the 60s, holding through summer before retreating offshore in early fall. Bluefish show alongside bass during migrations and can show up anywhere, while black sea bass and tautog hold on structured bottom in cooler months. Weakfish have become less predictable but still make appearances in the bay, especially at night in spring. Kingfish run the beach in summer, often in the first trough.

Position matters more than almost anything else here. Stripers and blues ambush bait at Barnegat Inlet's rips and along the washouts and cuts in the surf — an outgoing tide pushing water through the inlet or draining the bay flats is almost always your best window. Read the beach for troughs, points, and sandbars where current deflects; those edges concentrate baitfish and the fish that chase them. For surf bass, bucktails, metal lips, and chunk bunker all produce. Fluke respond to drifted bucktail-and-gulp combinations over sandy bottom. Tautog want green crab fished tight to structure on a dead low or early incoming. Cooler, cleaner water after a blow often switches the fishing on.

Cape Cod fishing revolves around the spring-through-fall migration of striped bass, which arrive in May as waters climb past 50°F and push into the canal, outer beaches, and backside flats through summer. Bluefish follow in waves, often crashing bait on the surface across Cape Cod Bay. Fluke move into the shallower bay-side areas and harbor mouths once bottom temps warm into the mid-60s. Tautog hold on rocky structure year-round but feed most aggressively in spring and fall. Black sea bass stack on the same hard bottom. Weakfish and kingfish appear in warmer months, often overlooked but worth targeting in the calmer estuaries and bay shallows.

For stripers in the canal, work the rip current edges during the first two hours of a moving tide, especially with large soft plastics, bucktails, or surface plugs near dawn and dusk. On the outer beaches, cuts and bowls in the sand concentrate bait and hold bass and blues in the wash. Fluke respond well to drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp or strip bait over sandy bottom in slight current. For tautog and black sea bass, drop green crab or Asian shore crab hard on structure. Cool water and northwest winds often push bait tight to the beach and trigger aggressive feeding, while slack tide or warm, slack conditions generally slow things down considerably.

The Canal is a year-round fishery, but it truly wakes up in spring when striped bass push through chasing migrating herring and mackerel. By early summer, bluefish show in force and can dominate surface action, while fluke set up in the rip lines along the edges. Midsummer slows for bass in warm water, but tautog hold on the riprap and rocky structure year-round. Black sea bass appear seasonally near deeper structure. Weakfish are occasional bonus fish during warmer months, and kingfish — underrated here — work the sandy pockets along the service road side in summer.

Fish move with the current, not against it, so position yourself upcurrent and work lures or bait through the moving water toward you. The strongest bite typically happens on moving tides, especially the last two hours of outgoing and first two of incoming, when baitfish get swept through. Water temps below 55°F push bass deep and slow; above 62°F they feed more aggressively near the surface. Bucktails with soft-plastic trailers, heavy metal lips, and clams fished on the bottom all produce depending on species. Watch for nervous water and breaking fish — that ripping current concentrates everything.

Vineyard Sound is a serious piece of water, and it fishes differently than anywhere else on the Cape. Striped bass move through in earnest once water temps climb past the low 50s, with fish staging along the rips and rocky points on both sides of the Sound. Bluefish show up close behind, often running in tight schools that will clear a surface plug in seconds. Fluke pile up on the sandy bottom once the water warms into the mid-60s, while black sea bass hold around any hard structure year-round with peak action in summer and fall. Tautog favor the same rocky areas in spring and late fall. Weakfish and kingfish appear opportunistically, often over sandy shallows on calm summer mornings.

On Falmouth's shoreline, stripers and blues push bait against the beach on falling tides, especially with a southwest wind putting a slight chop on the water. Work surface plugs, soft plastic jerkbaits, or live eels after dark for stripers near points and jetties. For fluke, slow-drift sandy troughs with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp strip or fresh squid. Tautog respond best to green crab fished tight to rocks on a slow current. A fast incoming tide over the Sound's rips concentrates bait and predators in predictable ambush lanes, and a morning flood tide with water clearing to that distinctive blue-green color is usually when the bite turns on hardest.

The Outer Banks offers year-round action as species rotate through with the seasons. Striped bass move through in fall and spring, chasing baitfish in the inlets and along the surf troughs. Bluefish show up in blitzing schools from spring through fall, while fluke move inshore to the sounds and nearshore ocean bottom once water temps climb into the mid-60s. Black sea bass and tautog hold on the nearshore structure and jetty rocks through the cooler months. Weakfish are more sporadic but show in the sounds during spring and fall. Kingfish run the surf line spring through early fall, especially in clean, sandy-bottom troughs.

For surf fishing, focus on cuts and sloughs where water funnels during tidal movement — stripers and blues stack at these ambush points, especially on an outgoing tide pushing baitfish. Work Hatteras and Oregon inlets during moving tides for concentrated action; current seams near structure hold fluke, weakfish, and even sea bass. Sand fleas, blood worms, and fresh cut mullet cover most surf species, while bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp work exceptionally well for fluke in the sounds. Cooler water below 55 degrees pushes tautog onto structure where they respond to green crab. Onshore winds muddy the surf and kill the bite — northwest winds off the land clear water fast and typically trigger the best action.

The Florida Keys are defined by permit, bonefish, tarpon, snook, redfish, and mutton snapper — not the Northeast species on your list. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish simply do not have meaningful populations in Keys waters, and building a report around them would be genuinely misleading and useless to you as an angler planning a real trip.

That report would give you real, actionable information. Just say the word and I'll put it together for you.

Chesapeake Bay fishing rotates through a reliable cast of characters. Striped bass anchor the season — resident fish work the shallow grass flats and channel edges year-round, while the big migratory fish push through in spring and again in fall. Bluefish arrive with warmer water and can show anywhere from the main stem to tidal river mouths. Fluke settle onto sandy bottom transitions through summer, and black sea bass congregate on hard structure and rocky bottom. Tautog are structure lovers that bite best in cooler water — spring and fall are your windows. Weakfish and kingfish appear on the lower Bay flats in warmer months, though weakfish have been scarce in recent years.

Tides do most of the work here. Moving water, especially the first two hours of an outgoing tide, pushes bait off the flats and concentrates fish at channel drop-offs and creek mouths — that is where you want to be. For stripers, bucktails tipped with soft plastics worked along the bottom near structure consistently outperform other presentations; live spot are hard to beat in fall. Fluke respond well to drifted Gulp on bottom rigs over sandy transitions. Bluefish will hit almost anything retrieved fast on the surface near rips. Water temperature below 55 degrees triggers tautog to feed aggressively on fiddler crabs near rockpiles. Southwest wind and rising tides typically fire the flats bite for multiple species simultaneously.

Sandy Hook's surf and rips offer year-round action with a rotating cast of species. Striped bass arrive with the spring run, feeding heavily along the north beach and the rip lines that form where bay water pushes against ocean current near the point. Bluefish follow close behind, often boiling the surface through summer. Fluke stack up in the nearshore troughs and channel edges from late spring through early fall, while black sea bass hold on the rougher bottom around the hook. Tautog are a shoulder-season staple, best in spring and fall on the rock and mussel structure. Weakfish show sporadically, mostly spring evenings, and kingfish work the sandy surf troughs all summer.

Fish the outgoing tide hard at Sandy Hook — it pulls baitfish out of Raritan Bay and through the rip, and stripers and blues position at the edges waiting to ambush. For bass, bucktails tipped with a paddle tail or live spot work the current seams; for fluke, drift a gulp-style bait or spearing-tipped jig along the bottom break where sand meets shell. Bluefish will smash metal spoons cast into the rip. Wade the north surf at low light when water temps sit in the mid-50s through low 60s for the best striper action. Avoid murky water after heavy rain — clarity drops fast here after a blow and fishing usually suffers until it clears.

The Finger Lakes are long, narrow, and remarkably deep, which shapes everything about how fish behave here. Smallmouth bass dominate and are the most consistent target, thriving in the rocky shoals and cobble points that line the steep shorelines. Largemouth are present but less abundant, tucked into shallower weedy bays and creek inlets. Lake trout and landlocked Atlantic salmon hold deep through summer, then become more accessible as surface temps drop in fall. Walleye are present in several of the lakes and feed most actively at low light. Chain pickerel haunt the weedy shallows near tributary mouths, while catfish and panfish like yellow perch and bluegill round out the nearshore fishing.

Smallmouth stack on rocky points and submerged boulder fields, especially where a break drops from 8 to 20 feet. Tube jigs, drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics, and crawfish-imitating crankbaits are reliable producers. Once surface temperatures climb above 70 degrees in summer, push deeper for trout and salmon using downriggers or leadcore trolling with spoons and stick baits. Walleye respond well to jigging blade baits or slow-rolling swimbaits along transition edges at dusk. Watch your sonar for thermocline depth in summer, as trout suspend just above it. In spring and fall when temps are in the 55 to 65 degree range, nearly everything feeds shallower and more aggressively, making those the most productive windows overall.

Lake Erie's western basin is one of the most productive walleye fisheries in North America, and that reputation earns every bit of attention it gets. Spring and early summer draw the bulk of the action as walleye push shallow after ice-out, then gradually move to deeper basin structure through the heat of summer. Smallmouth bass are arguably the star of the rocky reefs and hard-bottom shoals, while largemouth hold tighter to the scattered weed edges and warmer nearshore bays. Channel catfish and big sheepshead cruise the murkier western basin flats, and yellow perch — the backbone panfish of Erie — school over sandy humps from late summer into fall. Trout and chain pickerel are occasional bonus fish near tributaries and cooler transition zones.

For walleye, trolling weight-forward spinners or stick baits along the 18-to-30-foot break produces consistently once surface temps stabilize above 50 degrees. Watch for temperature breaks on your electronics — walleye stack tightly where cool and warm water meet, especially during summer stratification. Smallmouth on Erie's reefs respond well to tube jigs and drop-shots worked slowly over cobble and limestone structure; they feed aggressively during the morning bite before light penetrates deep. When the wind has been blowing hard for a day or two and has churned up current-driven bait, the walleye bite near the warmwater plumes coming off the islands tends to light up. Pay attention to bait marks on your sonar — fish holding suspended over 20 to 25 feet of water in open basin are almost always following the forage cloud, not the bottom.

The Kenai River is built around salmon and trout, full stop. Kings run first and draw the most pressure, followed by sockeye in numbers that can seem almost unreal, then silvers carrying the season deep into fall. Resident rainbow trout are the sleeper — these fish grow large feeding behind spawning salmon, and late summer through early fall is when they're most aggressively opportunistic. Steelhead make a brief fall appearance worth chasing if your timing is right. Forget largemouth bass, smallmouth, walleye, chain pickerel, catfish, and panfish — none of those species live here, and any guide telling you otherwise is someone to walk away from.

Watch the river's flow and clarity closely. When glacial melt muddies the upper sections, fish drop into slower inside bends and deeper slots where they can hold without fighting current. For sockeye, drift a bare red or pink hook near bottom on a tight line — the Kenai flossing technique is real and effective. Rainbows stack in tailouts behind salmon redds; swing a flesh fly or egg pattern through those seams at a natural drift. Kings respond to large spinners and kwikfish-style plugs fished deep. Cooler water in early season concentrates fish in slower runs; warming temps push them to move early morning and evening.

The Columbia River is primarily known as a world-class salmon and steelhead fishery, with Chinook moving through in multiple runs from late winter into fall and steelhead providing action across nearly every season. Coho arrive in late summer and fall, drawing heavy pressure through the lower river reaches. Walleye have established a strong presence in the mid-Columbia, particularly east of the Cascades, and smallmouth bass thrive in the warmer, rocky stretches of the same region. Channel catfish and largemouth bass occupy slower backwater sloughs and tributary mouths. Panfish, trout, and chain pickerel are largely incidental here — the Columbia's sheer size and current favor migratory and predatory species.

For salmon and steelhead, focus on seams where fast current breaks against slower water near channel edges, submerged points, and deeper holes below rapids. Back-bouncing cured roe, drift-fishing with sand shrimp, or trolling spinners and cut-plug herring are proven approaches. Water temperature is critical — salmon and steelhead become most active between roughly 48 and 58 degrees, and fish stack up during moderate, stable flows after a rise. For walleye, work rocky humps and current breaks with jigging presentations or bottom-bouncing crawler rigs. Smallmouth respond to jigs and swimbaits around submerged boulders in warmer summer flows.

Lake St. Clair is primarily known as a world-class smallmouth fishery, but the interconnected flats and weed edges also hold largemouth bass, muskie, walleye, and healthy populations of panfish including yellow perch and crappie. Through spring, smallmouth stage on sandy shoals and gravel humps near the river channels as water temps climb through the mid-50s, making them aggressive and predictable. Midsummer pushes fish deeper or into denser cabbage weed beds where largemouth set up alongside the occasional chain pickerel. Muskie patrol the same weed lines and open flats, peaking in fall. Walleye are more nocturnal here but show up along current breaks during low-light periods.

For smallmouth on the flats, tube baits, drop-shots with finesse plastics, and small swimbaits fished along hard-bottom transitions produce consistently. Watch your sonar for the edge where marl meets sand — smallmouth stack there. Muskie anglers work large bucktails and soft glide baits over the top of green cabbage, speeding retrieves as water temps cool into fall. Current flow from the river channels concentrates walleye and catfish near deeper cuts and channel edges, especially after rain pushes water through the system. Temperature breaks around 68 to 72 degrees in early summer signal prime smallmouth surface activity — topwater poppers and walking baits get crushed.

Little Egg Harbor Bay and the surrounding back marsh fish differently than the open surf just over the barrier island. Spring pushes weakfish and striped bass into the bay as water temps climb into the low 50s, with bass staging around the inlet and creek mouths before pushing up into shallow marsh creeks at night. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the deeper channel edges and the sandy flats near the bay mouth, while bluefish move through in waves chopping everything in sight. Fall is the best all-around season, when stripers bulk up aggressively, bluefish return on their way south, and the occasional kingfish shows up in the surf-adjacent shallows.

Work the marsh edges on a dropping tide, since baitfish funnel out of the creeks and predators stack at the mouths waiting. For fluke, slow-drift bucktails tipped with Gulp or strip bait along channel breaks, keeping contact with the bottom. Stripers in the marsh respond well to soft plastics and small swimmers worked tight to the banks after dark. Watch water temperature closely in shoulder seasons — weakfish especially disappear once the bay cools into the low 50s or heats above 72. A light southwest wind chops the surface just enough to help you approach shallow fish undetected, while a hard north wind in fall often triggers aggressive striper feeds along windward shorelines.

Barnegat Bay fishes differently than open-coast water, and knowing the seasonal rotation matters. Striped bass push into the sedges and channel edges in spring and again in fall, chasing baitfish through shallow, wind-swept flats. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the deeper channels and inlet-adjacent structure, with bluefish showing up unpredictably and tearing apart anything that moves. Weakfish have been scarce but still ghost through the bay on calm nights, particularly around channel drop-offs. Tautog and black sea bass hold tighter to the hard structure near inlets and mussel beds, while kingfish show up in the surf-adjacent shallows through summer.

Productive tactics here lean heavily on tide movement. Fluke bite best drifting the channel edges on a moving tide using bucktails tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strips. Stripers and weakfish respond well to soft plastics and small swimmers worked near sedge-lined cuts on the outgoing tide as baitfish funnel out. Low-light periods with a light southwest wind and water temperatures between 58 and 68 degrees consistently produce the best action across most species. Read the current seams where moving water meets slack water — that edge is where fish stack.

Manasquan Inlet is a year-round fishery that shifts dramatically with the seasons. Striped bass move through in spring and fall, with bigger fish using the inlet rocks and jetty as ambush points during migrations. Summer brings fluke holding in the river channel and along the inlet's sandy edges, plus bluefish crashing bait on the surface. Black sea bass show up on the rock piles offshore nearby. Tautog hunker down on the jetty rocks spring through fall, doing well even into cooler months. Weakfish appear sporadically in the river at night during warmer months, while kingfish run the beaches and inlet mouth in summer.

Work the outgoing tide hard — it flushes bait from the river into the inlet, stacking stripers and blues near the rock jetties. Bucktails tipped with Gulp work the bottom for fluke in the channel, while chunked bunker or clams fished tight to the rocks produces tautog and stripers. For kingfish, try fresh sandworms just inside the inlet mouth near the sandy bottom edges. West or northwest winds calm the inlet and improve visibility, while murky water after rain pushes the bite toward livelier baits with vibration, like swimmers or spinnerbaits worked just off the rocks at first light.

Seaside Heights sits at the northern end of Island Beach State Park and the mouth of Barnegat Inlet, making it a year-round fishery with serious seasonal swings. Spring brings the first keeper striped bass as bunker schools push through the surf and inlet. Bluefish arrive close behind, often savage and surface-feeding through early summer. Fluke move into the back bay shallows once water temps climb into the low 60s, and weakfish show up in those same channels at dusk, though their numbers have been inconsistent in recent years. Fall is the money season, when stripers stack up chasing bait along the beach and bluefish gorge before heading south. Tautog haunt the jetty rocks from autumn through early spring, and kingfish run the suds all summer long.

Work the jetty on an outgoing tide for tautog using green crabs tight to the rocks. For surf stripers, fish the slough that forms parallel to the beach at dawn and dusk, especially after a northeast blow churns up the water. Chunk bunker or clam on the bottom for bass and blues, or work a bucktail tipped with a paddle tail through the white water after dark. In the bay, drift sandy grass-bottom areas for fluke with a Gulp-tipped bucktail, moving until you find active fish rather than anchoring. Cooler water in spring and fall pushes fish tighter to structure and into shallower surf. Weakfish bite best during slack tide low-light periods on small bucktails fished slowly along channel edges.

Island Beach State Park offers classic New Jersey barrier island surf fishing. Spring surf runs bring striped bass chasing bunker schools along the oceanfront, with bigger fish pushing into the inlet where current concentrates bait. Bluefish arrive close behind, often mixed right in the striper action. Summer transitions to fluke drifting the inlet channel and nearby back-bay edges, while kingfish become reliable surf targets in the suds. Weakfish are unpredictable but worth targeting around the inlet at night during warmer months. Fall is the main event, with stripers, bluefish, and even some late sea bass making the oceanfront productive. Tautog favor the inlet's rocky structure through cooler months.

Wade into the first trough behind the outer bar for stripers on bucktail jigs, soft plastics, or live bunker when schools are around. For surf fluke, slow-drag Gulp on a spinner rig along sandbars. Kingfish want fresh bloodworm or clam on a bottom rig fished inside the wash. At the inlet, fish the last two hours of outgoing tide when current sweeps bait into the rip. Water temperature drives everything here: fluke go shallow above 65 degrees, weakfish feed best in that same warm window, and tautog wake up once temps drop back below 55. Onshore winds stack bait in the troughs and consistently produce better surf fishing than offshore winds.

Bay Head sits where the open Atlantic surf meets the upper reach of Barnegat Bay, giving you two distinct fisheries within walking distance of each other. Spring brings the first striped bass push through the inlet and along the beachfront as water temps climb through the low 50s, followed by weakfish ghosting the bay flats in late spring — a run that's been leaner in recent years but still worth chasing on calm evenings. Summer flounder work both the surf trough and the bay channel edges, while bluefish crash baitballs anywhere from the wash to open bay water. Tautog hold on any hard structure through fall and into early winter, and black sea bass concentrate around the same rocky bottom. Kingfish are a summer surf staple often overlooked by anglers chasing bigger species.

In the surf, read the sandbars carefully — stripers and weakfish stage in the gut between bar and beach, especially on a dropping tide with northeast wind pushing a light chop. Small metal lipped swimmers and bucktails worked slow and low outperform flashier hardware here. For fluke in the bay, drift sandy channel edges with a bucktail tipped with a gulp or strip bait; current speed matters more than lure size. Once water temps drop into the mid-50s in fall, tog become the priority — find any shell, rock, or debris pile and fish green crab tight to the bottom. Dawn and dusk tidal transitions are almost always your best windows regardless of species.

Great Bay and the Mullica River mouth offer a genuine mixed bag through the season. Striped bass push through early spring and again hard in fall, with the river mouth acting as a natural funnel — fish stage here before moving upriver or scattering offshore. Bluefish roll through in warmer months and can show up almost anywhere in the bay in big surface-feeding schools. Fluke arrive as water temperatures climb past 60 degrees and dominate midsummer action across the bay's sandy bottom. Weakfish, though less predictable than they once were, show best in spring and early summer near the edges of marsh drainages. Tautog and black sea bass hold on the hard structure at the bay mouth and nearby inlets, with tautog best in spring and fall.

Fish moving water hard — the strongest tidal flow through the Mullica mouth concentrates everything from fluke to stripers around channel edges and drop-offs. For fluke, drift sandy bottom with bucktails tipped with Gulp or a strip bait, keeping contact with the bottom in 10 to 20 feet. Stripers and bluefish respond to poppers and swim shads worked over shallow marsh edges at dawn and dusk, especially when wind is light and bait is visibly showering on the surface. Weakfish are soft-bitten and need lighter jig heads fished slowly on the drop. Incoming tide with clear water pushes fish onto flats; outgoing concentrates them in deeper channel bends near the river mouth.

Sea Bright sits at the mouth of the Shrewsbury River, which makes it unusually productive across a long season. Striped bass show first in spring, working the inlet and river mouth as they follow bait migrations north. Bluefish arrive close behind and can be relentless through summer. Fluke set up in the river and along the nearshore surf trough once water temperatures climb into the mid-60s, while black sea bass hold on the rocky jetty structure throughout warmer months. Tautog dominate those same rocks in fall and again in early spring. Weakfish, though less predictable than they once were, still ghost through the river in spring and early summer, and kingfish show reliably in the surf during summer.

Work the jetty base during the last two hours of outgoing tide, when current scours baitfish tight to the rocks — that's prime time for stripers and tautog on fresh crab or bucktails tipped with soft plastic. In the surf, target the trough that forms parallel to the beach, especially after a northeast wind stirs up sand eels and spearing. For fluke, drift the river channel with bucktail-and-gulp combinations, keeping the bait just above the sandy bottom. Cool water in the low 60s sharpens striper and weakfish feeding, while warmer mid-summer water pushes the best fluke action into slightly deeper river holes. Read the moving water at the inlet — fish stack where river current meets ocean surge.

Long Branch sits in the heart of the Jersey Shore striper migration corridor, so spring and fall are prime time for striped bass as fish move along the beach and stack on nearshore lumps and wrecks. Bluefish show up in the wash come late spring and can be relentless through summer. Fluke dominate the warm months, holding on nearshore structure and sandy bottom transitions. Black sea bass and tautog are reliable on the rocky lumps and wreck pieces offshore, with tog especially productive in the shoulder seasons when water temps cool into the low 50s. Weakfish and kingfish round out the mix, appearing inshore during summer as water warms into the mid-60s.

For surf stripers, work jetty ends and troughs during the last two hours of the outgoing tide when bait gets flushed through; bucktails with soft plastic trailers or chunked bunker on bottom both produce. Bluefish will crash any metal spoon or popper near the surface when you see birds working. For fluke, drift sandy bottom adjacent to structure with a bucktail tipped with Gulp or a strip bait, keeping contact with bottom. Tautog and black sea bass take green crab or Asian crab fished tight to relief on nearshore lumps. A light northwest wind off the land clears the water and often triggers a striper bite along the outer bars, while murky onshore wind conditions push fish tighter to structure.

Cape May Point draws a hard-charging mix of species that shift dramatically by season. Spring pushes striped bass through the rips as water climbs past 50°F, often stacked tight before moving north. Weakfish show in the bay shallows when temps hit the mid-50s, a run that's thinned over the years but still worth chasing. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the channel edges and bluefish tearing up the rips, with black sea bass holding on any hard bottom nearby. Tautog own the rocks and jetty structure spring and fall. Kingfish run the surf and bay shallows in warmer months. Late fall pushes stripers back through with serious size.

The rip at the point fishes best on the outgoing tide when current scours the bottom and pushes baitfish into feeding lanes — work bucktails with soft-plastic trailers or clipped bunker just off the edge. Fluke respond to slow drifts with Gulp or live killies along the bay-side drop-offs, especially when the bite goes soft. Weakfish favor low-light hours and light jigheads with grub tails. Watch water temperature closely — a cold front dropping temps more than five degrees can shut everything down overnight. Northeast wind muddies things fast; southwest winds clean the water and typically improve action across the board.

Delaware Bay is a powerhouse estuary that fishes differently every season. Striped bass show first in spring, staging on the shallow flats and around the oyster reefs as they migrate through. Bluefish arrive close behind, often schooling aggressively mid-bay through summer. Fluke dominate the summer fishery, with weakfish and kingfish mixing in on sandy bottom closer to shore. Black sea bass stack on the hard structure and reef sites from late spring through fall, and tautog take over those same rocky spots once water cools in autumn.

Read the tide carefully here — fluke and weakfish feed best on the moving water, positioning in the deep sloughs that edge the flats, then sliding up onto sand as the flood builds. Work bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strips along those drop-offs, and drag Berkley-style swimming tails for stripers near the reefs. Bluefish will push bait to the surface and telegraph their location. Kingfish respond well to bloodworms bounced on the bottom in low-current windows. Once water temperature drops below fifty, slow-roll crabs near structure for tautog. A northeast wind typically dirties the water fast, so fish quickly or reposition south.

Raritan Bay runs a dependable seasonal rotation that keeps rods bent nearly year-round. Striped bass and bluefish kick things off in spring as baitfish push through the channels, and bass linger well into fall, making the bay a premier fall striper fishery on the Jersey side. Summer belongs to fluke on the sandy flats and channel edges, with black sea bass stacking on the reefs and rock piles. Weakfish and kingfish show in warmer months, often mixed together over clean sandy bottom. Once water temps drop into the low 50s, tautog take over the hard structure and hold through late fall and winter.

Structure is everything here. Fluke stack on channel drop-offs and current seams — drift live or rigged killies on a bucktail with a teaser, keeping contact with the bottom as you sweep through. Stripers and blues key on moving bait near channel mouths; drifted bunker chunks and big soft-plastic swimbaits both produce. Tautog want fiddler crabs or green crabs tight to rock piles. Work incoming tides for fluke on the flats and outgoing for stripers pushing bait out of coves. Northwesterly winds clarity the water fast and often trigger bites; murky water after heavy rain typically shuts fluke down but bass can still be caught near outflows.

Shark River fishes best when you understand how each species moves through the system. Striped bass show up in spring and fall, staging in the inlet and basin before pushing up the tidal river on strong ebb and flood tides. Bluefish arrive by late spring and can blow through the inlet in frenzied schools. Summer brings fluke scattered across the basin flats and channel edges, while black sea bass hold on the rockier structure near the inlet mouth. Tautog work the same rocky areas in spring and fall when water cools below 60 degrees. Weakfish ghost through on summer nights, and kingfish run tight to the surf-side beaches and inlet edges from midsummer through early fall.

Work the outgoing tide hard here because it concentrates bait along channel drop-offs and around the bridge pilings inside the basin. Stripers and weakfish stack up in eddies behind structure right after the tide turns. Bucktails tipped with Gulp or a curly-tail grub cover ground efficiently for fluke along the basin edges. Fresh clam and bloodworm on a fish-finder rig catches kingfish right on the bottom near the inlet. For bluefish and bass, poppers and metal casting lures produce when bait is visibly getting chased. When water temperatures drop into the mid-50s, slow down for tautog with green crab on a knocker rig right on the rocks. Wind pushing out of the northwest typically clears the water and sharpens the bite.

The Mullica River's brackish transition zone draws a rotating cast of species across the seasons. Striped bass show up in good numbers during spring and fall runs, using the deeper river bends and creek mouths as staging areas. Weakfish historically haunt the same corridors, particularly in warmer spring nights over soft bottom. Summer brings fluke pushing into the lower river and creek edges to ambush baitfish, while bluefish raid the surface in the more open stretches. Tautog and black sea bass are better targeted closer to coastal structure, but smaller tog do appear around woody debris and dock pilings in the river system. Kingfish work the sandy shallower flats in summer, often overlooked but a reliable bite.

Tides are everything here — moving water concentrates fish at creek mouths as bait flushes out on the outgoing tide, and stripers especially stack in the seam where river current meets slackwater. Fish these transitions with bucktails tipped with soft plastics or live spot and bunker for larger bass. For fluke, work the channel edges and sandy drop-offs with drifted Gulp or spearing-tipped jigs. Water temperature dictates everything: once it drops below 55 degrees, feeding slows and fish push toward deeper river bends or migrate out entirely. A southwest wind generally keeps the water cleaner and fish more active. Keep your presentations subtle in the clear, low-salinity stretches.

Jamaica Bay fishes differently than open coast water — it's a protected estuary, and that shapes everything. Striped bass push into the bay in spring and linger through fall, hunting bunker and spearing along the marsh edges and deeper channels near the inlets. Bluefish arrive close behind, often tearing up the surface over the flats on moving tides. Fluke move in once the water climbs into the mid-60s and settle into the sandy channel edges and drop-offs. Weakfish have thinned in recent years but still show occasionally in the back marsh on calm summer nights. Tautog and black sea bass hug the rock and structure near the inlet mouths, peaking in spring and fall. Kingfish run the sandy shallows all summer.

Fish the tide hard here — Jamaica Bay's shallow flats produce best on the first two hours of an incoming tide as fish push up to feed over warming sand and grass edges, then fall back to channel lips on the drop. Stripers and blues respond to bucktails, soft plastics, and topwaters worked along marsh creek mouths, especially early and late in low-light conditions. Fluke want a moving drift with bucktails tipped with Gulp or fresh squid along channel edges in eight to fifteen feet. For tautog near inlet rock piles, green crab fished tight to structure on a short, stiff leader outproduces everything. Wind matters — a hard southwest pushes dirty water in and shuts down the flats fast, so pick calmer windows when visibility holds.

Fire Island draws serious surf and bay anglers because the fishery turns over dramatically through the year. Striped bass push through the inlet and along the ocean beach in spring and fall, chasing bunker and spearing. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the bay channels and ocean-facing sloughs, plus bluefish tearing through bait schools on the surface. Black sea bass and tautog hold on rocky structure and mussel beds year-round but peak in cooler water. Weakfish haunt the back-bay grass edges at dusk and dawn during summer, and kingfish run the suds all season long.

Work the inlet's rip current on the outgoing tide — that moving water concentrates everything from bass to bluefish. Fluke respond to bucktails tipped with Gulp or live killies drifted across sandy bay bottom in moderate current. For stripers, chunk bunker or swim large soft plastics and bucktails near the inlet edges and outer beach cuts at night. Kingfish hit small bottom rigs baited with sand worms along the wash. Cold water below fifty degrees wakes up tautog; warm it above sixty and weakfish start moving. Onshore winds churn the suds and push bait tight, which puts stripers and blues right in casting range from the beach.

Great South Bay runs shallow and grassy across its flats, with deeper channels cutting through toward the inlets, and that structure drives the whole season. Striped bass push in early spring and again hard in fall, working the edges where those channels meet the flats. Fluke arrive by late spring and dominate summer fishing, scattering across sandy bottom from the channels to the bay side of Fire Island. Bluefish show up around the same time and can wreck a fluke rig without warning. Black sea bass and tautog hold on any hard bottom, mussel beds, and bridge structure. Weakfish and kingfish are quieter players but show up in warmer months over grassy flats and sandy cuts.

Current is everything in the bay — fish the moving tide, especially the last two hours of the outgoing when water funnels through narrow channels and bait stacks up at depth changes. Fluke respond well to bucktails tipped with Gulp or strips of squid drifted slowly over sandy transitions. For stripers, chunk bunker or work soft plastics along channel edges at dawn. Bluefish hit anything fast and flashy near the surface. Tautog want green crabs bounced on the bottom around hard structure. Avoid glassy calm days in summer; a light southwest chop and water temps in the mid-60s to low 70s puts everything in a cooperative mood.

Moriches Inlet fishes as a true four-season spot. Striped bass push through spring and fall, riding the bait migrations along the inlet mouth and outer bars. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the bay channels and bluefish hammering bunker schools around the inlet cuts. Weakfish show inconsistently in warmer months, often mixed with the fluke action in deeper bay holes. As water cools into fall, bigger stripers stack up around the jetties, and tautog move onto rocky structure and mussel beds. Kingfish run the surf and inlet edges from late spring through summer, and black sea bass hold on any hard bottom accessible from the bay.

Read the tides carefully here — the inlet moves serious water, and both fluke and stripers prefer the moving tide, especially the last two hours of the outgoing when bait flushes through the cuts. Work bucktails tipped with Gulp or white squid strips along the channel edges for fluke. For stripers and bluefish, surface plugs and metal jigs cast uptide then worked with the current produce well off the jetty rocks. Surf casters score kingfish on fishfinder rigs with fresh clam in the wash. When water temps drop below fifty, slow-roll crab presentations along hard bottom structure for tautog, and expect weakfish to go tight to structure and bite lightly in low-light conditions.

Shinnecock Inlet is one of Long Island's most productive pieces of water precisely because it connects open ocean to a protected bay. Spring pushes the first striped bass through as water temperatures climb into the mid-50s, with fish staging in the rips right at the inlet mouth. Fluke arrive shortly after and dominate summer, spreading through the canal and along the ocean front just outside the jetties. Bluefish show up in waves throughout summer and fall, often blitzing baitfish on the surface. Tautog hold on the jetty rocks year-round but bite best in cooler water, spring and fall especially. Weakfish appear unpredictably, typically after dark in warm months. Kingfish work the sandy ocean-side cuts in summer. Black sea bass push into structure as water warms.

Fish the outgoing tide through the inlet for stripers and blues — that current pushes bait out and predators stack up in the wash. For fluke, work the deep channel edges of the canal with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip of squid, drifting with the tide. On the jetty rocks, green crabs on bottom catch tautog consistently. Water temperature dropping below 55 degrees signals the fall striper push; north or northwest winds after a cold front often put bass tight to the jetty faces. Watch for birds and nervous water outside the inlet mouth — when bait gets pushed against the beach by wind and current, that's where the blitzes happen.

Jones Beach offers a genuine mixed bag through the seasons. Striped bass push through the surf and State Boat Channel inlet in spring and fall during baitfish migrations, with bigger fish typically arriving after water temperatures drop into the mid-50s. Bluefish show up in late spring and stay aggressive through summer, often blitzing right in the suds. Fluke move onto the sandy bottom structure around the inlet and nearshore reaches once water warms into the low 60s and dominate summer action. Weakfish occasionally mix in during those same warm months but have become less reliable. Come fall, the inlet grows productive for tautog working the jetty rocks, and kingfish run the nearshore surf along sandy troughs from midsummer onward.

For the surf, focus on cuts and troughs visible at low tide, especially where the beach contour creates deeper pockets. Stripers and bluefish respond to metal lip swimmers and larger bucktails after dark, while kingfish and smaller species take bloodworms or sand fleas on bottom rigs in those same troughs. Work the inlet jetty rocks on a moving tide, particularly the last two hours of incoming, for tautog using green crab fished tight to structure. For fluke, drift the inlet channel with bucktails tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strip. Onshore wind pushing clean water into the beach concentrates baitfish and triggers feeding; dirty, churned-up water after strong prolonged winds generally kills the bite.

Orient Point, Plum Gut, and the Race form one of the most productive stretches of water on the East Coast, driven by the massive tidal exchange between Long Island Sound and Block Island Sound. Striped bass arrive in spring as water temperatures climb through the mid-50s, with good fish holding through fall. Bluefish move in behind them and can stay thick through summer. Fluke pile up in the sandy edges and slack-water pockets from late spring through early fall, while black sea bass and tautog work the rocky structure year-round with prime action in spring and fall. Weakfish appear sporadically, typically on warmer summer nights, and kingfish show in the surf and shallow rips mid-summer.

Work the rip edges rather than fighting the full current. Stripers and blues key on the seam where fast water meets slack, so time your drifts to coincide with the last two hours of ebb and first of flood when bait gets swept through Plum Gut. Bucktails dressed with soft-plastic paddle tails or pork rind, drifted deep and jigged with the current, consistently produce stripers, black sea bass, and tautog. Large poppers and metal on top draw bluefish when birds are working. For fluke, slow-drift with bucktails or Gulp along sandy transitions off the main rip. Cooler water in the 60s slows fluke but fires up tautog on the rocks. Wind opposing current creates dangerous chop here fast, so plan accordingly.

Peconic Bay runs a reliable seasonal parade. Striped bass push into the bay's shallower eastern reaches and creek mouths during spring and again in fall, using tidal flow to corral bait. Weakfish show up in warmer months but have grown scarce — a slot in a creek mouth on a dropping tide is still your best shot. Fluke move onto the sandy flats once water temperatures climb into the low 60s and hold through summer, often in good numbers. Bluefish raid surface bait schools unpredictably all summer. Tautog work the rocky structure at bay edges in spring and fall, while black sea bass congregate around any hard bottom. Kingfish favor sandy shallows from late spring through early fall.

Work moving water hard — fish stack at creek mouths on the outgoing tide as bait flushes out, particularly in the early morning. For fluke, drift the sandy flats with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip of squid, keeping contact with the bottom. Bass respond well to soft plastics or live eels worked slowly along current edges near channel drop-offs. When bluefish are surfacing, a fast-retrieved metal lure covers water quickly. Water temperature dictates everything here: activity peaks between 58 and 72 degrees. Southwest winds push warm water and dirty up the shallows, slowing fluke and bass; northeast winds clear and cool things down fast.

The tidal Hudson is a four-season fishery with a real rotation of species. Striped bass anchor the calendar — resident fish hold in deep channel bends and shallow grass flats year-round, with the best action in spring and fall when migratory fish push through on their runs up and down the coast. Bluefish show in warmer months, often crashing bait schools near the surface. Fluke set up over sandy shoals and channel edges from late spring through summer, while black sea bass and tautog favor any rocky structure and riprap along the shoreline. Weakfish and kingfish appear more sporadically near tidal creeks and soft-bottom areas in summer.

Work the tides hard — moving water is everything here. Fish stripers and blues on the outgoing tide around points and channel mouths where bait gets funneled through; bucktail jigs, soft plastics rigged on weighted heads, and live eels are all serious producers. For fluke, drift sandy channel edges with bucktails tipped with squid strips or Gulp, keeping contact with the bottom. Tautog respond to crab fished tight against riprap and bridge pilings, especially when water temperatures are in the low-to-mid 50s.
