Avoid fishing during extreme runoff — muddy, freshwater-heavy conditions push most species downstream or off the bite entirely.

Lake Ontario's open water and river mouths offer a diverse fishery that shifts dramatically with the seasons. Spring staging draws brown and lake trout tight to river mouths as they intercept baitfish pushing in with warming currents, while smallmouth bass move onto shallow rocky points and breakwalls as water temps climb through the 50s. Summer pushes warmwater species like largemouth, catfish, and panfish into the warmer, shallower bays and lower river stretches, while trout and walleye drop to cooler thermocline depths offshore. Fall triggers aggressive feeding across the board, with walleye and smallmouth especially active along the piers and rocky structure before ice-up slows things down.

For open-lake trout and walleye, trolling spoons, stickbaits, or paddle tails along depth contours where temperature breaks occur consistently outperforms blind casting. Pier anglers do well drifting live or cut bait along the bottom for catfish and using small jigs or crappie tubes for panfish staging in current seams near river mouths. Smallmouth on the breakwalls respond well to tube jigs and drop-shot rigs worked slowly over cobblestone bottom. Chain pickerel lurk in any weedy backwater connected to the lake system, and a simple spinnerbait or jerkbait retrieved through emergent vegetation produces reliably. Watch water temperature and flow — rising flows after rain events push baitfish and draw predators tight to current edges.

The lower Niagara is a multi-species fishery that earns its reputation year-round. Smallmouth bass dominate warm months and are arguably the star of the river, holding in current seams and rocky structure with impressive size. Largemouth push into slower eddies and slack water near woody cover. Walleye are a prime target from late winter through spring and again in fall, moving with baitfish schools along the current edges. Brown and rainbow trout work the deeper, oxygenated runs. Chain pickerel haunt the quieter backwater margins. Channel catfish take over the deep holes after dark in summer, and crappie, perch, and rock bass fill out slower days.

Fish position themselves by flow and temperature in this river, so reading the water matters as much as your presentation. When flow is high and cold, walleye and trout stack in deep eddies just off main current — slow-roll jigging with soft plastics or blade baits works well. As water warms into the 60s, smallmouth go aggressive on current-edge rocks and gravel runs; swimbaits, tube jigs, and drop-shot rigs all produce. Drift the main current breaks with nightcrawlers or leeches for consistent panfish and walleye action. Pickerel and largemouth reward anglers who slow down and work soft plastics or spinnerbaits through woody slack-water pockets well off the main flow.

Buzzards Bay runs a full seasonal menu. Tautog hold on the rocky structure and mussel beds through late fall and early spring when water temps are cold, then give way to striped bass pushing in from the Canal and deeper holes as things warm. Fluke scatter across the sandy flats and channel edges through summer, often mixing with occasional weakfish in the deeper softer-bottom areas. Bluefish show up unpredictably but can overwhelm a flat fast when they move through. Black sea bass stack on any hard bottom or structure, and kingfish work the sandy shallows, often overlooked but worth targeting in summer.

Tides matter more here than almost anything else. Fish the Canal on the moving tide, never slack, and position yourself so current does the work. On the bay flats, outgoing tides concentrate stripers and fluke at channel edges and drop-offs as water drains. Squid strips and live menhaden produce broadly, while bucktails with soft plastic tails cover fluke and bass efficiently. Watch water temp closely: bass feed aggressively once surface temps hit the mid-50s, while fluke activity peaks in the 60s. Westerly winds push bait against the eastern shoreline, a pattern that consistently stacks fish.

Boston Harbor offers a genuine multi-species fishery that shifts hard with the seasons. Striped bass arrive in spring as water temps climb through the low 50s, staging around the harbor islands and deep channel edges before scattering onto the flats come summer. Bluefish push in behind them and can be thick through midsummer. Fluke settle onto the sandy patches between the islands once the water warms into the mid-60s. Tautog hold on the rocky rubble and mussel-covered structure throughout the season, peaking in spring and fall. Black sea bass favor similar hard bottom. Weakfish and kingfish show up as warm-water bonus fish in summer, typically over sandy bottom.

Work the tide transitions hard — the last two hours of the outgoing and first hour of the incoming move bait through the channels and concentrate predators at current seams off the island points. Stripers and blues respond well to topwater plugs and soft plastic paddletails fished on the swing through rips. For fluke, drift the sandy flats with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strips. Tautog and sea bass demand bottom rigs with green crab or fiddler crabs worked tight to rocky structure. Wind above 15 knots from the northwest pushes cleaner water into the inner harbor and often triggers a bite.

Casco Bay runs a reliable seasonal parade. Tautog show first around the rockpile ledges as water temps climb through the upper 40s in spring, followed by striped bass pushing into river mouths like the Presumpscot and Royal as baitfish stage there. By midsummer, bluefish churn the open bay, fluke settle onto sandy transition zones between the islands, and black sea bass stack on deeper structure in 60 to 90 feet. Weakfish appear sporadically in warmer summers near eelgrass flats, while kingfish work the sandy shallows. As water cools into fall, stripers bulk up aggressively before moving south.

Work the two hours before and after a moving tide — slack water kills the bite. Tautog respond to green crabs fished tight to boulder structure; fluking means slow drifts with bucktail-and-trailer combos over the sandy edges off the islands. Stripers and blues will blow up on surface plugs and large soft plastics around current seams at ledge edges, especially when water hits the mid-50s to 60s range. Onshore wind piles bait against island shorelines; fish those windward sides hard. Black sea bass hit jigs and squid strips on bottom rigs over hard structure.

Kennebunkport draws serious anglers chasing a solid rotation of species. Striped bass arrive with warming spring waters, staging around the river mouth and harbor structure before spreading along the rocky coast through summer. Bluefish show in blitzing schools once water temperatures climb into the mid-60s, often pushing bait to the surface near Goat Island and the outer ledges. Fluke settle into sandy bottom near channel edges through summer, while black sea bass and tautog work the deeper offshore structure and mussel-encrusted rocks. Weakfish and kingfish appear sporadically in warmer water, typically inside the harbor or along sandy tidal flats in summer's peak.

Fish the Kennebunk River on moving tides, particularly the last two hours of incoming and the first of outgoing, when stripers and fluke stack behind current breaks near pilings and channel drop-offs. Soft plastic paddle tails and bucktail jigs tipped with strip bait cover both species effectively. Bluefish want fast-moving metal spoons or poppers worked aggressively. Tautog respond best to green crab or Asian crab fished tight to structure on slack tide. Wind from the southwest tends to push bait against the rocky shoreline, concentrating stripers in the wash. Watch water clarity after heavy rain, as river runoff pushes fish temporarily toward saltier coastal water.

Penobscot Bay runs cold and deep, and that shapes everything. Striped bass arrive first in spring, moving up from the southern reaches and stacking on shallow rock piles and eelgrass flats as water temps climb toward 55 degrees. Bluefish push in through summer and can show up anywhere, often crashing bait near the outer islands. Fluke and black sea bass hold over sandy and mixed-bottom ledges once things warm up. Tautog are around all season but fish best in spring and fall when they're actively feeding around mussel-covered rocks and pier structure. Weakfish and kingfish make occasional appearances in warmer summers, typically in shallower, quieter coves and protected bights.

For stripers, work the rocky points and island corners on moving tides with soft plastics like 9-inch paddle tails or big bucktails dragged slow along bottom. Bluefish want fast-moving metal or poppers retrieved aggressively. Tog require patience — drop green crab tight to structure and stay in contact with the bottom. Fluke and black sea bass respond well to bucktails tipped with squid strip over ledges in 30 to 60 feet. An outgoing tide that pushes bait off shallow structure into deeper current seams is consistently the most productive window across nearly every species here.

Moosehead is first and foremost trout water — lake trout and brook trout define this fishery, along with a strong landlocked salmon population that keeps things interesting through ice-out and again in fall when water temps drop back into the 50s. Smallmouth bass are your bread-and-butter warmwater target in the coves and rocky points from late spring through early fall, while chain pickerel haunt the weedy shallows year-round. Walleye exist here but run secondary to the trout fishery. Largemouth are present but less dominant than smallmouth given the cold, clear character of this deep glacial lake. Panfish fill in the coves nicely for kids or slow afternoons.

In early season, focus trout and salmon near tributary mouths and surface temperatures in the upper 50s — they'll be shallow and aggressive. As summer pushes surface temps into the 60s and 70s, lakers drop to the thermocline, typically 40 to 60 feet down, and jigging tube baits or slow-trolling smelt-imitating spoons near structure produces. Smallmouth stack on the rocky points and submerged boulder fields — drop-shot rigs and soft plastic crawfish work well here. Pickerel are ambush predators hiding in emergent vegetation in protected coves, so run weedless spoons or shallow-running minnow plugs tight to the edge. Watch for cooling fall temps to push trout and salmon back into accessible depths.

Rudee Inlet fishes differently depending on time of year, and knowing that rhythm makes all the difference. Spring pushes striped bass through the inlet channel as water temps climb through the 50s, often stacking them tight to the rock jetties before they push north. Bluefish show up choppy and aggressive through spring and summer, blitzing baitfish near the inlet mouth. Fluke dominate summer — nearshore structure and sandy bottom edges off the inlet produce well — while weakfish and kingfish haunt the shallower sandy stretches if you're patient enough to target them. Fall belongs to black sea bass and tautog around the nearshore wrecks, with toggin picking up as water cools into the low 50s.

On the wrecks, black sea bass and tautog hold tight to structure — drop green crab or fiddler crabs straight down and stay right on the edge. For fluke, work a bucktail with a Gulp trailer along sandy bottom transitions, drifting with a light southeast wind that keeps you moving at the right pace. Stripers in the inlet respond to eels at night or paddle tails worked through the current seams near the jetty rocks. Outgoing tide concentrates baitfish and gamefish both in the inlet channel — that rip is your friend. Watch water clarity after rain; dirty runoff from the back bay kills the bite fast, especially for weakfish.

The CBBT draws a remarkable mix of species throughout the year. Striped bass move through during spring and fall migrations, with fish stacking hard against the pilings and in the shadow lines during low light hours. Summer brings fluke sliding up onto the sandy flats near the islands and along the tube openings, along with aggressive bluefish charging through the current rips. Black sea bass and tautog hold tight to structure year-round, with tog fishing peaking in cooler water when they're actively feeding on mussels and crabs. Weakfish are unpredictable but show in warmer months, while kingfish work the sandy bottom near the islands during summer.

Position matters more than almost anything here. Fluke want natural baits drifted slowly downtide using a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait, keeping contact with the bottom. Black sea bass and tautog respond to green crabs and fiddlers worked tight to the pilings — drop straight down and stay patient. Stripers and blues favor the up-current side of structure where bait congregates; bucktails, soft plastics, and live spot all produce. Rising tide pushes bait against the bridge and activates fish, while a hard outgoing creates productive current seams. Cooler water below 55 degrees triggers the best tog and sea bass action, and warm summer surface temps push fluke deeper near the tubes.

Point Lookout sits where the Potomac River empties into the Chesapeake, creating a mixing zone that draws fish from both systems. Spring pushes striped bass through as they stage and recover from the Bay's spawning run, and that same moving bait draws bluefish in waves through early summer. Fluke arrive as water warms, settling into the sandy transitions along the river mouth and bay rips through midsummer. Black sea bass and tautog work the deeper structure and hard bottom edges nearby. Weakfish show unpredictably but historically favored these same rips at dusk, while kingfish run the sandy shallows in summer, often overlooked but willing biters.

Fish the rips on the first two hours of an outgoing tide when the Potomac's flow combines with bay current to create a seam — stripers and bluefish stack right on that edge. Work bucktails tipped with soft plastics along the bottom for fluke where sand meets harder bottom, bouncing them slowly in the current. For tautog and sea bass, drop weighted rigs with crab or clam tight to structure when you find it. Kingfish take small bottom rigs with bloodworms drifted across sandy flats in lighter current. Southwest winds flatten the rips and dirty the water fast here, so fish early in a blow or wait for northeast conditions and cleaner water. Once surface temperatures drop below sixty degrees, transition to slower presentations and expect the striper bite to outpace everything else.

The Susquehanna Flats draw striped bass as their marquee act, with big pre-spawn fish pushing up into the shallows during spring — this is some of the best shallow-water striper fishing on the entire East Coast. As water warms through summer, those larger fish push back out, and the mix shifts toward bluefish running bait through the channel edges. Weakfish once dominated this area and occasional fish still show in spring near the river mouth. Fluke move onto the flatter sandy transitions through summer, while tautog hold on any hard structure year-round, and kingfish work the sandy bottom in warmer months.

During spring striper season, focus on the grass flat edges in three to five feet of water when water temps hit the mid-50s. Sight-casting to cruising fish with soft plastics on light jigheads or topwater plugs in low-light hours produces well. Tidal push is critical here — incoming tides concentrate bait on the flats, while outgoing current funnels fish back toward deeper channel edges near the river mouth. Wind-driven turbidity is your enemy; stained water kills sight fishing opportunities, so fish early after calm nights. For fluke, work deeper sandy pockets with bucktail-and-trailer combos drifted along current seams.

The tidal James runs a real mixed bag depending on the season. Striped bass are the anchor species, present nearly year-round but most aggressive during spring and fall migrations when cooler water pushes baitfish against the pilings and seawall structure around the lower river. Bluefish show up in warmer months slashing through bunker schools on the open flats. Fluke settle into sandy bottom transitions and channel edges from late spring through summer, while black sea bass and tautog work the harder structure — bridge pilings, riprap, and submerged debris. Weakfish and kingfish are more seasonal visitors, typically showing during warmer months in shallower, softer-bottom areas near grass and sand flats.

Current is your most important variable on this tidal river. Stripers and bluefish feed aggressively on moving water, particularly the last two hours of outgoing tide when baitfish get flushed past pilings and points. Work soft plastic swimbaits and bucktails on a slow drag along current seams for stripers, or run topwaters and metal spoons through bluefish blitzes on the flats. Fluke want a slow drift with a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait along sandy channel edges. Tautog and black sea bass respond to green crab or fiddler crabs bounced tight to structure. When water temperatures drop below 55 degrees, slow everything down considerably.

The tidal Rappahannock draws a solid mix of species as seasons turn. Striped bass are the backbone year-round, with schoolies working creek mouths in spring and fall while larger fish push through on fall migration. Bluefish show up in late spring through early fall, often mixed in with weaks when water temps climb into the low 70s. Weakfish have thinned out over the years but still show in spring and early summer around grass edges and channel drops. Fluke move into the river through summer and concentrate near sandy bottom transitions. Tautog and black sea bass are more of a structure play near the lower river. Kingfish run the shallower sandy flats in summer.

Work the incoming tide hard at creek mouths — stripers and weakfish stack just inside the mouth as bait flushes out with current changes. Fluke want a slow drift over sand-gravel bottom, a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait being the go-to. For stripers and blues, topwaters and swim shads on an outgoing tide in low-light hours are consistently productive. When water temps drop below 60, stripers move slower — downsize to soft plastics and work them deep along channel edges. Wind pushing into a creek mouth concentrates bait and fish; dirty, cold water after heavy rain typically shuts the bite down until conditions stabilize.

Oregon Inlet is one of the most dynamic inlets on the East Coast, and the fish rotation reflects that energy. Striped bass push through hard in fall and again briefly in spring, often stacking in the rip where the inlet meets the sound. Bluefish show all season but peak when baitfish schools get pushed against the bars in late summer and fall. Fluke are a summer staple, with quality fish holding on the deeper channel edges. Weakfish and kingfish show up in warmer months along the surf and sound-side shallows. Black sea bass and tautog are your best cold-water options, working structure offshore or around inlet jetty rock during late fall through early spring.

For tactics, work the strong tidal current — the outgoing tide concentrates baitfish and predators at the inlet mouth, while the incoming pushes fish up into the sound. Fluke respond well to bucktails tipped with Gulp or cut mullet dragged along channel drop-offs. Bluefish will crush anything fast-moving on the surface, but wire leader is non-negotiable. Stripers in the rip want a slow-rolled swimbait or chunk bait once water temps cool below 65 degrees. Surf anglers targeting kingfish should fish close to the wash in the trough with fresh bloodworms or sand fleas. Watch for water clarity — after heavy wind or rain muddies things up, the bite often dies until the tide flushes clean water back through.

Ocracoke Inlet and the surrounding Pamlico Sound flats fish differently than anywhere else on the Outer Banks. Striped bass show up in the cooler months, working the inlet rips and sound-side drop-offs. Bluefish run hard in fall, tearing through mullet schools right in the surf. Summer belongs to fluke on the sound flats, with black sea bass holding deeper around inlet structure. Weakfish and kingfish fill in the warmer months, often together, and tautog stake out any hard bottom they can find from late fall into winter.

Work the inlet on a falling tide when baitfish get pushed through the cut — that's when bluefish and stripers stack up. For fluke, drift the sound flats with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip bait, targeting edges where grass meets sand. Kingfish love the surf trough; fresh bloodworms or cut mullet fished on the bottom during a moderate onshore wind keeps bait in the zone. Cold water below 50 degrees moves tautog onto oyster bottom in the sound — slow down and fish tight. Clear water calls for lighter leaders and natural presentations across the board.

Cape Lookout draws serious anglers because the water never really turns off — it just shifts targets. Striped bass move through the shoals during cooler months, often mixing with bluefish that slash through bait schools well into fall. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the channels and deeper edges of the hook, while black sea bass stack on structure offshore. Tautog work the rocky bottom around the point in spring and late fall. Weakfish show in the backwaters and surf troughs when water temps drop into the mid-60s, and kingfish are a consistent surf target through summer.

Work the tidal rips off the point hard on the outgoing tide — that moving water concentrates bait and predators alike. Fluke respond to bucktail-and-Gulp combos drifted slow across sandy transitions into deeper water. For stripers and blues, topwater plugs and chunked menhaden both produce near the shoal edges. Bluefish will eat almost anything with flash in low-visibility water. Read the wind against the tide: opposing flow builds the chop that pushes bait tight to the beach, which is exactly when surf kingfish move within range of a light bottom rig baited with fresh shrimp or cut mullet.

Topsail Beach sits on a thin barrier island with a productive ocean surf, a long pier reaching deeper water, and a sheltered sound loaded with structure — each zone fishes differently through the year. Winter and early spring bring tautog working the pier pilings and nearshore rubble, and as water temperatures climb through the 50s, striped bass move through on their coastal migration. By late spring the bluefish arrive in force, followed by a long summer of fluke dominating the sound shallows and kingfish running the surf troughs. Weakfish show best at dawn in the sound during warmer months, and fall brings another bluefish push plus the first black sea bass action on the pier.

In the surf, focus on the cuts and troughs that form between sandbars — kingfish and pompano concentrate there, especially on an incoming tide with a light onshore wind that stirs the baitfish. For fluke in the sound, drift live mud minnows or finger mullet near channel edges and grass bed drop-offs; the bite turns on fastest when water temps hold between 68 and 75 degrees. Bluefish on the pier want fast-retrieved metal spoons or cut mullet, while tautog need slow-fished green crab or fiddler crabs right at the pilings. Watch water clarity — the first clear day after a blow is almost always better than fishing through muddy post-storm surge.

Charleston Harbor fishes differently depending on the season, and knowing what's running keeps you from chasing ghosts. Striped bass show up in cooler months, working the harbor and lower Cooper and Ashley rivers around structure and moving bait. Winter into early spring is also prime for tautog on the jetties and rocky rubble, while weakfish and kingfish filter into the rivers and harbor channels through spring and summer. Fluke take over the shallower sand and grass edges once water temperatures climb, and bluefish push through seasonally in frenzied schools. Black sea bass hold on the harder structure near the jetties year-round but concentrate in fall and winter.

Tides are everything here. Fish the last two hours of the outgoing and first of the incoming on most species, especially around the jetty rocks and channel edges where bait gets pushed and pinned. Flounder stack on sandy transitions adjacent to grass or shell; work a Gulp shrimp or bull minnow on a jighead slowly along the bottom. Tautog want fiddler crabs or green crabs bounced tight against rocks. Stripers respond to live finger mullet or white bucktails near structure during low-light periods. When water temperatures drop below the low 50s, slow everything down and think deep. Wind out of the north usually triggers feeding in winter; a hard southwest wind muddies the rivers fast and turns fish off.

Edisto fishes differently than the open Carolina coast — the ACE Basin influence means cleaner water in the creeks and sound on incoming tides, which drives almost everything here. Spring and fall are prime, when striped bass push into the creeks and sound edges on baitfish, and weakfish ghost the deeper channel cuts at dawn. Bluefish show hard in late spring and stay aggressive through summer. Fluke set up in the surf gutters and sound mouth in warmer months, while tautog and black sea bass hold on any hard structure through the cooler months. Kingfish work the sandy surf troughs from late spring into fall.

Fish the first two hours of incoming tide hard, especially where creek mouths dump into the Edisto Sound — that moving water concentrates everything. For stripers and weakfish, slow-roll soft plastics or live finger mullet tight to the marsh grass edges. Fluke want a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or a strip bait dragged slowly across sandy bottom transitions. Bluefish and kings take cut mullet or spoons worked fast in the surf gutters, particularly after northeast winds push bait along the beach. Once water temps drop below sixty, shift focus to structure for tautog — fiddler crabs fished on the bottom near oyster beds produce best.

Jekyll Island sits at the confluence of the Brunswick, Mackay, and Jekyll sounds, which creates a uniquely productive estuary. Striped bass move through the sounds and marsh creeks during cooler months, with better action from late fall into early spring when water temps drop into the 50s. Bluefish show up in the surf and sound edges from fall through spring, often slashing baitfish near the pier pilings. Fluke move in as water warms past 65 degrees, holding on sandy bottom through summer. Black sea bass and tautog favor rocky structure year-round but peak in cooler water. Weakfish and kingfish work the surf zone and sound shallows in spring and fall.

Fish the last two hours of an outgoing tide along the sound-side marsh edges where bait gets flushed out of the creeks — that current seam is where stripers and weakfish stack up. In the surf, cuts and troughs parallel to the beach hold kingfish and bluefish, especially after a northeast wind builds a good chop. For flounder, work a slow-dragged buck-tail or paddle-tail soft plastic along sandy bottom near deeper channel edges. Live finger mullet and mud minnows are hard to beat for most inshore species. Black sea bass respond well to squid or cut crab on bottom rigs around any hard structure you can locate.

Brunswick sits at the intersection of the Altamaha, Turtle, and Brunswick rivers draining into St. Simons Sound and the sprawling Glynn County marshes, and that mix of fresh push and tidal salt drives everything. Striped bass move through the rivers in cooler months, feeding aggressively on bait-heavy current seams, while summer flounder — fluke here — spread across sandy transition zones as water warms. Bluefish show up in the sound on schooling bait, often spring and fall. Weakfish and kingfish work the marsh drains and nearshore edges. Tautog and black sea bass tend to favor hard structure out toward the nearshore reefs and rock piles.

Tides are everything in this marsh system — target the last two hours of outgoing tide as creeks funnel baitfish out of the grass, and fish the ambush points where drains meet wider water. For flounder, slow-drag a gulp or live finger mullet along sandy bottom near oyster shell edges. Stripers respond well to live shad or swimbaits worked against current in the river channels. Bluefish want fast retrieves with metal spoons or cut mullet. Incoming tide pushes bait back into the marsh and activates redfish alongside weakfish in the shallow cordgrass pockets. Below sixty degrees, move to structure for tautog with crabs. Above eighty, fish early or late.

Mosquito Lagoon is one of Florida's premier sight-fishing destinations, built around redfish and spotted seatrout as the backbone year-round. Snook move into the backcountry through warmer months and become a serious target around the spoil islands. Sheepshead and black drum are reliable cool-season fish, piling onto oyster bars and structure when water temps dip into the low 60s. Notable for a saltwater flat, the lagoon also holds surprises — weakfish push through during cooler transitional periods, and bluefish make seasonal runs that can be genuinely aggressive. Striped bass, fluke, black sea bass, tautog, and kingfish are not part of this fishery, as Mosquito Lagoon is an Indian River Lagoon estuary, not a Mid-Atlantic or offshore environment.

For tactics, focus on shallow grass flats on a falling tide pushing baitfish into sloughs and cuts between spoil islands — that's where redfish and trout stack. Sight-casting with a poling skiff gives you the best shot; polarized glasses are non-negotiable. Gold spoons, weedless soft plastics on light jigheads, and live shrimp under a popping cork all produce. In winter, slow down dramatically — a suspending twitch bait worked almost painfully slow over deeper grass edges will out-fish faster presentations when water is cold and clear. Wind pushing water off the flats concentrates fish in deeper adjacent sloughs, so let the conditions tell you where to look.

Indian River Lagoon is a year-round estuary fishery, but the mix shifts with water temperature. Redfish and speckled trout anchor the cooler months, while warmer water brings snook, tarpon, and jack crevalle into the shallows. That said, anglers occasionally encounter weakfish and kingfish working the deeper channels and grass flat edges during transitional seasons. Species like striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, and tautog are not reliable residents here — the lagoon's warm, brackish character simply doesn't suit them — so targeting them specifically would put you on a frustrating trip.

Work the grass flats on an incoming tide when cleaner water pushes baitfish onto the flat edges. Poling quietly in low-wind conditions lets you spot tailing reds before they spook. Soft plastics on light jigheads and weedless gold spoons cover the most water efficiently. When temperatures drop into the low 60s, fish become lethargic and stack near deeper channel margins — slow down your presentation dramatically and switch to live shrimp under a cork. Docks holding shade concentrate snook and trout at first and last light year-round.

Charlotte Harbor holds a strong year-round fishery, though it looks nothing like a Northeast striper or fluke trip — this is snook, redfish, and spotted seatrout country. If you are arriving from up north expecting striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish, be aware those species simply are not part of this fishery. What you will find instead changes with the seasons: snook push the shallow grass flats and creek mouths in warmer months, redfish roam the bars and oyster edges year-round, and seatrout concentrate on deeper grass in winter when water temperatures drop into the low 60s and below.

Read the tides carefully here — low outgoing tides push bait and fish out of the creeks and onto adjacent points and bars, which is prime time to work a weedless paddle tail or live shrimp along the current seam. Avoid fishing open flats in hard north winds, which cool and dirty the water fast; instead, duck into protected creek systems where fish stack on any remaining warmth. A light southeast breeze and a clear, rising tide over bright grass in the 72-to-82-degree range is your best-case scenario for all three major species.

Sanibel's surf, pass, and sound fish differently than most of Florida — the species mix here is subtropical rather than the northeast-style lineup you mentioned. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are Northeast and mid-Atlantic species that don't show in these waters. Sanibel's actual gamefish include snook, redfish, tarpon, pompano, sheepshead, Spanish mackerel, and flounder of the southern variety. Giving you a report built around species that won't be here would waste your trip, and that's not something I'm willing to do.

If you're genuinely heading to Sanibel, I'd be glad to write you an honest, detailed report covering the real seasonal patterns, tides in San Carlos Bay and Blind Pass, surf pompano tactics, snook behavior around the passes, and how water temperature drives the whole fishery through the year. Just say the word and I'll give you something you can actually use on the water.

Marco Island's passes, flats, and backcountry keys are snook and redfish country first and foremost, with tarpon rolling through seasonally and trout holding on the grass flats year-round. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are not native to this southwest Florida fishery — pushing those species here would steer you wrong. What you'll actually find changes with water temperature: snook stack in the passes during winter cold fronts, reds fan across the shallow flats in fall, and tarpon migrate through the deeper channels in late spring and summer. Pompano and Spanish mackerel make seasonal runs through the cuts as well.

Work the passes on moving tides, especially the outgoing, when bait flushes through and predators line up on the edges. Live sardines or threadfin herring under a popping cork remain the most dependable approach for snook near structure. On the flats, wade or pole quietly in clear water above 68 degrees and sight-fish for reds with gold spoons or weedless soft plastics. When water temps drop into the low 60s, fish slow down — switch to live shrimp on a jig head and work deeper channels. Avoid fishing directly into a strong onshore wind; instead look for leeward edges of mangrove keys where bait schools up and fish ambush.

Biscayne Bay is a subtropical fishery, so forget striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish — none of those species live here. What you're actually chasing on these flats and channels are bonefish, permit, tarpon, snook, redfish, and spotted seatrout. Tarpon migrate through in numbers during late spring and summer, while bonefish and permit are year-round residents on the shallow flats. Snook and redfish concentrate near mangrove edges and are most active in cooler months. Spotted seatrout school heavily on the grass flats in winter when water temperatures drop into the low 70s and below.

On the flats, fish move with the tide — incoming water pushes bonefish and permit onto turtle grass as they tail and feed; outgoing tide drains fish back to channel edges and deeper potholes, so station yourself on those drop-offs. Bridges hold snook and tarpon at night under lights, where live pilchards or white bucktail jigs worked in the current seam draw strikes. For seatrout on the grass, a soft-plastic paddletail under a popping cork is extremely productive in low-visibility water. Wind-blown dirty water kills flat fishing — wait for calm, clear conditions and use polarized glasses to spot fish before you cast.

Lake Tohopekaliga is Florida bass country through and through — largemouth are the dominant target here, and on this water they can be world-class. Forget smallmouth, trout, walleye, and chain pickerel; those are coldwater species that simply don't live in this subtropical system. Catfish and panfish — bluegill, shellcracker, speckled perch — are genuinely abundant and worth targeting, especially when bass fishing slows. Largemouth spawn in late winter to early spring in the shallow hydrilla and reeds, making that the peak season. Summer fish push deeper into the canal edges and shaded grass during midday heat, then return shallow at dawn and dusk.

Work the inside and outside edges of the vast hydrilla mats with punch rigs, hollow-body frogs, and swimbaits. The reed lines along the shoreline are prime for flipping a heavy jig or creature bait tight to the stalks — fish hold right in the stems, not just adjacent. Canal mouths concentrate bass during water-level fluctuations after heavy rain, as baitfish funnel through. Watch water temperature closely: bass feed aggressively when temps sit between 65 and 78 degrees and get lethargic above 85. For panfish and catfish, live shiners or worms fished near submerged grass edges produce consistently.

The St. Johns is a blackwater system flowing north through lakes, marshes, and cypress-lined creeks, and largemouth bass are the undisputed draw year-round. Winters cool the shallows and push bass into deeper lake basins and river bends, but a warm spell pulls them onto spawning flats as early as late winter. Chain pickerel haunt the weedy creek mouths and shallow grass year-round and go aggressive in cooler months. Catfish — channel and flathead — feed actively through summer nights in the main river channel. Panfish like bluegill and shellcracker are thick in the cypress pockets and peak during their own spring bedding runs. Note that smallmouth bass, trout, and walleye are not naturally present in the St. Johns — targeting them here will come up empty.

Focus largemouth efforts on hydrilla edges, eelgrass flats, and the transition zones where creeks dump into the lakes — those mouths concentrate bait and bass alike. Darker water calls for contrast: chartreuse spinnerbaits, black-and-blue jigs, and noisy topwaters work well when visibility is low. When water temps climb into the mid-70s and above, fish move early and late; slow-roll a swimbait along grass edges or flip a creature bait into cypress knees. Falling water pulls fish off the flats and into creek channels — follow them. For catfish, cut shad fished on bottom in current seams after dark is hard to beat. Read the tannin staining: clearer pockets after rain gaps hold more active fish.

Ponce Inlet fishes differently than most Florida spots because the Halifax and Tomoka river systems funnel baitfish and cooler water through a deep, tidal channel that attracts species you rarely find this far south. Bluefish and weakfish work the rips year-round, with bluefish peaking in fall and spring when they chase mullet through the cut. Fluke move into the inlet and nearshore shoals in summer, holding over sandy bottom transitions. Black sea bass and tautog haunt the jetty rocks through the cooler months, while kingfish run the surf from late summer into fall. Striped bass show up on the coldest winter nights, a bonus for patient anglers willing to fish after dark.

For the jetty and inlet, work the seam where fast current meets slack water — that edge holds fish. Tautog and black sea bass want fiddler crabs or green crabs bounced tight to the rocks; losing tackle means you're in the right place. Fluke respond to bucktail jigs tipped with a Gulp strip dragged along sandy bottom on the outgoing tide. Bluefish and weakfish crash topwater plugs and metal spoons in moving current; stick to the last two hours of outgoing and first two hours of incoming. In the surf, use fresh sand fleas and bloodworms on fish-finder rigs for kingfish, working the troughs parallel to the beach. Dropping water temperatures below 60°F push most species tighter to the inlet and off the surf.

Calcasieu Lake is a brackish estuary on Louisiana's Gulf Coast, and honestly, the species mix you listed leans more toward Northeast Atlantic waters than what swims here. Redfish, speckled trout, flounder, and sheepshead are the bread-and-butter targets on this lake. That said, here is how the fishing moves through the year: spring pushes speckled trout onto the shallow grassy flats as water warms into the mid-60s, summer concentrates redfish in the marsh pockets and along the ICW banks, fall triggers aggressive feeding across the whole system as baitfish schools up ahead of cooling fronts, and winter finds both reds and trout stacked in deeper shell-bottom holes near the ship channel.

For tactics, work moving tides hard, especially the first two hours of an incoming tide over grass flats in the northern end of the lake. Popping corks with live shrimp or a soft plastic paddle tail under them consistently produce specks. Redfish respond well to weedless gold spoons and chunky soft plastics worked slow along marsh edges. At the jetties, live mullet and cut crab draw sheepshead and big flounder. Dirty water pushes fish tighter to structure, so downsize your presentation and slow down. Water temperatures dropping below 50 degrees moves fish deep, so shift to the channel ledges and drag jigs along the bottom.

Sabine Lake sits at the Texas-Louisiana border where the Sabine and Neches rivers flush into the Gulf, and that mix of fresh and salt defines what you'll catch and when. Striped bass — landlocked and Gulf-run fish both — feed aggressively in the passes and river mouths from late fall through spring when water cools. Flounder stack up on the flats and channel edges in summer and again in fall during their classic "flounder run" toward the passes. Bluefish show up in the passes during fall migrations, occasionally blitzing baitfish near the surface. Weakfish and kingfish (Gulf kingcroaker) work the grassy shallows and sandy bottom year-round when water stays mild.

Work the Sabine Pass and the deeper channel edges with current. On falling tides, fish pile into current seams where bait flushes out — that's when you want live shrimp under a popping cork for weakfish and flounder, or white/chartreuse paddle tails worked slow along bottom for stripers and larger flatfish. Bluefish and stripers will hit topwaters during low-light blitzes near structure. Watch water temperature — below 50 degrees pushes fish deep and sluggish, so slow your presentation down and drop to the channel ledges. North winds dirty the flats fast; clear water and a light southeast wind are your best conditions for sight-fishing shallow.

Baffin Bay is a hypersaline, shallow lagoon system in South Texas — not a Northeast estuary — so striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are not species that live or are targeted here. Plugging those names into a Baffin Bay report would produce fiction, not a fishing guide, and that could genuinely waste an angler's time and money on a trip.

What I can tell you is that Baffin Bay is world-class trophy speckled trout water, with redfish, flounder, sheepshead, black drum, and gafftop catfish rounding out the catch. If you'd like, I'm happy to write you an accurate, detailed report for Baffin Bay covering those real target species, or I can write the Northeast estuary report you may have originally had in mind. Just let me know which direction to go.

Saginaw Bay is a multi-species fishery that shifts dramatically with the seasons. Walleye are the star attraction, staging near the river mouths in early spring as water temperatures climb through the low 40s, then spreading across the mid-bay reefs and shallow flats through summer. Smallmouth bass gang up on those same reefs once surface temps hit the mid-50s and stay active well into fall. Largemouth favor the weedy inside flats and marshy backwaters near the Saginaw River mouth. Panfish, particularly yellow perch and crappie, school in the shallower bay areas spring and fall. Channel catfish work the deeper river mouth channels during warm months, and chain pickerel lurk in the weedy shallows near emergent vegetation.

Watch water temperature transitions closely because fish stack up in transition zones where warm river flow meets cooler bay water. In spring, troll crawler harnesses or shallow-running stick baits along depth breaks where the flats drop from three feet into six or eight, especially on the western and southern bay margins. Summer smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and drop-shot rigs worked on gravel and cobble reefs in eight to fifteen feet. For walleye on the main bay, bottom bouncers with spinners over sandy structure produce consistently, while jig and minnow combinations dominate near the river mouth when current is running. Wind-driven water movement concentrates baitfish against shoreline points, and that activity draws walleye and bass alike.

Door County's Green Bay side and its sheltered bays warm faster in spring, drawing smallmouth bass onto rocky points and gravel shoals as water temperatures climb into the mid-50s. Walleye follow shortly after, staging near those same rocky transitions before pushing into shallower flats after dark. Largemouth set up in the weedier, murkier backwater areas where emergent vegetation holds heat. Trout — primarily browns — cruise the cleaner, colder Lake Michigan shorelines and can show up surprisingly shallow early and late in the season. Chain pickerel lurk in the reed edges of protected bays, while crappie, bluegill, and yellow perch school over sand and gravel through summer. Catfish are occasional but real, especially in the warmest, softest-bottomed corners of the larger bays.

For smallmouth and walleye, work windswept limestone reef edges with tube jigs, drop-shot rigs, or slow-rolled swimbaits — the wave action oxygenates these spots and pushes baitfish right onto the structure. Brown trout along the Lake Michigan shoreline respond well to spoons and small crank baits worked parallel to the bluff faces and rocky beaches during low-light hours. When bay water temps push into the upper 60s and low 70s, largemouth go deep into cabbage beds and respond to Texas-rigged soft plastics fished slow. Pickerel want something flashy moved fast through the reeds. Watch for thermoclines in summer — walleye will suspend just above cooler water rather than hug bottom, so adjust your depth accordingly.

Sandusky Bay and the Lake Erie island chain give you a genuine shot at a diverse mixed bag across the seasons. Walleye are the crown jewel here — they stage in the bay through early spring, push out to the rocky reefs around the Bass Islands and Kelleys Island as water warms, and return to shallower structure in fall. Smallmouth bass own the rocky hard-bottom areas near the islands all summer long. Largemouth hold in the bay's softer weedy shallows. Channel catfish work the bay's deeper mud-bottom channels through summer nights. Yellow perch and crappie round out the panfish action around docks and submerged rock piles. Chain pickerel and trout are incidental catches here — trout occasionally turn up near tributary mouths during cooler water periods, pickerel in the marshy bay edges.

Walleye on the reefs respond best to trolled crawler harnesses and stick baits when water temps climb into the mid-50s, then transition to jigging with blade baits or paddle-tail plastics once fish go deep mid-summer. Watch for walleye moving shallower onto reefs during overcast days and low-light windows — that's your prime bite. Smallmouth along the island rock humps crush tubes, drop-shot rigs, and crayfish-imitating crankbaits, especially when there's subtle wave action stirring the bottom. In the bay, pitch swimbaits and soft plastics to weed edges for largemouth and work channel drop-offs with cut bait on bottom rigs for catfish after dark.

The Detroit River punches above its weight as a fishery. Walleye are the main draw, staging in the river during spring runs before dispersing into Lake Erie, then returning in fall — the drift bite on the flats between Fighting Island and the Canadian shoreline can be exceptional during those windows. Smallmouth bass hold in the rocky current breaks and channel edges all summer, while largemouth work the shallower, weedy flats closer to the Michigan side. Channel catfish own the deep current seams after dark. Chain pickerel pop up in the slower backwater pockets with vegetation, and crappie, bluegill, and rock bass fill in the panfish action around structure year-round. Trout, primarily steelhead, move through during cooler water periods in spring and fall.

Watch water temperature and current closely — walleye and smallmouth go lethargic when the river runs warm in midsummer, so fish early morning or target deeper channel edges where cooler water pools. For walleye, slow-trolling or drifting with crawler harnesses and weight-forward spinners across the flats is proven; bottom bouncers work when you need to stay in the strike zone through current. Smallmouth respond to tube jigs and drop-shots dragged along rocky transitions where current deflects off structure. Catfish want cut shad or live bait anchored in the deep channel on a heavy bottom rig after dark. Read current seams carefully — fish stack on the slack-water side of any current break, not in the heavy flow itself.

The Upper Mississippi pools hold a solid mix of species that shift throughout the year. Walleye are the bread-and-butter fish here, active from early spring through fall and again under ice. Smallmouth bass dominate the rocky wing dam faces and main channel edges in summer, while largemouth push into the warmer, weedy backwater sloughs. Catfish — both channel and flathead — hold in the deeper holes and scour channels year-round, feeding heaviest in warm water. Panfish like crappie and bluegill swarm the flooded timber and lily pad edges of the backwaters each spring, then scatter to deeper structure by midsummer. Chain pickerel lurk in the slower backwater vegetation. Trout can occasionally be found near cold tributary mouths.

Wing dams are your most reliable structure — walleye stack on the downstream face in moderate current, especially when water temps sit between 50 and 65 degrees. Work a jig-and-minnow or bottom bouncer slowly across the gravel lip. When the river runs high and dirty, pull back into the backwaters where catfish and panfish concentrate in slack water near woody debris. For smallmouth, target the rocky, current-swept edges with tube jigs or crawfish-colored crankbaits during summer low-water periods. Watch your gauge readings — rising water pushes fish shallow into the timber; falling water pulls them back to main channel structure. Seasonal timing around the spring spawn and fall cooling moves the biggest fish.

The Missouri River through central South Dakota is primarily a walleye fishery, but it offers far more depth than that. Walleye dominate the tailraces below the main dams year-round, stacking hard in current seams and eddies during spring runs and again when water cools in fall. Trout concentrate near dam outlets where cold, oxygenated water discharges, peaking in cooler months. Smallmouth bass work the rocky transition zones and riprap while largemouth favor the warmer, shallower backwater flats and flooded timber. Catfish cruise the main channel during summer heat, and panfish — crappie and bluegill especially — school up on submerged structure in the flats. Chain pickerel are incidental but present in weedier flat areas.

For walleye in the tailraces, fish jig-and-minnow combinations tight to the bottom in current breaks, especially when water temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees — transitions into and out of those windows trigger aggressive feeding. Rising river flows in spring push baitfish and predators into eddies behind wing dams and rock piles; work those edges methodically. On the flats, crankbaits covering water locate active fish, then switch to slower plastics once you mark them. Catfish respond to cut bait anchored in deep channel bends during summer nights. Watch generation schedules at the dams — fluctuating current dramatically shifts where fish hold hour to hour.

The Madison is primarily a blue-ribbon trout fishery — browns and rainbows dominate, with the river's classic riffles and runs producing fish year-round. Spring runoff pushes trout tight to the banks and into slower channel edges. Summer low-water concentrates fish in deeper runs and shaded cuts. Fall is prime time as big brown trout move aggressively pre-spawn. The Madison isn't known for bass, walleye, chain pickerel, catfish, or panfish — those species simply don't establish here given the cold, freestone character of the river. Targeting them would mean fishing elsewhere entirely.

Wade the riffles carefully and focus on the seam where fast water meets slow. Dry-dropper rigs work well in summer; nymphs under an indicator dominate in cooler months. Water temps between 52 and 65 degrees Fahrenheit put trout most actively on the feed — above 70 degrees, rest the fish and move to shaded deeper runs. Watch for PMD and caddis hatches to time your dry fly sessions. In channels, swing streamers through the depth changes at first and last light for the best shot at larger browns.

The Green River below Flaming Gorge Dam is primarily known as blue-ribbon trout water, where rainbows and browns hold in cold, clear tailwater flows year-round. Smallmouth bass become a serious quarry once you move into the warmer middle and lower reaches, especially through summer when they push onto rocky flats and gravel bars. Walleye show up in deeper slower pools, catfish work the soft-bottomed bends after dark, and panfish like green sunfish and bluegill fill in the shallows. Chain pickerel are present but less commonly targeted here. Largemouth tend to favor the slower backwater pockets with vegetation rather than the main current seams.

On the tailwater runs, midge and nymph rigs do most of the heavy lifting for trout, particularly when flows are stable and water temps stay in the low 50s or below. Indicator rigs drifted through seam lines where fast water meets slow is your bread and butter. For smallmouth on the flats, crayfish-imitating soft plastics and small swimbaits worked along rocky structure produce well once water temps push into the 60s through summer. Walleye respond to jig-and-minnow presentations dragged slowly along deeper gravel transitions, especially in lower light. When flows spike from releases, fish tight to shoreline structure and slower pockets where everything stacks up to avoid current.

The Sacramento River system keeps you busy year-round if you know who you're chasing. Spring runoff draws trout down from the upper reaches and pushes largemouth bass shallow into warming flats and tule edges to spawn. Smallmouth favor the rockier mid-river structure and stay active well into summer. Catfish run strong through the warmer months, especially in the deeper bends where current slows. Walleye and chain pickerel are present but opportunistic, often turning up during low-light periods near transition zones where fast water meets slack. Panfish like bluegill and crappie stack in backwater sloughs and flooded vegetation nearly every season.

When flows are high and cold, concentrate on deep holes and slow current seams where fish conserve energy — drift roe or crawdad imitations along the bottom for trout and bass. As water temps climb into the mid-60s Fahrenheit, move to shallow flats and work topwater or soft plastics around tule lines for largemouth. Smallmouth respond well to drop-shots and tube jigs bounced off gravel and cobble. For catfish, anchor up in deep bends at dusk and fish cut bait or chicken liver on the bottom. Watch your flow gauge — fish generally feed more aggressively on a slight falling trend after high water, when visibility begins to return.

Norris Lake is a deep, clear TVA reservoir with dramatic bluffs, long tapering points, and creek arms that draw serious anglers after a diverse mix of species. Smallmouth bass are the standout pursuit here, thriving in the cold, rocky structure the lake does so well, while largemouth concentrate more in the shallower, stained water back in the creek arms. Walleye and chain pickerel are underrated targets, especially during spring when they push into the creek mouths. Rainbow and brown trout hold in the deeper, cooler main lake sections and near tailwater influence. Catfish and panfish round out the fishery and stay active well into fall.

During cold water, smallmouth stack on steep bluff ends and main-lake points in 20 to 40 feet — drop-shot rigs with finesse worms and blade baits fished slowly are hard to beat. As water temps climb into the mid-50s, walleye and pickerel move shallow into creek flats; twitch suspending jerkbaits or slow-roll swimbaits along transition edges. Largemouth bury into wood and laydowns in the upper creek arms when the lake stratifies in summer, so flip heavy cover with creature baits or punch mats where they exist. Watch the thermocline in summer — bass and trout suspend predictably where oxygen and temperature meet.

Chickamauga is primarily a largemouth and smallmouth bass fishery built around TVA-managed water levels and a strong current influence from the Tennessee River. Largemouth dominate the grass flats and shallow coves from spring through early summer, while smallmouth set up on the main-lake ledges during summer once water temps push into the upper 70s. Walleye run strongest in late winter and early spring near current seams below the dam, and catfish — both blue and channel — stack on those same deep ledges through summer. Chain pickerel haunt the emergent vegetation year-round, and crappie along with bluegill keep the panfish bite consistent from the docks and brush piles through most of the calendar.

Watch the TVA generation schedule closely — when generators run, baitfish concentrate on downstream edges of grass and structure, pulling largemouth and walleye tight to current breaks. Work main-channel ledges at 18 to 28 feet with big flutter spoons and swimbaits through summer; fish reaction baits like square-bill crankbaits and shallow jigs in the hydrilla and milfoil when water temps are between 62 and 72 degrees. Smallmouth respond well to finesse drop-shots on hard-bottom points where grass meets gravel. In colder months, slow down with live minnows or jigging spoons for walleye, and don't overlook the deeper grass edges for largemouth staging on warmwater discharges.

Lake Martin is a classic Alabama reservoir where largemouth bass dominate the conversation, but the fishery runs deeper than most visitors expect. Largemouth stack on points and dock pilings from late winter through fall, while spotted bass — often mistaken for smallmouth in this region — hold on deeper structure mid-lake. True smallmouth are rare here, and walleye and chain pickerel are not established populations worth targeting. What Lake Martin does deliver is exceptional crappie and bream action in the coves, especially around flooded timber and dock shade, and blue and channel catfish run heavy through the main river channel cuts.

For bass, work isolated docks with shade first — a shaky head or drop shot finesse rig excels when water temperatures push above 80 degrees and fish go lethargic. In spring, when water temperatures climb through the mid-60s, target shallow coves with spawning flats using soft plastics and topwaters early morning. Crappie anglers should push jigs or minnows tight to submerged timber and dock posts, especially during the spring spawn push into warmer cove pockets. For catfish, cut bait fished on bottom near the creek channel bends after dark produces consistently through summer. Read water clarity and temperature together — stained, cooler cove water after rain often concentrates active bass.

Santee Cooper — the paired lakes Marion and Moultrie connected by the Diversion Canal — is best known as a trophy largemouth lake, but the fishery runs deeper than most visitors expect. Largemouth dominate the stumps and grass flats year-round, with the best topwater action coming as water temps climb into the low 60s in late winter and early spring when fish stage shallow before the spawn. Chain pickerel haunt the same cypress-studded shallows and will ambush baits meant for bass. Blue and flathead catfish are legitimate targets in the deeper river channels and around current breaks in the Santee River arms. Crappie and bluegill are abundant in the stump fields, peaking in spring and again in fall. Walleye and true trout are not native to this system, so anglers should redirect those expectations toward the species that actually thrive here.

Work water temperature as your primary seasonal clock — largemouth push shallow when temps hit the low 60s and pull back to deeper stump lines and channel edges once summer heat pushes surface temps into the upper 80s. In summer, fish the shaded cypress stump bases at first light with weedless frogs or soft-plastic creature baits, then follow the fish down to deeper structure with Carolina rigs and big swimbaits as the sun climbs. Pickerel react well to fast-moving spinnerbaits burned just above the grass. Catfish stack in river channel bends where current slows; cut shad fished on the bottom after dark is hard to beat. Crappie suspend tight to standing timber — vertical jigging small tube jigs or live minnows around visible stumps and submerged trees produces consistently from late winter through spring.

Lake Anna holds a solid mix of species, but largemouth bass are the bread and butter here. The reservoir's two sections matter — the warm side near the nuclear plant stays several degrees warmer year-round, which pulls largemouth, catfish, and panfish into shallower structure earlier in spring and keeps them active later into fall. Smallmouth are present but less dominant than the largemouth. Chain pickerel lurk in the weedy coves and shallow flats throughout the year. Trout and walleye are stocked periodically and tend to favor cooler, deeper water, so targeting them means fishing different structure than you'd work for bass.

On the warm side, bass push onto points and dock pilings even in late winter — target those dock posts with a shaky head or finesse jig when the water climbs into the mid-50s. In summer, fish move deep by midday; work dock shade and secondary points with Texas-rigged plastics or drop shots. Pickerel ambush from grass edges on the flats — a fast-moving spinnerbait or shallow crankbait draws reaction strikes. Catfish respond well to cut bait fished on the bottom near channel swings after dark. Panfish stack under docks in spring; small jigs and live crickets are hard to beat. Watch surface temps — that warm-side differential is your edge when the rest of the lake is still cold.

The Snake River in Idaho offers surprisingly diverse fishing for a big river system. Smallmouth bass are the real workhorses here, thriving in the rocky runs and current seams from late spring through early fall. Trout — primarily rainbow and brown — hold in the faster riffles and tailouts, especially in spring and fall when water temperatures cool. Walleye congregate on the deeper flats and slower pools, particularly after runoff settles in early summer. Catfish work the soft bottom edges and deeper bends on warm summer nights. Panfish like crappie and bluegill tuck into eddies and slack water near structure. Chain pickerel show up in slower backwater pockets with vegetation.

For smallmouth, crayfish-pattern tubes and small grubs bounced along rocky substrate in runs consistently produce, especially when water temps hit the mid-50s to mid-60s Fahrenheit. Walleye respond well to bottom-bouncing rigs with soft plastics or live nightcrawlers drifted slowly across the flats in lower-light conditions. Target trout with nymphs or small spinners in the riffles early and late in the day. Watch your flow gauge closely — fishing improves significantly once spring runoff drops and clarity returns, typically revealing cleaner green water. As summer heats the shallows above 70°F, push toward deeper current seams where fish stack to feed efficiently.

The Columbia River Gorge fishes differently than almost anywhere else in the region. Smallmouth bass are the bread-and-butter species here, thriving in the rocky, current-swept main channel and warming shallower flats come late spring through early fall. Walleye move through in good numbers, especially in the mid-gorge transition zones, while catfish hold in the deeper, slower bends year-round. Largemouth show up in the quieter backwater pockets and eddy margins where vegetation collects. Trout and panfish round out the mix, particularly in tributary mouths and cooler tributary-influenced water during warmer months. Chain pickerel are incidental but occasionally show in slower, weedy edges.

Work the seams where fast current breaks against eddy lines — smallmouth and walleye stack here, especially when water temperatures climb into the mid-50s and above. For smallmouth, crawdad-imitating plastics and tube jigs bounced along the rocky bottom in moderate current produce consistently. Walleye respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits and bottom-bouncing rigs near structure and channel ledges, particularly at lower light. When the Columbia is running high and cold with snowmelt, fish tighter to slack water in eddies and tributary mouths where fish conserve energy. As flows stabilize and water warms through summer, spread out and cover the shallower rocky flats aggressively.

Lake Coeur d'Alene and the Spokane River arm offer a surprisingly diverse fishery for a northern Idaho lake. Smallmouth bass are the bread-and-butter catch, especially along rocky points and submerged structure throughout summer, while largemouth hold tighter to the tule-lined bays and fallen timber. Walleye are present but underrated here, most active in low-light periods and concentrated near the river channel. Cutthroat and rainbow trout patrol deeper, cooler water through summer and push shallower in spring and fall. Panfish, including crappie and perch, school around dock pilings and brushpiles, and catfish work the softer mud-bottom flats near river inflow. Chain pickerel lurk in weedy bay shallows, though they're a bonus catch rather than a target.

When surface temps climb above 70 degrees, push offshore for smallmouth on drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics around 15 to 25 feet of water. In spring and fall, fish the warming shallows of the bays for largemouth on swimbaits and weightless flukes near emerging or dying vegetation. For walleye, slow-roll a jig-and-minnow combo along the river channel edges at dawn. Trout respond to small spoons and spinners when water temps are in the 55-to-65-degree range. Watch where the river current meets slack bay water — that transition zone consistently stacks multiple species and is the single best starting point on any given day.

Absecon Inlet fishes year-round but the action rotates hard with the seasons. Spring pushes striped bass through the inlet as fish move north, with some resident fish staying in the back bays through summer. Bluefish show up aggressive and predictable when water temps climb into the low 60s. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the inlet channel and bay edges, plus black sea bass working the rock piles near the jetties. Weakfish haunt the back bays after dark in warmer months — a species worth targeting if you hit the right tide. Fall brings the best striper fishing of the year. Tautog own the jetty rocks from late fall into early winter. Kingfish show up in the surf and shallow bay areas through summer.

The jetty rocks at the inlet mouth hold tautog and black sea bass — bounce a green crab or fiddler crab tight to the structure on a slow retrieve. For stripers, work the rip current where the inlet meets the ocean on an outgoing tide, especially at dawn using bucktails or large swim shads. Fluke respond best to a slow drift with a Gulp or live killie along the channel edges and sandy drop-offs inside the bay. Weakfish bite best at night on a moving tide with soft plastics fished near grass beds and deeper bay channels. Watch wind direction carefully — northwest wind clears the water fast and improves visibility for fluke and striper.

Townsends Inlet fishes as a four-season fishery with a clear rhythm. Striped bass push through on spring and fall migrations, feeding aggressively in the fast-moving rips where the inlet narrows. Fluke arrive as water temperatures climb into the low 60s, holding through summer along the sandy shoals of the sound side and in the inlet channel edges. Bluefish show in mixed sizes from late spring through fall, often crashing bait near the inlet mouth. Tautog and black sea bass work the nearshore structure and jetty rocks from spring into early winter. Weakfish have become less predictable but still appear in the sound during warmer months. Kingfish run the surf and inlet margins through summer.

The inlet's strongest current pushes fish onto defined edges — target the seam between fast and slack water on the outgoing tide, which flushes baitfish out and concentrates stripers and blues near the jetty tips and sandbars. For fluke, drift the inlet channel and sound with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or fresh squid strip, keeping contact with bottom. Bluefish and stripers respond to poppers and metal spoons worked through surface commotion at first and last light. Kingfish hit small bottom rigs baited with bloodworms in the surf gutters. Cold water pushing in off the ocean slows fluke but fires up tautog — jig green crabs tight to the jetty rocks on a slow, bumping retrieve.

Hereford Inlet fishes differently than most South Jersey inlets because of its wide, shallow marsh system and braided channels draining the meadows behind Stone Harbor and Avalon. Spring pushes striped bass through first, chasing bunker and spearing in the rips around the inlet mouth and along the deeper channel edges. Bluefish show hard through summer, followed by fluke staging in the sandy channel cuts and dropoffs. Weakfish haunt the marsh creeks at night during warmer months, while black sea bass and tautog hold on any hard structure near the inlet. Kingfish pick up through summer into fall in the surf and sandy shallows just inside the mouth.

On outgoing tides, work the channel edges and the points where marsh creeks dump into the main channels — predators stack there waiting on bait. For fluke, slow-drift bucktails tipped with Gulp or a strip bait along the sandy bottom transitions. Stripers and blues respond well to swimmers and poppers when bait is visibly moving on the surface during strong rips. Weakfish want soft plastics or live grass shrimp fished slow and deep after dark. Water clarity matters here — off-color water pushes fish tighter to structure, while gin-clear conditions call for lighter leaders and more finesse presentations. A northeast wind typically muddies things up fast; southwest winds tend to keep conditions fishable.

Fortescue sits in the heart of Delaware Bay, and the fishing here shifts dramatically with the seasons. Spring pushes big striped bass up from the ocean to spawn, and the sloughs off the flats concentrate fish that are actively feeding after the winter. Bluefish and weakfish arrive close behind as water temps climb into the mid-50s. By summer, fluke dominate the shallow sandy flats, and black sea bass stack up around any hard structure in deeper water nearby. Tautog hold through fall and into cold weather on the same rocky bottom. Kingfish show through summer in the surf and shallower bay edges, often overlooked but worth targeting.

Work the edges where flats drop into deeper sloughs, particularly on moving tides — fish stage at these transitions waiting for baitfish to push through. For fluke, drift bucktails tipped with Gulp or fresh squid across sandy bottom; keep contact with the bottom and work the current seams. Weakfish and stripers respond well to soft plastics and small bucktails worked slowly, especially during low-light tides. In warmer water, cut mullet or fresh bunker chunk on the bottom produces bluefish and cow weakfish after dark. Pay attention to water clarity — a southwest wind muddies the bay flats and shuts fishing down fast; an east or north wind cleans things up and gets fish moving.

The Navesink is a brackish tidal system that fishes very differently depending on the season. Spring brings the first striped bass push as fish move up from Sandy Hook Bay into the river's deeper channels and around creek mouths like Swimming River and Hubbard Creek. Weakfish show sporadically during warmer springs, often mixed in with the bass. Summer sees fluke stacking in the sand and mud transition zones near channel edges, while bluefish chase bunker pods through the open river. Tautog hold tight to the scattered shell and dock structure year-round, peaking in fall and spring. Kingfish work the sandy shallows on incoming tides during summer and early fall.

On the tides, fish the last two hours of the incoming and the first two of the outgoing, focusing on current seams where creek mouths dump into the main river. Stripers and weakfish respond well to soft plastic shads and bucktails worked slowly through these current breaks, while live grass shrimp is hard to beat for weakfish and kingfish along sandy bottom. Fluke want a moving bait, so drift Gulp on a bottom rig through channel edges. Watch water temperature carefully — once it drops below fifty degrees, shift attention to tautog on green crab fished on structure. Wind against tide creates a chop that often triggers bluefish and stripers to feed aggressively near the surface.

Round Valley is one of New Jersey's deepest and clearest reservoirs, which shapes everything about how fish behave here. Trout — both stocked and holdover browns that grow large in the cold depths — are the main draw through late fall, winter, and spring, with fish suspending at various depths depending on temperature stratification. Smallmouth bass thrive in the rocky structure and points, peaking in spring and early fall. Largemouth are present but secondary to smallies given the cold, clear water. Walleye patrol the deeper basin and transition areas, especially at low light. Chain pickerel lurk in shallower weedy pockets near the shoreline. Catfish and panfish round out the catch, active in warmer months.

Follow the thermocline closely — trout suspend just above it in summer, often 30 to 50 feet down, and jigging tube baits, small spoons, or live nightcrawlers on drop-shot rigs at those depths produces. Smallmouth stack on rocky points and submerged structure; finesse plastics and drop-shot work when the water is gin-clear. Walleye respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits or live bait along deeper edges at dusk and dawn. In spring and fall when surface temps are in the 50s, trout move shallow and can be taken trolling or casting near the banks. Match your depth to the season — this reservoir rewards anglers who work the water column methodically rather than fishing one depth all day.

Spruce Run holds a surprisingly diverse fishery for a central Jersey impoundment. Largemouth dominate the shallow coves and weedy flats, while smallmouth relate more to the rocky points and harder structure along the main basin. Early spring triggers aggressive feeding from both bass species as water climbs through the low 50s, and that same cold water produces some of the reservoir's best trout action near the surface before summer stratification pushes them deep. Walleye and chain pickerel are present but overlooked — pickerel haunt the cove edges year-round, while walleye activity peaks at dawn and dusk during cooler shoulder seasons. Catfish and panfish round things out, with bluegill and crappie concentrating around any submerged wood and dock structure.

Work the flats with soft plastics like creature baits or Senkos rigged weedless when largemouth are buried in vegetation, and switch to finesse drop-shots or tube jigs on the rocky points for smallmouth. Trout respond well to small spinners and live nightcrawlers worked slowly in spring before the thermocline sets up. For pickerel, toss weedless spoons or flashy spinners tight to cove edges with sparse vegetation. Walleye are best approached with a slow-trolled or drifted live shiner or a paddle-tail swimbait after dark. Pay attention to water clarity — Spruce Run can fluctuate after rain events, and stained water often pushes largemouth shallower and makes reaction baits more productive than finesse presentations.

Manasquan Reservoir is a multi-species fishery built around a flooded landscape that holds fish year-round if you know what each season demands. Largemouth bass dominate the shallower timber edges and flats through spring and fall, while smallmouth favor harder structure and cleaner bottom near the points. Stocked trout fish best in cooler months before surface temps climb past the mid-60s, after which they push deep or disappear from practical range. Chain pickerel lurk tight to the timber and weed fringes in cold water and again in fall. Walleye are present and underrated, best targeted low-light and after dark. Catfish and panfish fill in the warm months across the deeper flats.

In spring, work the timber edges with slow-rolled swimbaits or Texas-rigged plastics as bass stage before the spawn, and focus the points where slightly warmer water concentrates fish first. The submerged wood holds pickerel and largemouth all year — keep your presentations tight to the structure rather than beside it. For walleye, dragging a jig-and-minnow combination along the deeper point transitions at dawn and dusk consistently outperforms midday efforts. When surface temps break 70 degrees, shift catfish and panfish setups toward the flats using nightcrawlers or cut bait on a slip-sinker rig. In fall, dropping water clarity and cooling temps push both bass species back shallow, making spinnerbaits and jerkbaits particularly effective along timber runs and wind-blown points.

Plum Gut is one of those places that rewards anglers who understand moving water. Striped bass are the backbone of the fishery, showing up in spring and staying through fall, with the biggest fish often arriving early in the season when the water is still cold. Bluefish and weakfish push through during warmer months, and summer brings quality fluke on the sandy edges flanking the channel. Black sea bass and tautog hold on the rocky structure throughout the season, with tog especially productive in fall when they fatten up before winter. Kingfish work the softer bottom near the gut's margins during summer.

Fish the tide changes hard here — stripers and bluefish stack in the rips when current is running strong, not slack. Position uptide and work eels, bucktails, or large swimming plugs through the boil. For fluke, drag a squid-strip-tipped bucktail across the sandy flats as current slows. Tautog and sea bass want fiddler crabs or green crabs bounced tight to submerged rock. When wind opposes the tide, the chop concentrates baitfish and gets everything feeding. Water temperature breaking above 55 degrees triggers the striper bite; once it climbs past 70, focus shifts to fluke and blues.

Cuttyhunk sits at the western end of the Elizabeth Islands chain, where Vineyard Sound, Buzzards Bay, and the open Atlantic converge.
