That mix of currents and structure draws a serious lineup of species. Striped bass show up in spring and stay through fall, with the best fishing often coming during the migrations. Bluefish run hard through summer, and tautog hold on the rocky ledges from spring into late fall. Fluke and black sea bass stack up over the sandy holes and mixed-bottom areas in summer. Weakfish and kingfish are less predictable but worth targeting in warmer months when water temps climb into the mid-60s and above.

Fish the rips hard on moving water, especially the last two hours of the outgoing tide when bait gets pushed through the cuts. Stripers and blues ambush from the downtide edges of the rips, so work swimmers, poppers, or live eels along those seams. For tautog, drop green crabs tight to the boulders and fish them slow. Fluke and black sea bass respond well to bucktails tipped with squid or soft plastics drifted over structure. Kingfish and weakfish favor softer bottom nearby. Avoid fishing the rips in heavy wind-against-tide chop — it kills the bite and makes boat positioning dangerous.

Watch Hill Reef and the surrounding passage draw a dependable rotation of species through the warmer months. Striped bass show first in spring as water temperatures climb into the mid-50s, feeding aggressively on the bait pushed through the rips. Bluefish follow close behind and can be relentless through midsummer. Fluke stack up in the sandy pockets around the reef structure once water warms into the low 60s, while black sea bass hold tight to the harder bottom. Tautog are best targeted during the shoulder seasons when they're actively feeding on crabs in the rocks. Weakfish and kingfish appear less predictably but show during warmer, calmer stretches, often at dawn near softer bottom edges.

The rips here are the key — fish position themselves at the edges where current deflects off the reef, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing tide when baitfish concentrate and get pushed into feeding lanes. For stripers and blues, work metal spoons, large bucktails, and surface plugs through the rip edges rather than straight through. Fluke respond well to drifting gulp-style baits or bucktails tipped with strip bait across the sandy transition zones. Tautog require slow-fished green crabs tight to structure. Wind against tide creates a chop that often switches the bite on for surface-feeding fish. Pay attention to water clarity — after a blow, dirty water pushes fish deeper and slows the bite considerably.

Charlestown Breachway draws striped bass from late spring through fall, with schoolie bass arriving first as water temps climb past 50°F, followed by larger fish through summer and into the October run. Fluke stack up in the deeper channel holes once water warms into the mid-60s, and bluefish crash the breachway mouth unpredictably all summer. The ponds — Ninigret especially — hold tautog around the rocky structure year-round, with spring and fall producing the best tog action. Weakfish and kingfish make quieter appearances in the warmer months, often overlooked but worth targeting in the calmer back-pond shallows.

For the breachway, work the outgoing tide hard — stripers and fluke both funnel through the channel as water drains from the pond. Bucktails tipped with a Gulp or squid strip cover both species efficiently. On the surf side, cut mullet and chunk bunker on the bottom catches stripers patrolling the wash, while metal lip swimmers and poppers work the slough on a northeast wind swell when bait gets pushed tight to the beach. Bluefish will hit nearly anything flashy, but wire leaders protect your knots. For tautog, go with green crab or fiddlers tight to the rocks; cold water slows their bite, so fish slow and deliberate.

Galilee sees a reliable parade of species through the warmer months. Tautog are the early-season stars, holding on the rocky structure around the harbor walls before water temps push past the mid-50s. As spring gives way to summer, fluke move into the channel and the sandy edges of the harbor mouth, and striped bass begin working the rips off the wall, especially at dawn and dusk. Bluefish show up unpredictably but can stack up thick when bait schools push through. Black sea bass tend to hold on deeper structure nearby. Weakfish and kingfish appear in warmer water, often in the quieter inside areas of the harbor around sandy bottom.

For fluke, drift the channel with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or strips of squid, keeping contact with the bottom. Bass along the wall respond well to swimming plugs, soft plastics on a light jig head, or live eels worked through the current seam during a moving tide. Tautog want green crabs fished tight to structure — patience matters. The outgoing tide is generally your best window here, as it pulls bait and smaller fish through the channel and concentrates predators along current edges. Avoid fishing slack water. Onshore wind muddies the harbor quickly, and when water temps drop sharply in fall, bass and blues stage heavily before pushing offshore.

Cape Ann offers a diverse season that kicks off in spring when striped bass push through on their northward migration, working the rocky points at Halibut and Straitsmouth Island. As water temps climb through summer, bluefish arrive and can be relentless at the outer ledges, while fluke settle into sandy pockets between the ledges and harbors. Black sea bass stack on any hard structure in 30 to 60 feet. Tautog are present spring and fall, hugging the same boulder fields. Weakfish and kingfish make occasional appearances in warmer inshore water, though both run thin here and should be considered a bonus catch.

Fish the first two hours of an incoming tide along rocky shorelines and harbor mouths — stripers and blues ambush baitfish pushed by the current. For tog, drop green crabs tight to submerged boulders. Fluke respond to bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or spearing, drifted slowly along structure edges. Cooler water below 65 degrees shuts down fluke but brings the best striper action. Onshore wind pushes bait against the rocks and concentrates fish; northwesterly winds typically produce cleaner water on the south-facing shores. Watch for diving terns — they mark bluefish and bass feeding below.

The Merrimack River mouth is a productive stretch that fishes differently through the year. Striped bass arrive with the spring bait run, often chasing herring and smelt through the jetty current, and hold here well into fall. Bluefish show up in summer, sometimes crashing bait schools on the surface flats. Fluke bury into the sandy bottom of those same flats once water temperatures climb into the mid-60s. Tautog work the jetty rocks in spring and again in fall. Weakfish and kingfish are less predictable but show up during warmer stretches, often mixed into the same sandy-bottom zones as fluke.

Work the jetty edges during moving tides, especially the last two hours of the outgoing when baitfish funnel through the channel. Stripers stack behind current breaks along the rocks — soft plastics on jigheads, bucktails, and live eels at night are reliable producers. For fluke on the flats, drift bucktail and Gulp combinations along the sandy drop-offs. Bluefish respond to fast-retrieved metal lures or poppers when they're pushing bait to the surface. Onshore winds can muddy the shallower flats and push fish deeper toward the channel edges, so read water clarity and adjust depth accordingly.

The Saco River mouth is a classic southern Maine striper fishery, with schoolie striped bass pushing into the estuary as early as late April and keepers showing up through summer into October. Bluefish arrive in earnest by midsummer, often crashing bait in the rip where the river meets the ocean. Fluke work the sandy bottom just outside the jetties and along the beach trough, while tautog favor the rocky jetty structure through spring and fall. Weakfish and kingfish make occasional appearances in the surf, particularly on summer evenings, and black sea bass can show up on the outer jetty rocks in warmer months.

Fish the outgoing tide hard — the river current flushing bait and warm water into the ocean consistently holds stripers along the south jetty rocks and in the channel edges. During incoming tides, fluke push into the calmer water behind the jetties; work bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or strip bait slowly along the bottom. For stripers in the surf, swimming plugs and soft plastics work well when bait is visibly moving; go topwater at dawn during flat conditions in summer. Wind out of the southwest pushes warmer water and bait up against the beach, concentrating fish in the nearshore trough. Water temperatures above 55°F reliably activate the bite.

The Damariscotta River is primarily a striper fishery, with schoolies pushing into the river on spring tides as early as late May, followed by larger fish through summer and into October. Bluefish move through the harbor and outer ledges in midsummer, often crashing bait near the surface. Fluke show up on sandy pockets near the river mouth once water temperatures climb into the low 60s, and black sea bass stack on the deeper offshore ledges through summer. Tautog haunt rocky structure year-round but bite best in spring and fall. Weakfish and kingfish are less predictable here, appearing in warmer years when baitfish concentrations are strong in the estuary.

Work the river channel edges on the moving tide, especially the last two hours of incoming when stripers push bait against the banks and bridge structure. Soft plastic swimbaits, white bucktails, and live menhaden or mackerel are reliable striper producers. On the ledges, jig with diamond jigs or Norwegian-style lures for bluefish and sea bass, and fish fresh crab on a dropper loop for tautog around the rocks. Fluke respond well to bucktail and squid strip combinations drifted slowly over mixed bottom near the river mouth. An east wind tends to muddy the harbor and push fish deeper, while calm westerly days with a running tide are prime. Water temperature is your calendar here.

Assateague's surf, channels, and bay give you a genuine mix of inshore species across the seasons. Striped bass push through in fall and again in spring, with bigger fish working the suds and channel edges after dark. Summer belongs to fluke along the channel drop-offs inside the bay and in the sloughs behind the island, while bluefish show up in waves from late spring through early fall, often cutting bait schools right in the surf. Black sea bass and tautog hold on the nearshore structure and jetty rocks, with tog fishing best when water cools in fall and early spring. Weakfish have thinned over the years but still appear in the back bay channels at dusk. Kingfish are a consistent surf target all summer and are often overlooked.

Wade the troughs that form between sandbars after storms for stripers and kingfish, using fresh clam, bloodworm, or cut mullet on a fish-finder rig. For fluke, drift the channel edges with bucktail jigs tipped with Gulp or a strip of squid when the tide is moving — slack water kills the bite. Bluefish respond well to metal lures thrown into breaking schools or chunk bait on the bottom at night. Read the wind carefully here: a strong onshore wind muddies the surf fast, but that same dirty water along a color line can hold stripers and blues right where the clear and dirty water meet. Water temps in the mid-50s trigger the best striper action; once it climbs past 70, shift your focus to fluke and bluefish.

Tangier Sound fishes differently than open Bay water — it's shallower, tidal-driven, and the mix of species shifts hard with the seasons. Spring pushes striped bass through the guts and channel edges as water temps climb out of the low 50s, and weakfish show up around the same time, working the grass flat margins after dark. Summer belongs to fluke on the sandy bottom transitions and bluefish tearing up baitfish on the flats, while black sea bass hold on any hard structure you can find. Tautog appear on oyster bottom and shell hash in cooler water, both spring and fall. Kingfish run the sandy shallows mid-summer into fall.

Read the tides carefully here — a moving tide, especially the last two hours of the outgoing, concentrates bait in the guts and draws stripers and weakfish to the current seams. Fish deeper channel edges on slack. For fluke, work the tide-swept flat edges with bucktails tipped with Gulp or strips of squid, bouncing bottom slowly. Stripers respond well to soft plastics and paddle tails worked through current breaks. Kingfish are almost always caught on bottom rigs with bloodworms or fresh shrimp tight to the sand. Wind pushing water onto the flats warms the shallows fast and activates feeding — pay attention to water clarity, as off-color water from wind chop can scatter fish significantly.

The Choptank draws a solid mix of species as the seasons turn. Striped bass show up in numbers during spring and fall migrations, with fish staging in deeper bends and around pilings as water temperatures swing through the 50s. Summer brings fluke onto the sandy flats and channel edges, along with bluefish slashing through baitfish schools in the more open reaches. Weakfish and kingfish move into shallower grassy areas during warmer months, often overlooked but very catchable. Tautog hunker around woody structure and pilings year-round but bite best in cool water. Black sea bass are occasional visitors near hard bottom closer to the river mouth.

Work the pilings on the moving tide, not the slack. Stripers respond well to bucktails, soft plastics, and live spot drifted along current breaks. Fluke want a slow bottom bounce with a gulp or live minnow on the up-current side of the flats. When water temps climb above 72 degrees, push toward dawn and dusk and fish deeper edges where cooler water holds. Kingfish and weakfish favor light tackle with small jigs or bottom rigs tipped with bloodworms in modest current near softer bottom. Wind pushing against the outgoing tide creates the kind of choppy, oxygenated water that stacks bluefish and draws stripers shallow. Read the bait — where the bunker nervous up, everything else follows.

Lynnhaven Inlet fishes differently with every season. Striped bass move through in fall and again in spring, using the inlet channel as a transit corridor between the Bay and ocean. Bluefish show up in warmer months, often blitzing baitfish near the bridges and on the shallow flats. Fluke spread across the sandy bottom through summer, with some quality fish holding in the deeper cuts. Weakfish and kingfish work the same flats, especially in late spring and early fall. Tautog settle around bridge pilings and hard structure when water temperatures cool, and black sea bass show up on rockier bottom closer to the inlet mouth.

Fish the moving tide, not slack water. Stripers and weakfish favor the outgoing tide as it sweeps bait through the inlet channel, so position upcurrent of the bridge pilings and let shad bodies or bucktails swing into the shadow line. For fluke, drift the sandy flats with a gulp-style bait or a bucktail tipped with a strip, keeping contact with the bottom. Kingfish respond well to fresh cut bloodworm drifted just off the bottom in moderate current. Bluefish and bass push bait against bridge structure on windy incoming tides. When water temperature drops below 55 degrees, slow down for tautog around pilings with fiddler crabs.

The York River fishes differently than open Bay water — the tidal current here is aggressive, and species move in and out with the seasons rather than staging offshore. Striped bass push into the river in fall and hold through winter, especially near the Coleman Bridge pilings and deeper channel bends. Spring brings weakfish into the shallower tributary mouths before water temperatures climb. Summer is prime time for fluke across the grass flats near the river's edges, bluefish slashing through baitfish schools mid-river, and black sea bass hanging tight to any hard structure. Tautog work the pilings year-round, and kingfish show up on sandy bottom during warmer months.

Work the pilings on a moving tide — tautog want fiddler crabs or green crab fished right against the structure, while stripers respond to bucktails and soft plastics drifted through the current seam. For fluke, drag gulp-style baits or spearing-tipped jigs along the flat edges where bottom transitions from grass to sand. Weakfish prefer lower-light periods and quieter current phases, so dawn tides on calmer days are worth targeting. Watch water temperature — fluke action drops off noticeably once surface temps push into the low 80s. An outgoing tide that pulls bait off the flats into deeper cuts concentrates almost everything that feeds here.

The New River runs cold and rocky through the Virginia highlands, and that unique character shapes everything about your fishing. Smallmouth bass are the heart of this river — aggressive, plentiful, and present year-round, peaking in activity from late spring through early fall when water temps climb into the mid-60s to low 70s. Largemouth hold in slower backwater pockets along the banks rather than the main current. Walleye move actively after dark, especially in spring during spawning runs near the larger ledge systems. Trout favor the colder, faster riffles year-round. Chain pickerel lurk in slack water near woody debris, flathead and channel catfish work the deep ledge pools after dark, and sunfish and rock bass fill nearly every crack in the cobble.

Wade the riffles and work the transition seams where fast water dumps into slower runs — smallmouth and walleye stack in those slack pockets behind ledges waiting to ambush baitfish. Tube jigs, crayfish-imitating soft plastics, and inline spinners in natural colors are consistent producers for smallmouth. For walleye, drift live shiners or nightcrawlers across ledges at low light. Watch the gauge: when flows run high and off-color, fish tight to current breaks and slower inside bends. When flows drop and clear in summer, finesse presentations — drop shots, small grubs — outperform anything bulky. Once water temps fall below 55 degrees, slow everything down; fish are still catchable but far less aggressive, especially bass.

Pamlico Sound is primarily a warm-season fishery, though it produces year-round if you know where to look. Striped bass push into the upper sound and marsh creeks during cooler months, feeding aggressively before retreating as temperatures climb. Late spring through summer belongs to fluke and bluefish, with fluke staging on sandy bottom near channel edges and blues tearing through open water in feeding frenzies. Weakfish show in the grassy shallows and creek mouths, particularly at dusk during warmer months. Kingfish work the sandy flats in summer. Tautog and black sea bass become targets around the sound's scattered structure — oyster reefs, bridge pilings, and rock piles — especially in fall when water cools.

Fish the incoming tide on the flats, particularly where marsh drains funnel baitfish into open water — that's where weakfish and stripers ambush prey. For fluke, drift sandy bottom near drop-offs using bucktail jigs tipped with squid or Gulp, keeping contact with the bottom. Bluefish respond well to fast-retrieved spoons and poppers over open water. In summer, midday heat pushes fish deep or into shaded marsh edges, so fish early morning or evening. Southeast winds push warmer, saltier water into the sound and activate feeding; northwest winds can dirty up the shallows fast. Water clarity is your best real-time indicator — stained water means work the current seams, clear water means go light and slow.

Albemarle Sound fishes like a different world from the coast — it's a vast, shallow, brackish system where striped bass are the year-round anchor species, running strong in fall and again in spring as they stage near river mouths on the Roanoke, Chowan, and Cashie. Bluefish push through in waves during spring and fall, sometimes thick enough to break bait on open-water flats. Weakfish show up in warmer months, especially around grass edges and soft bottom at the mouths of tributary creeks. Fluke work the sandy transition zones where river current meets sound bottom in summer. Kingfish are an underrated find on shell-sand flats in warmer months, while tautog and black sea bass favor any hard structure you can locate.

Wind and tide move this water hard — a sustained southwest wind can stack fish on the north bank shallows or blow the flat completely dry, so always fish with wind direction in mind. Stripers in the river mouths respond well to slow-rolled swimbaits and bucktails worked along current seams, especially when water temps drop into the low 50s. Fluke want a slow drag across transition bottom using gulp or live finger mullet on a Carolina rig. For weakfish and kingfish, light bottom rigs with shrimp or cut mullet on shell bottom near channel edges are tough to beat. Clear, moving water consistently outfishes stained slack water here.

The Roanoke River system offers a diverse fishery that shifts dramatically with the seasons. Largemouth bass dominate the slack backwater flats and flooded timber, while smallmouth favor the rocky runs and faster current seams. Spring is the headline season — walleye push up from Albemarle Sound into the river corridor to spawn, drawing serious attention, and chain pickerel haunt the shallow grass edges throughout the cooler months. Catfish — both channel and flathead — hold in the deeper holes year-round and become especially active in summer. Panfish and the occasional stocked trout round out the cooler-water months in the upper reaches.

Flow is everything on the Roanoke. Rising water pushes largemouth tight into flooded willows and cypress — work shallow-running crankbaits and soft plastics along wood edges. Dropping flows concentrate fish in deeper current breaks and channel bends, where a slower presentation with jigs or live bream pays off for big cats and walleye alike. For walleye, fish the swift gravel runs at dusk during the spawn push with shallow jerkbaits or hair jigs swung across current. When water temps dip below 50°F, slow down dramatically — drop-shotted finesse plastics in slack eddies behind structure will consistently outfish aggressive presentations. Read the stain: off-color water calls for darker, rattling lures; clear flows favor natural colors and lighter line.

Bogue Inlet fishes differently through the seasons than most Carolina inlets because of how the sound behind it connects to the ICW and the broad shallow flats of Bogue Sound. Striped bass push through in late fall and early spring, staging in the deeper inlet cuts before moving toward the sound. Fluke are the bread-and-butter summer target, especially along the sandbars flanking the channel. Bluefish show up in late spring and again in fall, sometimes blitzing the surf hard enough to scatter bait into the wash. Black sea bass and tautog hold on the nearshore structure and jetty rock through the cooler months. Weakfish are present but inconsistent, usually picking up after dark in the sound. Kingfish own the surf from late spring through summer.

Work the outgoing tide hard in the inlet — that current sweeping bait out of the sound is when the fish really turn on. Fluke stack on the down-current edge of the channel bars, so drag a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or a strip of belly meat along the bottom and let the tide do the work. The surf kingfish bite best when you get a light southeast breeze pushing clean water in; fresh sand fleas or small pieces of shrimp fished right in the trough just inside the break are your best bet. For stripers and weakfish at night in the sound, slow-roll soft plastics along the edge of the grass flats where the bottom drops off. Cold water below about 55 degrees moves the flounder and weakfish off, so pay attention to the thermometer before rigging up.

Cape Fear River draws serious anglers because the species mix shifts dramatically with season. Spring pushes striped bass up into the tidal stretches as water temperatures climb through the 50s, and weakfish show in the lower river around the same time. Summer belongs to fluke holding on sandy flats near channel edges, with bluefish tearing through baitfish schools in open water. Black sea bass and tautog claim the rockier structure year-round but fish most aggressively in cooler water. Kingfish move into shallower flats in warmer months, especially where sandy bottom gives way to shell. Fall brings bluefish back hard and often sees stripers staging again as temperatures drop.

Fish the rock walls on an incoming tide when current pushes bait tight against structure — tautog and black sea bass sit right in the rubble, so bounce a green crab or fiddler crab directly on bottom. Fluke want a moving bait drifted across flat sandy bottom; a bucktail tipped with a Gulp or strip bait matched to current speed is reliable. Work topwaters and spoons for bluefish when you see birds diving. Stripers respond to live shad or herring worked near the bottom in tidal current seams. When water temperatures drop below 55 degrees, slow everything down significantly — fish tighten to structure and feed less aggressively but are still very catchable.

Winyah Bay fishes like a different world depending on the season. Spring pushes striped bass through the bay and up the Pee Dee and Waccamaw river mouths as fish stage between wintering grounds and cooler upriver haunts. Bluefish arrive close behind and tear through baitfish schools near the jetties well into fall. Summer belongs to fluke drifting the sandy channel edges and black sea bass stacking on the jetty rocks. Weakfish show unpredictably but reward patient anglers working deeper holes after dark. Tautog claim the rockier jetty structure through cooler months, while kingfish run the surf and shallower bay bottom from late spring into early fall.

Work the outgoing tide hard, especially where the Sampit or Pee Dee river flow meets saltwater, because that current edge concentrates baitfish and predators stack underneath. Fluke respond well to gulp-style soft plastics bounced slowly along sandy drop-offs, and tautog demand fiddler crabs or green crabs wedged tight to the jetty base. For stripers, suspending plugs and live spot or mullet fished in moving water near channel bends are reliable. When water temperature climbs above eighty degrees, fish move deep or nocturnal, so target dawn tides. Persistent southwest wind pushes murky river water across the bay and kills bite quality, while a shift to north or northeast clears things quickly and turns fish active.

Port Royal Sound fishes differently than most South Carolina waters because of its sheer depth and tidal volume. Striped bass show up in cooler months, stacking along channel edges and near structure where baitfish concentrate. Bluefish move through in late fall and early spring, often aggressive on the surface. Fluke arrive with warming water and hold through summer on sandy transition zones between flats and deeper cuts. Weakfish and kingfish work the surf edges and creek mouths, particularly in spring and fall. Black sea bass and tautog hold on hard bottom and shell rock when water temperature drops.

Fish the incoming tide on the flats for reds and flounder, drifting DOA shrimp imitations or live finger mullet across sandy bottom near grass edges. On the outgoing, drop into the deeper channel mouths where stripers and bluefish ambush bait being flushed out. Wind-driven muddy water pushes fish tighter to clean creek banks. In summer, target flounder early morning before heat pushes water temps above the mid-80s. For tautog and sea bass, anchor over shell rock with fiddler crabs or sand fleas and fish dead on bottom. Read the rips where current breaks to find fish stacking at any season.

The Altamaha drains a massive Georgia watershed, which means fish follow baitfish and water temperature more than the calendar. Striped bass stack in the lower river during cooler months, pushing well upriver when water temps drop into the 50s. As spring warms the marshes, weakfish and flounder slide into the creeks and grass edges ahead of summer. Bluefish show up in the sounds with the first serious baitfish pushes, and black sea bass hold on nearshore structure where the river meets saltwater. Tautog are a cooler-water fish here — oyster reefs and bridge rubble hold them in fall and winter. Kingfish work the sandy shoals near the sound's mouth through warmer months.

Wade or pole the marsh drains on a falling tide — fish push bait against those banks hard. For flounder and weakfish, slow-dragged Gulp shrimp or live finger mullet along channel edges in two to six feet is hard to beat. Stripers upriver want big swimbaits or cut shad worked near structure on the bottom. Bluefish respond to fast, aggressive retrieves with spoons or topwaters during a strong incoming tide. Read the water color — the tannin-stained river water mixing with cleaner sound water creates a visible line, and predators stack right on that edge. Wind against tide creates chop that concentrates baitfish, and that's when bluefish and weakfish get aggressive.

Ten Thousand Islands holds snook, redfish, tarpon, spotted seatrout, and mangrove snapper as its bread-and-butter species, with the mix shifting hard through the seasons. Winter pushes trout and redfish deep into backcountry creeks and onto dark-bottom flats where they can absorb heat. Spring wakes up the passes with rolling tarpon and snook pushing onto the flats to spawn through summer. Fall is prime time across the board, with cooler water firing up aggressive feeding before the cycle resets. The species you listed — striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish — are not resident species in this water and will not be encountered here.

Work the mangrove edges on an incoming tide, when baitfish stack along the roots and snook slide tight to the shade. Weedless soft plastics and live pinfish or pilchards pitched within inches of the prop roots produce best. On the flats, a falling tide drains baitfish out of the grass and concentrates redfish at flat edges and drain cuts — watch for tailing fish in water under two feet. Water temps below 60 degrees lock fish into deep creek bends; when temps climb above 85, work early-morning low-light windows. Wind above 15 knots muddies the flats fast, so prioritize leeward shorelines when conditions get sloppy.

Flamingo sits at the southern tip of Everglades National Park, where the freshwater glades meet Florida Bay, and the fish here are not your typical inshore suspects. Redfish, snook, and tarpon dominate the fishing calendar. Snook stack in the mangrove creeks through warmer months and push onto shallow flats at dawn and dusk. Redfish are present year-round, schooling on the backcountry flats in fall and winter when water cools and bait concentrates. Tarpon roll through the bays during spring and summer migrations. Seatrout fill the grass flats in cooler months. Species like striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are simply not part of this ecosystem and do not belong in a Flamingo fishing report.

Honest advice matters more than a polished report built on wrong information. Flamingo is remote, shallow, and tidal-driven, and success depends on reading falling tides that funnel bait out of creeks into waiting ambush predators, watching water clarity, and approaching skinny water quietly with a push pole. DOA shrimp, weedless soft plastics, and live finger mullet are proven producers. But stocking this report with northeastern species would send you chasing fish that do not exist here, and that helps nobody. Fish the water in front of you, not the species list on a template.

Florida Bay is not striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish country — those are Mid-Atlantic and Northeast species with no natural presence here. Presenting them as Florida Bay targets would be genuinely misleading, and misleading information is the opposite of useful for someone planning a real trip.

What Florida Bay actually holds, and holds well, are redfish, spotted seatrout, snook, tarpon, bonefish, permit, and sharks. The shallow marl flats, basin edges, and tidal channels create some of the best sight-fishing opportunities in North America, and the seasonal movements of those species through this system are worth a serious report.

I am glad to write you an accurate, detailed fishing report covering real Florida Bay species, their seasonal patterns, flat and channel tactics, tide and wind reading, and appropriate presentations. Just say the word and I will put it together for you.

Anna Maria Island sits at the mouth of Tampa Bay where Longboat Pass and Bean Point funnel tidal current across grass flats and sand bottom — and the fish here are Gulf and Bay species, not Northeast Atlantic fish. Snook, redfish, trout, tarpon, flounder, Spanish mackerel, and cobia are what these waters actually produce. Snook stage in the passes through winter, move onto the flats and into the surf as water warms past 70 degrees, then spawn near the passes in summer. Redfish school on the shallow grass flats year-round, while trout favor deeper grass edges in cooler months. Tarpon roll through the passes and along the beach in late spring through summer. Spanish mackerel and cobia follow the warming water inshore each spring.

Fish the passes on a moving tide, either direction, positioning near structure like the rocks and jetty edges where snook and flounder ambush baitfish in the current seam. Live pilchards are the universal bait here — free-lined or under a popping cork for trout and redfish on the flats. DOA shrimp, paddle tails, and gold spoons cover the grass flats effectively. Wind from the east keeps the flats calm and clear, making sight-fishing for reds possible on low tide. A northwest wind muddies the water fast and pushes fish off the shallow grass, so work the deeper edges and pass channels instead. Water temperature below 60 degrees slows snook and trout into a near-dormant state near warm discharge areas and deeper holes.

Estero Bay is a subtropical estuary on Florida's Gulf Coast, and the honest truth is that striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish simply don't live here. This bay runs warm and shallow, and its residents are snook, redfish, spotted seatrout, tarpon, sheepshead, and mangrove snapper. Trying to shoehorn Northeast species into this water would send you home empty-handed and frustrated.

What actually works here: snook and redfish hold tight to mangrove roots and oyster bars, especially on falling tides that funnel baitfish out of the shallows. Work DOA shrimp or live pilchards along shadow lines in low light. Tarpon roll the passes from late spring through summer — free-lined crabs or live pinfish fished on the bottom of the outgoing tide are your best shot. When water temps drop below 60 in winter, focus on deeper channels where trout and sheepshead stack up on structure.

Fort Pierce Inlet runs hard, and the species mix shifts with the seasons. Winter and early spring bring weakfish working the deeper holes of the inlet channel, along with black sea bass stacked around the jetty rocks. Bluefish show through much of the year but peak in fall and spring as water temps swing through the 60s and 70s. Summer flounder move in when water warms, lying in ambush along sandy transitions between the jetty base and open bottom. Tautog are a cold-water species here, best targeted during winter cool-downs. Kingfish work the nearshore surf. Striped bass, while at the far southern edge of their range, do occasionally appear during hard cold fronts pushing south.

The rock pile on either jetty is the single most consistent holding structure. Fish the last two hours of outgoing tide, when water funnels through the inlet and pinbait gets swept into feeding position. Drop a bucktail or a chunk of fresh-cut mullet tight to the rocks on the bottom for flounder and sea bass. Bluefish and weakfish respond well to drifted live finger mullet or a swimming plug worked in the current seam where the inlet meets the nearshore shelf. In the surf, pompano rigs with sand fleas will catch kingfish, but focus your casts near sandbars and cuts where wave energy concentrates bait. Dirty water kills the bite here, so let post-storm turbidity clear before making the trip.

Lake Kissimmee is primarily a largemouth bass fishery, and that is where you will focus most of your energy here. Largemouth move shallow into the emergent vegetation and reed lines during the spring spawn, then pull back to deeper hydrilla edges and canal mouths as summer heat builds. Panfish, particularly bluegill and shellcracker, hold year-round in the reeds and along grass edges, and chain pickerel will ambush from the same cover. Catfish work the canal bottoms and deeper basin areas. Smallmouth bass, trout, and walleye are not native to this water and are not realistic targets here.

Work topwater frogs and punch rigs through the matted hyacinth and kissimmee grass during low-light hours when fish are actively feeding shallow. When surface temps push into the upper eighties and beyond, slow down and flip heavy jigs or Texas-rigged creature baits tight to reed clumps and canal edges where fish seek shade and slightly cooler water. Canal mouths concentrate baitfish and draw largemouth during any wind or current movement, especially in cooler months. For panfish, live crickets and small jigs fished under a float along reed edges produce consistently.

Mobile Bay and the surrounding delta system hold a diverse mix of species that shift dramatically with the seasons. Speckled trout and redfish get most of the local attention, but anglers willing to target different species will find striped bass staging near the causeway bridges and delta mouth in late fall through early spring when water temps drop into the mid-50s. Bluefish move through during spring and fall migrations, often erupting on surface bait in the main bay. Flounder — locally called fluke by transplants from up north — are present spring through fall and stack up around structured areas before moving offshore as temperatures fall below 65 degrees. Weakfish and kingfish appear inshore during warmer months, while black sea bass and tautog tend to hold on the deeper rock and shell bottom toward the bay mouth and nearshore structure.

Tides are everything in this system. An outgoing tide pulling dark, tannin-stained delta water into the bay concentrates baitfish along current seams, and that is exactly where stripers and bluefish will be feeding. Fish the downcurrent edges of the causeway pilings on the outgoing, using swimbaits, bucktails, or live pogies. Flounder hold tight to shell bottom and riprap — work a quarter-ounce jig head with a white or chartreuse paddle tail slowly along the bottom. When westerly winds push water out and clarity drops, predators often move shallow into grass edges. In summer, fish early before surface temps climb past 85 degrees, when fish go deep or sulk until evening.

Barataria Bay is redfish and speckled trout country at its core, so those seven northeastern species you mentioned simply don't belong here — and giving you false intel would burn your trip. What this bay genuinely produces is outstanding. Redfish roam the grassy shorelines and back lakes year-round, running in pods through the cuts in fall. Speckled trout stack on deeper grass edges when summer heat peaks, then push shallow in the cooler months of late fall and winter. Flounder — southern flounder here, not fluke — stage in the passes and around shell during the fall migration southward, making October and November prime time to target them along bottom structure.

Work the outgoing tide hard in Barataria. Falling water drains the marsh, funneling baitfish through cuts and along points where redfish and trout ambush them. In summer, early morning with a light southeast wind keeps the surface calm enough to work topwater lures across shallow flats before the sun climbs. When water temperature drops into the upper 50s, slow your presentation way down — a paddle tail on a jighead dragged along shell is deadly for flounder and late-season trout. Dirty water after a north wind calls for louder, darker lures and natural baits like shrimp or mullet strips worked near structure.

Trinity Bay sits at the upper end of Galveston Bay, and the main gamefish here are speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum — not the Northeast coastal species you listed. I want to be straight with you rather than hand you a report stuffed with fish that simply don't live in this Texas estuary. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, tautog, weakfish, and black sea bass are not realistic targets in Trinity Bay, and building a trip plan around them would waste your time on the water.

What I can tell you is that Trinity Bay fishes best for specks and reds in fall when baitfish push into the shallows, flounder stack in the passes during their fall migration, and summer heat pushes fish to deeper shell reefs. If you want a honest, useful report built around what actually swims here, just ask and I'll give you the real picture.

Aransas Bay is redfish and speckled trout country at its core, but the species mix shifts considerably through the year. Spring pushes trout onto shallow grass flats as water warms into the mid-60s, while fall brings some of the best slot-red action of the year around the ICW spoil islands and back-lake drains. Flounder stack in the passes and along drop-offs during fall migration, making them a reliable secondary target. The listed northeast species like striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, and kingfish are not resident Aransas Bay fish and targeting them here would be a wasted trip.

For the flats, wade quietly during incoming tides with light southeast wind, throwing gold spoons or soft plastics on quarter-ounce jigheads along current seams at grass edges. Reefs and shell pads hold trout when water temps dip below 60, and that's when slow-rolled paddle tails outfish topwaters. Dirty water after north winds pushes fish tight to structure and into back-lake pockets. Clear, slower-moving incoming tides with stable pressure give you the best shot at multiple species in a single wade.

Port Mansfield targets speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum as the bread-and-butter species in the Laguna Madre and surrounding flats. Spring and fall are peak seasons when trout and reds push onto shallow grass flats in gin-clear hypersaline water. Summer heat pushes fish into deeper channels and potholes during midday, while flounder stack near channel edges before their fall migration. Winter concentrates big trout in deeper cuts and drains when cold fronts roll through. The species you listed — striped bass, fluke, bluefish, weakfish, tautog, black sea bass, and kingfish — are genuinely not part of this fishery and would mislead any angler planning a trip here.

For practical success, fish the skinny flats on an incoming tide with light southeast winds that keep water clear and temperatures stable. Sight-cast to tailing reds using DOA shrimp, gold spoons, or soft plastics on light jigheads. Trout hold over submerged grass and potholes — work topwaters early, then switch to suspending plugs or shrimp under popping corks. Flounder ambush prey near channel drop-offs; drag a live finger mullet or a paddle-tail slowly along the bottom. When water temperature climbs above 90 degrees, shift to fishing dawn and dusk near deeper drains where cooler, oxygenated water concentrates baitfish and predators alike.

Kewaunee Harbor and the adjacent Lake Michigan waters draw a diverse crowd of species through the year. Spring brings brown trout and steelhead staging near the harbor mouth before pushing into the Kewaunee River, while summer transitions to coho and chinook salmon running offshore. The harbor itself holds smallmouth bass along its rock riprap and pier pilings from late spring through fall, and walleye move through the harbor channel during low-light periods especially in spring and autumn. Panfish like yellow perch and crappie congregate around structure year-round, catfish work the deeper harbor mud in summer, and chain pickerel and largemouth bass favor the weedy shallows upriver where the Kewaunee River slows and widens.

For smallmouth, work the pier pilings and riprap edges with drop-shot rigs, tube jigs, or crawfish-colored crankbaits, especially when lake temperatures reach the mid-50s and above. Walleye respond well to jigging with twister-tail grubs or live minnows drifted near the harbor channel edges at dawn and dusk, particularly when river flow is moderate and water clarity improves after rain runoff settles. Perch and crappie stack near submerged dock structure and the pier base — small jigging spoons and wax worms on a drop rig produce consistently. When lake temps push into the upper 50s, trout and salmon move closer to shore, making spoons and stick-baits cast from the pier a legitimate option before they scatter to cooler deeper water.

Frankfort Harbor and Betsie Lake offer a surprisingly diverse fishery for a small Lake Michigan port. In spring, steelhead and brown trout push through the harbor channel on their way upriver, drawing serious attention from shore anglers on the pier. As water warms through early summer, smallmouth bass become the main attraction along the rocky pier pilings and harbor edges, while largemouth move into the shallower, weedy backwaters of Betsie Lake. Walleye show up reliably in low-light periods through summer and into fall. Panfish — perch, bluegill, and crappie — stay active nearly year-round in the calmer protected water. Chain pickerel lurk in the lily pad margins of the lake, and catfish work the deeper harbor mud after dark.

Watch the temperature break where cold Lake Michigan water meets the warmer harbor — that transition edge holds baitfish and attracts predators, especially walleye and trout. Drift spawn sacs or small spinners along the harbor channel in spring for trout. For smallmouth, work tube jigs and drop shots tight to the pier base and riprap. Walleye respond well to slow-trolled stick baits or jigging with paddle-tail plastics near bottom during low-light hours. Pickerel want weedline presentations — spinnerbaits and shallow-running stick baits along the Betsie Lake vegetation edges. When flow picks up through the harbor after rain, catfish and big perch stack near current seams — cut bait on bottom gets them.

St. Joseph sits where the St. Joe River meets Lake Michigan, and that confluence drives everything here. Spring brings steelhead and brown trout pushing up from the lake into the river current, followed by walleye staging near the piers during cooler water. As temperatures climb into summer, smallmouth bass become the main attraction along the rocky harbor walls and pier pilings, while largemouth move into quieter backwater pockets upriver. Channel catfish feed actively through the warmer months in deeper river bends. Panfish — bluegill and crappie — hold in calmer harbor edges year-round. Chain pickerel show up in slower, weedy stretches upriver and are often an overlooked surprise.

Watch water temperature closely: smallmouth on the pier pilings bite best when lake temps settle in the mid-50s to mid-60s, so fish tube jigs and drop-shot rigs tight to the structure. For walleye and trout, drift spawn sacs or jigging spoons near the river mouth when current is pushing steadily outward — fish stack where moving river water meets the lake's calmer surface. In summer, the harbor's shadow lines and current seams near the pier heads concentrate baitfish, making swimbait and crankbait retrieves along depth transitions productive. Catfish respond well to cut bait fished on the bottom in deeper river holes, especially on warmer nights with a slight current bump.

Michigan City sits where Trail Creek meets the southern tip of Lake Michigan, and that creek-to-harbor-to-open-lake progression drives everything. Spring brings coho and steelhead staging near the pier ends and harbor mouth, with walleye moving through Trail Creek as water temperatures push into the low 50s. Summer shifts focus toward smallmouth bass along the rocky pier base and harbor riprap, plus catfish and panfish holding in slower harbor water. Chain pickerel stay tucked in weedy shallows near creek inflows. Come fall, trout and salmon return in force, drawing the biggest crowds to the pier.

For pier and harbor smallmouth, crawfish-colored tubes and drop-shot rigs dragged along the riprap bottom consistently produce. Walleye respond to jig-and-minnow presentations drifted through the creek mouth, especially during low-light periods when current from Trail Creek pushes baitfish against the harbor walls. Watch water temperature closely — steelhead and coho fishing really fires when surface temps cool below 55°F in fall. Catfish stack up near the creek channel bottom; cut sucker or chicken liver on a Carolina rig fished after dark is a proven producer. Panfish congregate wherever dock pilings create current breaks in the harbor interior.

Conneaut Creek and the harbor fish best in spring and fall when steelhead and brown trout push in from Lake Erie on their spawning runs — that's when you'll find the most action along the lower creek stretches. Walleye move through the harbor and nearshore lake structure in spring and again in fall, following the same temperature-driven migrations. Largemouth hold in the harbor's quieter backwaters and dock edges through summer, while smallmouth favor the rocky lake shoreline and creek mouth. Chain pickerel show up in slower, weedier sections of the lower creek year-round. Channel catfish work the deeper harbor holes at night, and panfish like crappie and bluegill fill in the gaps through warmer months.

Watch water temperature closely — steelhead and browns become most active when creek temps drop into the upper 30s to mid-40s, and fish tend to stack in deeper pools below riffles during low, clear flows. Drift spawn sacks, beads, or small streamers through those seams for trout. For walleye, work the harbor channel edges and lake points at dawn and dusk with jig-and-minnow rigs or shallow-running stick baits. Smallmouth respond well to tube jigs and crawfish imitations bounced along rocky lake structure. When creek flow runs high and stained, switch to brighter attractor patterns and add weight to get down to where fish are holding near bottom out of the current.

Henderson Harbor sits on the eastern end of Lake Ontario's Black River Bay, and the mix of warm, protected shallows and cold, deep lake access makes it unusually productive year-round. Smallmouth bass dominate the rocky shoals and gravel points from late spring through fall, while largemouth hold in the weedy backwater bays and around dock structures. Walleye run strong through the bay in spring and again in fall as they chase baitfish. Chain pickerel haunt the shallow weedy coves all season, catfish work the murkier bay bottom at night, and panfish — yellow perch especially — school up over deeper flats in summer and late fall. Lake trout and brown trout become realistic targets when you push out into deeper Ontario water.

When water temps in the bay climb above 55 degrees, smallmouth move onto the shoals and gravel humps and respond well to tube jigs, drop-shots, and crawfish-colored crankbaits worked slowly along bottom. Walleye in the bay favor live crawlers on bottom rigs or slow-trolled stick baits near the deeper channel edges, particularly low-light morning hours. Pickerel and largemouth ambush prey along weedline edges — topwater lures at dawn or spinnerbaits just beneath the surface draw explosive strikes. For perch, find the right depth break, go with small jigs or live minnows, and work methodically until you locate the school.

Sodus Bay offers a diverse fishery that shifts noticeably as the seasons turn. Largemouth bass dominate the weedy shallows and dock lines through summer, while smallmouth move between the rocky points along the bay mouth and out onto the Lake Ontario shoreline. Walleye run through the bay during spring and again in fall, often staging near the deeper channel before pushing onto the flats. Chain pickerel lurk year-round in the thicker vegetation along the marshy northern edges. Trout, primarily brown and lake trout, are more of a lake game, best intercepted near the bay mouth in cooler months. Channel catfish and panfish, especially yellow perch and crappie, fill out the warmer-water seasons in the bay's softer-bottomed areas.

When water temps climb into the mid-60s, work topwater frogs and weedless rigs through the matted vegetation for largemouth. Smallmouth respond well to drop-shot rigs and tube baits dragged along the rock transition zones where the bay meets open lake. For walleye, troll crawler harnesses or shallow-diving stickbaits along the channel edges at dawn and dusk, especially when water temps are dropping in autumn. Pickerel will nail spinnerbaits and flashy spoons retrieved through the weeds. Target perch and crappie over soft bottom near docks and weed edges with small jigs or minnows under a slip float. Read current flow at the bay outlet — active movement concentrates predators, particularly walleye and smallmouth, right at the transition.

The Au Sable is primarily known as blue-ribbon trout water, and brown and brook trout define the upper and middle reaches through spring and summer. As you move downstream toward Oscoda and the Lake Huron mouth, the fishery shifts dramatically — walleye stack up in river-mouth current seams, especially during spring and fall runs, while smallmouth bass dominate the rocky riffles and mid-river runs through summer. Largemouth show up in slower, woody edge water. Chain pickerel haunt the weedy backwaters, catfish work deeper bends after dark, and bluegill and perch fill in the panfish action near the mouth through warm months.

For trout in the riffles, swing soft-hackle wet flies or drift small nymphs and minnow-pattern streamers through the bubble lines where current breaks behind rocks — water temps in the low-to-mid 50s trigger the best feeding. Smallmouth in summer runs respond well to crawfish-pattern tubes and hair jigs bounced along gravel transitions. For walleye near the mouth, target the downstream edge of current seams with jig-and-minnow rigs or bottom-bouncing crawler harnesses, especially when river flow drops and clears in early fall. Read the color change where river current meets lake water — fish stack hard along that transition.

The Pere Marquette is best known as a world-class steelhead and salmon river, but it holds much more. Brown and rainbow trout are year-round residents, most active in cooler water. Smallmouth bass dominate the warmer stretches and gravel runs through summer, while largemouth haunt slower backwater edges and woody structure near the lower river. Walleye move through in spring and again in fall, following baitfish. Chain pickerel ambush from bankside vegetation in the slower pools, channel catfish work the deeper holes at night, and bluegill and rock bass fill the gaps wherever insects hatch or crayfish are crawling.

In summer, wade the gravel and fish smallmouth with crayfish imitations, soft plastics, or small spinners through the fast chutes and tail-outs. Trout key on hatches in the riffles and hold in the seams where current breaks against deeper water. As water temps drop into the low 50s, steelhead push in from Lake Michigan and stack in the deeper runs and pools. Work egg patterns, nymphs, and small spoons near bottom with a natural drift. Walleye and catfish respond well to live or cut bait drifted slowly through the deepest holes, especially after dark in fall when flows pick up and water clarity drops slightly.

Great Sacandaga is a big, flood-control reservoir with constantly fluctuating water levels, and that fluctuation shapes everything. Largemouth dominate the shallower bays and weedy flats from late spring through summer, while smallmouth stack on the rocky points and harder structure throughout the warmer months. Walleye are present but underrated here — they push into shallower water during low-light periods, especially in spring and fall. Chain pickerel lurk in the same weedy bays as largemouth, often closer to the vegetation edges. Trout, mostly stocked rainbows and browns, favor the cooler, deeper reaches and are most accessible in spring and late fall. Catfish and panfish fill in the bays and softer-bottomed coves.

Read the water level closely — when the lake drops, fish that were using flooded vegetation get pushed to whatever remaining structure exists near the old river channel cuts and harder points. For largemouth and pickerel, work weedlines with weedless soft plastics or spinnerbaits along the edge rather than into the weeds. Smallmouth on the rocky points respond well to drop-shots and tube jigs bounced slow. Walleye come alive at dusk with a slow-rolled grub or crawler harness along those channel breaks. When surface temps climb past 75 degrees, go deeper or go early. Panfish and cats cluster near softer bottom in the bays — a simple hook and nightcrawler fished slow is hard to beat.

Raystown is a deep, clear, canyon-style impoundment where structure and depth change everything. Smallmouth own the rocky bluff faces and submerged points year-round, while largemouth favor the shallower flats and brushy coves, especially in spring and early fall. Walleye push onto the main-lake points and transitions at dusk and dawn, more so in the cooler shoulder seasons. Stocked trout hold in the deeper, cooler sections through winter and into early spring before the water warms. Chain pickerel lurk in weedy flat edges, catfish work the deeper channel bends after dark, and crappie, bluegill, and perch suspend near timber and dock structure.

For smallmouth along the bluffs, work tube jigs and drop-shots tight to the wall from mid-depth down, especially when surface temps push past 65 and fish slide deeper. On the points, a slow-rolled swimbait or blade bait tipped with a trailer produces walleye during low-light transitions. Largemouth on the flats respond well to topwater early morning in summer and soft plastic crawfish ripped along bottom edges in fall. Trout anglers do best trolling spoons or jigging blade baits over the deeper basin structure when water temps dip below 55. Watch your electronics for the thermocline in summer — most active fish stack just above it.

Wallenpaupack is a sprawling glacial lake with plenty of structure to keep you busy. Largemouth dominate the shallow weedy coves and dock lines, while smallmouth favor the rocky points and harder substrate. Chain pickerel shadow the same weed edges as largemouth and will surprise you year-round. Walleye run active in spring and evening hours through summer, suspending over deeper structure. Stocked trout fish best in spring near tributaries and cooler coves before surface temps climb. Catfish and panfish — yellow perch, crappie, and bluegill — provide consistent action around docks and deeper cove transitions.

Work topwater frogs and weedless rigs tight to dock pilings and cove edges for largemouth early and late in the day. When surface temps push past the mid-60s, drop a tube or finesse worm along rocky points for smallmouth and walleye transitions. Slow-roll a paddle tail swimbait at dusk along deeper cove mouths to intercept walleye. Pickerel respond well to fast-moving spinnerbaits burned through vegetation. Watch for dock shade holding bass and perch during midday heat. As water cools into fall, points concentrate baitfish and predators stack up — that is prime time to work a crankbait parallel to structure.

The Susquehanna holds a serious mix of species, and knowing the season separates a good day from a blank one. Smallmouth bass are the backbone here — they dominate the rocky ledges and current breaks and fish hard from late spring through fall. Largemouth move into slower backwater flats and shallow weedy pockets, especially in summer. Walleye run stronger in spring and again in fall when water temps cool into the low 50s. Trout hold near tributary mouths and cooler spring-fed stretches. Channel and flathead catfish own the deep holes after dark, and chain pickerel lurk in slack, weedy flats year-round alongside panfish like redbreast sunfish, which are abundant in this river.

For smallmouth on the ledges, work downstream edges with tube jigs, crayfish-pattern crankbaits, or drop-shot rigs in 4 to 10 feet of broken rocky structure — they stack where current deflects around big rock. When flows run high and off-color, switch to darker bulkier presentations and target slower seams near shore. Walleye favor deeper channel edges and gravel transitions at low light; slow-rolled swimbaits and live shiners work well. In summer heat, fish early morning and late evening when surface temps climb above 80 degrees — bass push deeper or into shadow. Catfish respond well to cut bait fished hard on bottom in slack holes after dark. Read the river's flow gauges consistently; rising water moves fish to edges, falling water concentrates them on structure.

The Juniata runs through limestone country, and that shapes everything. Smallmouth bass are the backbone of the fishery — aggressive in summer riffles and runs, sluggish when water temps drop below 50°F. Trout hold in cooler spring tributaries and deeper runs, especially in the upper reaches where limestone springs moderate temperatures. Walleye slide into ledge areas and deeper tailouts after dark and during low-light periods, particularly in spring and fall. Channel catfish own the deeper holes through summer. Chain pickerel ambush from slower backwater edges and slack water off main current. Panfish — rock bass and sunfish — pack the riffles and rocky margins year-round.

Fish the Juniata by reading flow. When the river runs clear and low in midsummer, smallmouth stack in the shade of ledges and current seams — finesse ned rigs, small tube jigs, and soft plastic crawfish work hard. In higher spring flows, crankbaits and swimbaits covering water fast will find active fish. For walleye, bottom-bounce jigs tipped with minnows or soft plastics along ledge drops after dusk. Catfish respond to cut bait or chicken liver fished on bottom in deep, slower runs. Water temperature is your compass — smallmouth feed aggressively between 60 and 75°F; push above or below that window and slow down your presentation accordingly.

The Allegheny offers a genuinely diverse fishery that shifts with the seasons. Smallmouth bass are the backbone of summer fishing, especially in mid-river runs and rocky structure, while largemouth favor the slower backwater flats near woody debris. Walleye run strong in spring and again in fall, often staging in deeper tailwater below dams. Trout, mostly stocked browns and rainbows, concentrate in cooler tributary mouths and shaded stretches during spring and early summer before warmth pushes them out. Chain pickerel haunt weedy flats year-round. Channel catfish own the deep holes after dark, and panfish like rock bass and crappie fill the gaps whenever other species go quiet.

Read the flow carefully — after rain events, smallmouth and walleye push tight to current seams where eddies collect baitfish, while catfish move into murkier slack water. When river temperature climbs above 70 degrees, target dawn and dusk and focus on shaded mid-river boulders. For smallmouth, tube jigs and crawfish-colored crankbaits worked through rocky runs are hard to beat. Drift live nightcrawlers or minnows through deeper eddies for walleye and trout in cooler months. Pickerel respond well to flashy spinnerbaits near emergent vegetation on the flats. In summer, drop a cut shad to the bottom of any deep slow bend after sunset and the catfish will find you.

The Delaware River through Pennsylvania offers serious diversity year-round. Smallmouth bass are the bread-and-butter species, thriving in the rocky riffles and ledge systems from late spring through fall. Largemouth push into slower eddy pockets near woody cover, while walleye favor deeper ledge breaks, especially at night and during low-light periods in spring and fall. Chain pickerel ambush from slack-water margins and weed edges in warmer months. Catfish, particularly channel cats, work the deeper holes and current seams after dark. Wild brown and rainbow trout inhabit the colder upper reaches and tailwater sections, with activity peaking in spring and again when fall temperatures drop back below 60 degrees. Panfish like rock bass and bluegill fill the gaps throughout.

Read the river's character carefully. When flows run high and fast, fish tuck behind current-breaking boulders and into the downstream tail of eddies where they can feed without fighting heavy water. As levels drop and clear, move toward the riffles and pick apart the downstream edges where oxygenated water meets calmer holding water. For smallmouth on ledges, crayfish-imitating crankbaits and tube jigs worked slowly along the bottom are consistently productive. Walleye respond well to twister-tail jigs and live minnows drifted through ledge breaks. For catfish, cut bait or nightcrawlers anchored in deeper holes work best on summer nights. Water temperature around 65 to 72 degrees signals peak smallmouth feeding; anything above 80 pushes fish deep and lethargic, so fish early.

The Lehigh River fishes differently than most Pennsylvania rivers because it shifts character so dramatically by season and by section. Spring brings quality brown and rainbow trout action through the colder upper reaches and catch-and-release stretches, with fish stacked in the deeper runs and slower tailouts. As water warms through late spring and summer, smallmouth bass become the dominant target throughout the gorge section, joined by walleye pushing through deeper pools and current seams after dark. Chain pickerel lurk in any slower backwater with woody structure, while channel catfish and bullheads work the soft-bottomed deeper holes overnight. Panfish like rock bass and sunfish fill in the gaps wherever you find moderate current over gravel.

For trout in colder flows, dead-drift nymphs like hare's ears and pheasant tails through the seams where fast water meets slow, or swing soft hackles at the tailouts. When flows drop and clear in summer, smallmouth push tight to large boulders and the broken pocket water in the gorge — crayfish imitations, small tubes, and inline spinners worked upstream and across are reliable. Walleye hold in the deepest pools during daylight and move into the riffles at dusk; twister tails on jigheads dragged slowly along bottom are effective. Watch your water temperature closely — smallmouth go sluggish above 80 degrees, and trout activity shuts down fast in warm summers. Fish early and target shaded runs.

Lake Almanor holds a surprisingly diverse fishery for a high-elevation Sierra reservoir. Rainbow and brown trout are the marquee species, thriving in the cold, clear water year-round, but the warm shallows also support solid largemouth and smallmouth bass, a decent walleye population, and panfish throughout the coves. Chain pickerel show up less predictably but are present, while channel catfish work the deeper soft-bottom flats after dark in warmer months. Spring and early summer are prime time across the board as snowmelt pushes baitfish shallow and predators follow. By midsummer, trout and walleye drop to the thermocline while bass push into weeds and structure.

The springs along the north end pump cold, oxygenated water that consistently holds trout even in late summer when the main basin stratifies — troll a small flasher-and-worm rig or a minnow-style plug near the cold inflows and you'll find fish stacked tight. Points extending into deeper water are classic transition zones for walleye and smallmouth at dawn and dusk; jigs with soft-plastic swimbaits bounced slowly along the drop are reliable. The shallow flats warm fastest in spring, drawing largemouth to sparse weed edges where a weightless Senko or small swimbait outfishes most other presentations. Watch your surface temperature — once it climbs past the low 70s, fish the deeper side of every structure.

Trinity Lake holds a surprisingly diverse fishery given its elevation and cold, clear water. Trout — both rainbow and brown — are the backbone through winter and into spring, especially when snowmelt keeps the arms cold and oxygenated. As surface temps climb into summer, largemouth settle into the timbered coves and brushy flats off the main arms, while smallmouth favor the rockier points and gravel transitions. Catfish and panfish fill out the warm-water bite in the shallower back ends of coves. Walleye and chain pickerel are present but opportunistic — they're not the primary draw, though you'll find them working low-light transitions near structure.

Work the arms by targeting submerged timber edges with Texas-rigged plastics or swimbaits for bass; trout respond well to inline spinners and small spoons fished along the cooler, deeper points. Watch your surface temperature — once the main lake stratifies in summer, bass push shallower at dawn and dusk while trout go deep and suspend. In spring and fall, that transitional water column is the sweet spot: slow-roll a swimbait through the 10-to-20-foot zone off rocky points and you'll contact both bass and roving trout. Current flow from the Trinity River arm after rain events concentrates fish near the inflow, especially catfish and smallmouth.

Henrys Fork is brown and rainbow trout water at its core, and those fish are the primary draw across all three areas you'll fish. The railroad ranch flats hold educated risers working PMD and callibaetis hatches through summer, while the riffles downstream warm slightly and see better midge and caddis activity in shoulder seasons. Spring and fall push fish into feeding lanes aggressively before runoff or the first hard frosts. Walleye and catfish show up in slower, deeper pockets off the main channel, and panfish concentrate near vegetation edges in warmer stretches. Bass, chain pickerel, and the occasional warmwater mix tend to favor spring-creek confluences where temperatures stabilize.

On the flats, long fine tippet and drag-free drifts are non-negotiable for trout. Watch water temps carefully — trout activity peaks between roughly 50 and 65 degrees, and when flows run high and cold post-runoff, concentrate on seams and softer inside bends where fish can hold without burning energy. In spring creeks, fish feed tight to undercut banks and weed edges; nymphing with scuds and sowbugs consistently outperforms dries. For walleye and catfish in slower pools, switch to bottom presentations with natural bait. Panfish and pickerel respond well to small spinners worked through vegetation at slower retrieves, especially during the warmest midday window in early fall.

The Deschutes is primarily known as a redband trout and summer steelhead river, and that shapes the entire season. Spring brings aggressive trout feeding in the riffles as flows drop from snowmelt and water temps climb toward the mid-50s. Smallmouth bass — not largemouth, which are uncommon here — become the canyon's other star from late spring through summer, going on a sustained bite that can rival any river in the Pacific Northwest. Catfish and panfish hold in slower, warmer side pockets. Walleye and chain pickerel are effectively absent from this system, so don't plan your trip around them.

For trout, focus on the seam where fast riffle water transitions into deeper runs — fish hold at that break to intercept drifting food. Dry-dropper rigs work well when surface temps are comfortable; when flows run cold and off-color, go subsurface with nymphs or small streamers swung on a tight line. Smallmouth stack behind mid-channel boulders in canyon stretches, especially once water temperatures consistently hit the low 60s. Crayfish imitations and 3-inch soft plastics rigged wacky or on a light drop-shot cover both rocky runs and slower tailouts effectively. Watch flows closely — high, turbid water pushes fish tight to softer inside edges, while dropping, clearing conditions pull them back into prime current seams.

The Rogue is a river that keeps you busy year-round. Spring brings Chinook salmon pushing upriver, and native coastal cutthroat and steelhead hold in the deeper runs during cooler months. Smallmouth bass are the surprise star here — they thrive in the warmer middle and lower river stretches through summer and early fall. Largemouth are less common but show up in slower, weedy backwater pockets near the mouth. Catfish and panfish — bluegill, crappie — congregate near structure and softer current seams, while walleye and chain pickerel remain rare incidental catches rather than reliable targets in this system.

For smallmouth, focus on rocky runs and tailouts where current breaks create ambush points. Crawdad-imitating soft plastics, small spinnerbaits, and hopper dropper rigs covering the seam between fast and slow water are proven producers. Watch your water temperature closely — smallmouth feed aggressively when temps sit between 60 and 72 degrees, and you'll find cutthroat stacked in shaded, deeper holes once summer heats the shallows. Near the tidal mouth, fish stage on incoming tides, so time your arrival accordingly and drift bait naturally through current seams rather than fighting the flow.

The Umpqua system offers a surprisingly diverse fishery that shifts dramatically with the seasons. Tidewater and the lower river hold good-sized smallmouth bass through summer, with largemouth tucked into slower backwater sloughs. Native cutthroat and sea-run cutthroat move through the estuary in late summer and fall, drawing serious attention from local fly anglers. Channel catfish work the deeper tidal holes year-round, while panfish — crappie, bluegill — concentrate in woody structure when water warms. Walleye show up in the main-stem pools, particularly where current softens, and chain pickerel lurk in slower, vegetated tidal pockets.

Reading water temperature is everything here — smallmouth become aggressive in the 60s, sluggish below 50°F, so time your effort accordingly. In higher spring flows, fish tight to current seams and deeper channel edges where fish hold out of heavy water; use four-inch soft plastics, drop-shots, and jigs worked slow. Sea-run cutthroat respond well to small spoons and bait-swung through tidal runs on an incoming tide. For catfish, anchored presentation with cut bait near deeper tidal bends after dark consistently produces. When flows drop and clear in summer, finesse techniques and lighter line outperform heavy gear.

The Willamette fishes like two different rivers depending on the season. Spring draws trout into the main channel as flows drop from snowmelt highs, while largemouth move shallow into the backwater sloughs and warm flats to spawn. Smallmouth prefer the rockier main-river structure and gravel bars, peaking through late spring and summer. Walleye tend to concentrate near deeper channel edges and current seams, especially in lower, slower stretches. Catfish work the deeper holes and soft-bottomed sloughs year-round, feeding heavily on summer nights. Chain pickerel and panfish — crappie, bluegill, and perch — thrive in the weedy backwater sloughs, most active when vegetation greens up in late spring.

Watch the gauge closely: rising or stained water pushes fish tighter to slack-water edges, flooded brush, and slough mouths. When flows stabilize and water temperature climbs into the low 60s, bass fishing turns on hard — work weedless soft plastics and swimbaits along slough margins and submerged timber for largemouth, and target current-facing boulders and gravel shelves with drop-shots or smallmouth crankbaits. Walleye respond well to jig-and-minnow presentations drifted along channel transitions at dusk. For catfish, cut bait or chicken liver fished on bottom in deeper slough holes after dark is hard to beat. Match your timing to water clarity and temperature swings — the fish will tell you where they are.

Puget Sound is cold, productive saltwater dominated by chinook and coho salmon, lingcod, halibut, rockfish, and Dungeness crab — not the mid-Atlantic species you listed. Striped bass, fluke, bluefish, weakfish, and kingfish simply do not occur here in fishable numbers, and tautog and black sea bass are Atlantic species entirely absent from Pacific waters. Writing a report pretending otherwise would waste your time on the water and cost you real fishing opportunity.

If you are planning a Puget Sound trip, I am glad to give you an honest, detailed report covering salmon timing on the rips and beach lines, halibut structure and tide windows, how lingcod stack up on hard bottom, and the bait and hardware that actually produces in this water. Just let me know and I will give you something genuinely useful.

Lake Washington holds a solid mix of species, but the fishery really revolves around largemouth and smallmouth bass as the primary draw. Largemouth favor the shallow weedy flats along the eastern shoreline, especially in spring when water warms into the mid-50s and fish move up to spawn. Smallmouth tend to push onto the rocky points and gravel transitions. Trout are present in cooler months, often targeted by trollers near the surface in winter and early spring before temperatures climb. Walleye exist here but are genuinely rare — treat them as a bonus. Panfish, particularly crappie and perch, school tight to structure year-round, and catfish prowl the softer muddy bottom in warmer months.

On the flats, weightless Senkos and shallow crankbaits in natural shad or crawfish colors account for most largemouth, especially when surface temps hit 58 to 65 degrees. Smallmouth on the points respond well to drop-shot rigs with finesse plastics worked slowly along gravel-to-sand transitions. The deeper drop-offs, particularly where the bottom falls quickly from 10 to 30 feet, concentrate fish during summer heat and late fall as bass suspend or go deep. A quality fish finder matters here — watch for baitfish marks near those ledges. Chain pickerel lurk in the weedier shallows and will ambush spinnerbaits and swimbaits meant for largemouth, so expect the surprise.

Bristol Bay is a wild sockeye and king salmon system — it holds no striped bass, fluke, bluefish, black sea bass, tautog, weakfish, or kingfish. Those are Atlantic coast species that do not occur in Alaskan waters. Writing a report that weaves them into a Bristol Bay context would be factually wrong and genuinely harmful to an angler trusting this advice.

If you want a useful Bristol Bay fishing report covering the species that actually live there — sockeye, Chinook, coho, chum, pink salmon, Dolly Varden, rainbow trout, Arctic grayling, and northern pike — I am glad to write that for you. Alternatively, if you want a report for the Atlantic coast species you listed, tell me which specific water you have in mind, such as the Chesapeake Bay, New Jersey coast, or Long Island Sound, and I will give you something genuinely useful.
